3.q: What is change control in PRINCE2 7?
o: The means by which an organization moves from its current state to a target state
The approach for planning communication with stakeholders affected by the change
The process of handing products into operational use and supporting their adoption
The procedure ensuring changes to the baseline are identified, assessed and decided
3.w: Change control is the procedure that ensures changes to the project baseline are identified, assessed and then approved, rejected or deferred (see manual 10.1, 10.2.3).

n.0: Moving the organization from its current state to a target state is change management, part of the people element (manual 3.2.1).
n.1: Planning communication with stakeholders is covered by the communication management approach (manual 3.4).
n.2: Handing products into use and supporting adoption relates to closing the project and the senior user's adoption responsibilities, not change control (manual 6.2.4, ch 19).

3.q:
Which two statements about the quality register are correct?

1. It records each quality activity and its result, typically pass or fail.
2. It lists every product in a plan together with its current status.
3. It is created during starting up a project, before the project brief.
4. It is updated when quality activities in a work package are completed.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
1 and 4
3 and 4
3.w: Statement 1 is correct because the register records the activity and its result, and statement 4 is correct because in managing product delivery the completed quality activities are notified and the quality register is updated (see manual 8.3.1.2, tab 17.3).

n.0: Statement 2 describes the product register, not the quality register (manual 8.5).
n.1: Statement 2 describes the product register, and statement 3 is wrong because the registers are set up in initiating a project (manual 8.5, ch 15).
n.3: Statement 4 is correct but statement 3 is wrong: the quality register is set up in initiating a project, not starting up (manual ch 15).

3.q:
Which two statements about the four organizational levels are correct?

1. The business layer is part of the project management team.
2. The project manager's primary responsibility is managing relationships within the project so that it produces the required products.
3. The project board works within the project tolerances defined by the business layer.
4. Team managers work within constraints set directly by the project board.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
3 and 4
2 and 3
3.w: The project manager's primary responsibility is managing relationships within the project so it delivers products in line with strategic objectives and agreed requirements (statement 2), and the board works within project-level tolerances set by the business layer (statement 3) (see manual 6.2, fig 6.2).

n.0: Statement 1 is false: the business layer sits outside the project management team (manual fig 6.2).
n.1: Statements 1 and 4 are both false: the business layer is outside the team, and team managers work within constraints set by the project manager (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is false: the delivering level works within constraints set by the project manager (manual fig 6.2).

3.q: A chief operating officer is described as the 'sponsor' of a new project being run with PRINCE2. How does PRINCE2 treat this sponsor?
o: PRINCE2 adds a sponsor role to the project board, next to the executive and senior user
The sponsor becomes the project manager, because the sponsor owns the outcome of the project
The sponsor takes the senior supplier role, because the sponsor funds the suppliers' work
PRINCE2 has no sponsor role; a sponsor typically becomes, or sits above, the executive
3.w: PRINCE2 has no role called sponsor; a sponsor or senior responsible owner typically becomes the executive or sits above the executive in the business layer (see manual 6.2.4, appendix B).

n.0: The board has three roles only: executive, senior user and senior supplier; PRINCE2 does not add a sponsor role (manual 6.2.1).
n.1: The project manager manages day to day on the board's behalf; a senior sponsor maps to the executive, and the two roles cannot be combined (manual 6.2.4.1).
n.2: The senior supplier represents those delivering the products; securing funding is an executive responsibility (manual 6.2.4.1).

3.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
In the 'managing product delivery' process, the team manager reports progress to the project manager at the agreed frequency by means of [?] reports.
o: highlight
checkpoint
exception
end project
3.w: The team manager keeps the project manager informed by checkpoint reports, produced in managing product delivery at the frequency agreed in the work package (see manual 17.4.2, 17.4.3).

n.0: Highlight reports are produced by the project manager for the project board in controlling a stage (manual 16.4.8).
n.2: Exception reports are raised by the project manager to the board when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded (manual 16.4.7).
n.3: The end project report is prepared by the project manager in closing a project, in evaluate the project (manual 19.4.4).

3.q:
Which two statements about delivery approaches in PRINCE2 7 are true?
1. PRINCE2 7 can govern projects using any of the three delivery approaches.
2. PRINCE2 7 requires an iterative-incremental approach for software projects.
3. An iterative-incremental project may have several delivery stages.
4. A linear-sequential project refines its acceptance criteria in parallel with development.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
3.w: PRINCE2 7 does not favour one delivery approach and can govern any of them, and an iterative-incremental project may use multiple delivery stages (see manual 1.5.3 and 7.2.3.1).

n.0: Statement 1 is true, but statement 2 is false: PRINCE2 7 does not require a particular delivery approach for any type of project.
n.2: Both are false: no approach is required for software projects, and refining acceptance criteria alongside development is a feature of iterative-incremental work.
n.3: Statement 3 is true, but statement 4 is false: linear-sequential projects define products in detail up front rather than refining criteria during development.

3.q:
Which two statements about the measures used to assess risks are correct?
1. Proximity describes when a risk might occur.
2. Velocity describes the estimated chance that a risk will occur.
3. Impact is estimated in the units used for the affected objective, such as days or pounds.
4. Exposure is a negative concept, as it applies to threats.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
3.w: Statement 1 is the definition of proximity, and statement 3 reflects how impact is estimated in the same units as the objective (see manual 9.2, 9.3.1.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the estimated chance of occurrence is probability; velocity is how quickly the impact would be felt (manual 9.2).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: exposure is neutral and can be positive or negative (manual 9.2).
n.3: Statement 2 is wrong: velocity is how quickly a risk would affect objectives once it occurs, not its probability (manual 9.2).

3.q:
Which two statements about handling issues formally or informally are correct?
1. Some matters raised as issues turn out to be risks and should be handled as risks.
2. Sensitive issues are placed in the issue register so that all stakeholders can see them.
3. Off-specifications are handled formally through the change control procedure.
4. An informal issue needs an issue report before it can be noted in the daily log.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
3.w: Statement 1 is correct: part of issue resolution is checking whether a matter is really a risk. Statement 3 is correct: off-specifications must be addressed through change control, so they are handled formally (see manual 10.2.2, 10.2.3).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: sensitive issues go in the daily log, where open access is not given (manual 10.1, 11.5).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: sensitive issues belong in the daily log, and informal issues are noted there without an issue report (manual 10.5, 11.5).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: issue reports are for issues needing formal review; informal issues are simply noted in the daily log (manual 10.5).

3.q: What are the steps of the PRINCE2 business case management technique, in the correct order?
o: Develop, check, maintain, confirm
Develop, maintain, check, confirm
Identify, assess, plan, implement
Capture, assess, decide, confirm
3.w: The business case management technique has four steps: develop, check, maintain and confirm (see manual 5.3.1).

n.1: The steps are right but the order is not: the business case is checked (for example to authorize initiation) before it is maintained in the delivery stages (manual 5.3.1).
n.2: These are steps of the risk management technique, which also includes communicate (manual ch 9).
n.3: Capture, assess and decide come from the issues technique; the business case technique is develop, check, maintain, confirm (manual ch 10, 5.3.1).

3.q: A project board hears about problems only when the project is already badly late and over budget. Which part of PRINCE2 is designed to address this challenge?
o: Defining the specialist techniques the team must use to build the products
Fixing the stage budget as one figure that the project manager may not vary
Setting tolerances so that forecast breaches are escalated to the board early
Having team members report directly to the board instead of to the manager
3.w: Under manage by exception, tolerances are set for each level and any forecast breach is escalated to the next level as early as possible, so the board is alerted before the problem becomes severe (see manual 2.5).

n.0: PRINCE2 does not prescribe specialist build techniques, and these would not give the board earlier warning of delays or overspend.
n.1: PRINCE2 allows a range of variation through tolerances rather than a fixed figure; it is the forecast breach of that range that triggers escalation.
n.3: Team managers report to the project manager, who reports to the board; bypassing the project manager undermines the defined roles and does not create early warning.

3.q: Which combination of roles is NOT permitted in a PRINCE2 project?
o: Executive and project manager held by one person
Project manager and team manager held by one person
Senior user role shared between two department heads
Project manager and project support held by one person
3.w: The executive role cannot be combined with the project manager role (see manual 6.2.4.1, 6.2.4.5).

n.1: Depending on scale, complexity, skill and capacity, the project manager may also perform the team manager role (manual 6.2.4.5).
n.2: More than one person may represent the users, depending on the scale and complexity of the user community (manual 6.2.4.2).
n.3: The project manager may also perform the project support role (manual 6.2.4.5).

3.q:
Which two statements about the influences on tailoring are correct?
1. The level of risk is one of the factors that tailoring takes into account.
2. Tailoring factors are set by the business layer in the project mandate.
3. A project that is part of a programme does not need to consider tailoring.
4. A supplier's own iterative-incremental framework can be a reason to tailor.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
3.w: Statement 1 is correct: level of risk is one of the seven named factors. Statement 4 is correct: a supplier wanting to use its own iterative-incremental or agile framework is an influence that may lead to tailoring, for example adding a coach role (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the factors are features of the project considered when tailoring is agreed in initiating a project, not items set in the mandate (manual 2.7, 15.4.1).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: tailoring is agreed in initiation, and a programme context is itself an influence that may cause tailoring (manual 2.7, 15.4.1).
n.2: Statement 3 is wrong: being part of a programme is one of the influences that may cause tailoring (manual 1.5, 2.7).

3.q: Which level of management sets the project-level tolerances, including the project's benefits tolerance, within which the project board must direct the project?
o: Project board
Business layer
Project manager
Project assurance
3.w: The business layer sets project tolerances across the seven performance targets, including benefits; the board then sets stage tolerances and the project manager sets work package tolerances (see manual 11.2.1, tab 5.1).

n.0: The project board sets stage tolerances within the project tolerances it is given by the business layer (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: The project manager sets work package tolerances for team managers, not project tolerances (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: Project assurance monitors and advises on behalf of the board; it does not set tolerances (manual 6.2.4, 11.2.1).

3.q: When is the authorize a stage or exception plan activity used?
o: At each stage end except the final stage, and to approve exception plans
At the end of every stage including the final one, before closure is authorized
At the end of starting up a project, to approve the initiation stage plan
At regular intervals during each stage, after each highlight report is received
3.w: A stage starts only when the board authorizes it. The board uses authorize a stage or exception plan at the end of each stage except the last to approve the next stage plan, and whenever it needs to approve an exception plan (see manual 14.4.4).

n.1: There is no next stage after the final stage; the board uses authorize project closure instead (manual 14.4.4, 14.4.5).
n.2: The initiation stage plan is approved with the project brief in authorize initiation (manual 14.4.1).
n.3: Highlight reports keep the board informed between decision points; responses during a stage are given in give ongoing direction (manual 14.4.3, 11.5).

3.q: Why might the way a project has been tailored be revisited at a stage boundary?
o: Because tailoring is first agreed in managing a stage boundary
Because the PID, including approaches and roles, may be updated
Because the business layer re-approves tailoring at each stage end
Because each delivery stage uses a different set of principles
3.w: Managing a stage boundary reviews and, if necessary, updates the PID, including the management approaches, project management team structure and role descriptions, so tailoring can be adjusted for the next stage (see manual 18.2).

n.0: Tailoring is first agreed in initiating a project; the stage boundary is where it may be revisited (manual 15.4.1).
n.2: The project board, not the business layer, authorizes each stage and approves an updated PID; the business layer is involved in project-level matters (manual ch 14, fig 6.2).
n.3: All seven principles apply in every stage; principles are not selected or tailored (manual ch 2).

3.q: Why does starting up a project include the plan the initiation stage activity?
o: The initiation stage plan stands in for the project plan until closure
The board uses the initiation stage plan to authorize the whole project
It lets team managers begin work packages for the first delivery stage
Initiation uses time and resources, so its work must be planned and approved
3.w: Initiating a project takes time and consumes resources, so the work is planned and approved in advance to make sure initiation is not aimless; starting up is not complete without this plan (see manual 13.4.7, 13.4.8).

n.0: The project plan is prepared during initiation and is approved when the project is authorized; the initiation stage plan covers the initiation stage (manual 15.4.4, 7.2.2.2).
n.1: The board authorizes the project on the basis of the PID at the end of initiation; the initiation stage plan supports the earlier decision to authorize initiation (manual 14.4.1, 14.4.2).
n.2: Work packages for a delivery stage are authorized in controlling a stage, after the board has authorized the project and that stage; team managers play no part in starting up (manual 12, 14.4.4, 16.1).

3.q: In PRINCE2's description of the organizational context, which party provides the resources and expertise needed to deliver the products?
o: Users
Business decision-makers
Project assurance
Suppliers
3.w: Suppliers provide the resources and expertise to deliver the products, while users specify what is wanted and business decision-makers keep the investment justified (see manual 1.5).

n.0: Users specify the desired outputs; they do not provide the resources to build them.
n.1: Business decision-makers ensure the investment is justified throughout the lifecycle.
n.2: Project assurance monitors the project on behalf of the project board; it is not one of the three parties described in the organizational context.

3.q: A change authority approves a request for change that will cost money to implement. According to the change control guidance, where should the funding for the change come from?
o: The approved change budget, or additional funding from the customer
The risk budget, because the change removes a threat to the stage
The cost tolerance of the current stage, treated as normal stage spending
The team manager's budget for the work package, agreed in the team plan
3.w: If a change has a cost, the source of funding must be identified as either the approved change budget or additional funding from the customer (see manual 10.2.3).

n.1: The risk budget pays for responses to identified risks, not for approved changes (manual 9.2, 10.2.3).
n.2: Cost tolerance is a margin for deviation in planned work, not the funding source for approved changes (manual 10.2.3, 11.2.1).
n.3: A work package budget covers its agreed products; new changes are funded from the change budget or extra customer funding (manual 10.2.3).

3.q: Before planning begins, a project manager wants a record of what went well and badly on earlier, similar projects. Which activity of starting up a project creates the log used for this?
o: Appoint the executive and the project manager
Plan the initiation stage
Request project initiation
Assess previous lessons
3.w: The assess previous lessons activity creates the lessons log and gathers lessons from people and teams with experience of similar projects and from lessons reports (see manual 13.4.2).

n.0: Appoint the executive and the project manager puts the two key roles in place; it does not create the lessons log (manual 13.4.1).
n.1: Plan the initiation stage produces the initiation stage plan, drawing on lessons already captured rather than creating the log (manual 13.4.7).
n.2: Request project initiation asks the board for authority to initiate; it is the last activity and creates no log (manual 13.4.8).

3.q:
Which two statements about baselines and change are correct?
1. The project baseline holds the current approved versions of products subject to change control.
2. Once a product has been baselined it cannot be changed for the rest of the project.
3. A change is a modification to an approved product that forms part of the project baseline.
4. Draft products still being developed in a work package form part of the project baseline.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
3.w: Statement 1 defines the project baseline and statement 3 defines a change: a modification to an approved product in that baseline (see manual 10.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: baselined products can change, through change control, with each approved change creating a new version (manual 10.2.1, 10.2.3).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: baselined products can be changed under change control, and drafts are not yet approved, so they are not in the baseline (manual 10.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the baseline holds approved versions, so a draft still in development is not part of it (manual 10.1).

3.q: Why might some of a project's benefits be confirmed before the project closes?
o: Because products may be released in stages and used while the project continues
Because benefits reviews are completed before the end project report is written
Because the full business case is confirmed by the board at the end of initiation
Because the senior user hands over responsibility for benefits when the project closes
3.w: Although most benefits are confirmed after closure, some may be realized and confirmed during the project when products are released iteratively or in phases and put into use (see manual 5.3.1, fig 5.3).

n.1: Post-project benefits reviews are carried out by the business after closure; the project plans them but does not complete them (manual 5.3.1, ch 19).
n.2: At the end of initiation the board checks and approves the full business case; that is not confirming realized benefits (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: The senior user remains responsible for the continued realization of benefits after closure; nothing is handed over that would bring confirmation forward (manual 6.2.4.2).

3.q: Which aspect of project performance is concerned with the project being affordable and with any possible overspend or underspend against its budget?
o: Costs
Scope
Risk
Quality
3.w: The costs aspect recognizes that the project has to be affordable and that many factors can lead to underspend or overspend against the cost budget (see manual 1.4).

n.1: Scope is about what the project will deliver, not the money spent.
n.2: Risk is about limits on the plan's aggregated risks, not the budget itself.
n.3: Quality is about products being fit for purpose.

3.q: How does PRINCE2 7 link the 'manage by stages' principle with the people involved in a project?
o: Each stage needs a new executive to bring a fresh view of the business
Each stage needs a new team so that working relationships stay simple
Stage boundaries are good points to review how people work together
Stage boundaries are when the business layer resets team tolerances
3.w: Stages often mark a change in influencers and key relationships, so they are good points to review how people interact with each other and the wider organization (manual 3.5.1).

n.0: A project has one executive throughout; stages do not require a new appointment (manual ch 6).
n.1: Stages do not require new teams; they are points to review how people are working together (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: The business layer sets project tolerances, and team (work package) tolerances are set by the project manager (manual 11.2.1).

3.q: Why does the organizational design and development technique begin by understanding the organizational ecosystem?
o: Because the project's products need business approval before any design work on them starts
Because the business layer has to agree the stage tolerances before the board can be appointed
Because projects bring together people from organizations with their own structures and governance
Because the project ecosystem replaces the organizational ecosystem for the life of the project
3.w: Projects unite people from organizations that already have structures and governance requirements, so these must be understood before the project organization can be designed as a distinct entity (see manual 6.3.1.1).

n.0: Product approval is part of quality and change control, not the reason the technique starts with the organizational ecosystem (manual 8.2, 6.3.1.1).
n.1: Stage tolerances are set by the project board, not the business layer, and are unrelated to this step (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: The project ecosystem is a temporary entity that exists alongside the organizational ecosystem and is transitioned back into it at closure; it does not replace it (manual 6.3.1.1, fig 6.5).

3.q: During closure, the project manager reviews the project log and produces a lessons report. What is the purpose of the lessons report?
o: To record lessons informally as they are identified during the project
To pass on lessons so that they can be applied on future projects
To review the project's performance against the baselined PID
To confirm that users have accepted the project product
3.w: The lessons report passes on lessons that can be used by other or future projects; in closing a project it is produced from a review of the project log, in consultation with the project management team (see manual 11.5, 19.4.4).

n.0: Recording lessons as they arise is the purpose of the lessons log, part of the project log (manual 11.5).
n.2: Reviewing performance against the PID used to authorize the project is the purpose of the end project report (manual 11.5).
n.3: Confirming acceptance of the project product is done in the 'confirm project acceptance' activity of closing a project (manual 19.4.3).

3.q: A large project has a dedicated project support team working for the project manager. According to the roles in the issues practice, who should maintain the issue register on this project?
o: The team manager
Project assurance
The senior user
Project support
3.w: Project support administers the change control and issue procedures by maintaining the issue register; the project manager does this when there is no project support (see manual 10.6, tab 10.2).

n.0: Team managers implement corrective actions in their work packages; they do not maintain the issue register (manual 10.6, tab 10.2).
n.1: Project assurance supports the board and must stay independent of the project manager; administering registers is project support work (manual 6.2, 10.6).
n.2: The senior user makes decisions on escalated issues, focusing on safeguarding the expected benefits, rather than keeping the register (manual 10.6, tab 10.2).

3.q: Which statement describes a tolerance in PRINCE2?
o: The permitted deviation from a plan's target before escalation to the next management level
Money held back in a plan to pay for responses to the project's threats and opportunities
Money, or agreed constraints, reserved in a plan to pay for approved changes to the baseline
How much risk, and of what kind, the business is prepared to accept to meet its objectives
3.w: A tolerance is the permitted deviation above or below a plan's target that is allowed before the matter needs to be escalated to the next level of management (see manual 7.2.4).

n.1: This describes a risk budget, which funds risk responses; it is not a permitted deviation (manual 7.3.1).
n.2: This describes a change budget, which funds approved changes (manual 7.3.1).
n.3: This describes risk appetite, which is set by the business (manual 9.2.1).

3.q:
Which two statements about tolerances in PRINCE2 7 are correct?

1. The project board sets the tolerances for each work package.
2. The business layer sets the tolerances for the project as a whole.
3. A team manager who forecasts a work package breach escalates it directly to the project board.
4. Tolerances can be set for sustainability as well as for time and cost.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
3.w: The business layer sets project tolerances (2), and PRINCE2 7 adds sustainability to time, cost, scope, quality, benefits and risk as an aspect for tolerances (4) (see manual 11.2.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is correct, but work package tolerances are set by the project manager, not the board (manual 11.2.1).
n.1: Neither is correct: the project manager sets work package tolerances, and a team manager escalates a forecast breach to the project manager (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is correct, but a team manager raises a forecast work package breach with the project manager as an issue, not with the board (manual 11.2.1).

3.q: On what does PRINCE2 base its approach to achieving the required quality in a project?
o: Defining each product and its quality specifications in a product description, then checking it against them
Inspecting the work done by each team member against a time-based schedule of activities in the team plan
Measuring the benefits achieved after closure against the forecasts in the original business case
Reviewing each stage plan's activities at every checkpoint to confirm that the work has been carried out
3.w: PRINCE2 takes a product-based view of quality: each product's purpose and quality specifications are defined in its product description and the product is then checked against them (see manual 8.1, 8.5).

n.1: PRINCE2 is output-oriented rather than work-oriented; quality is defined for products, not for the activities in a schedule (manual 2.6, 8.1).
n.2: Measuring benefits after closure is part of the business case practice and the benefits management approach, not the basis of quality (manual ch 5).
n.3: Checking that activities were carried out is progress monitoring; quality is judged against the product's specifications, not completion of activities (manual ch 11, 8.1).

3.q: How does PRINCE2 7 suggest that data can support the risk practice?
o: Analytics can replace the risk owner by choosing and carrying out the responses to each risk
Data analysis can set the business's risk appetite on behalf of the business layer
Data is gathered after closure to confirm which risks occurred, for the benefits review
Data and analytics can help the project identify and assess risks, giving evidence for its decisions
3.w: PRINCE2 7 encourages the use of data and analytics to identify and assess risks, for example to forecast exposure, which also helps to counter decision bias (see manual 9.3.2.6).

n.0: Data informs decisions, but risk owners and risk action owners are still identified and agreed for each risk (manual 9.3.1.4).
n.1: Risk appetite is determined by the business; data supports identifying and assessing risks (manual 9.2, 9.3.2.6).
n.2: The guidance is about using data during the project to identify and assess risks, not about a post-project check (manual 9.3.2.6).

3.q: A trainer is listing the elements of the purpose of the progress practice. Which is NOT part of the purpose of the progress practice?
o: Monitoring and comparing actual achievements against those that were planned
Seeking lessons from earlier projects and passing them on to future ones
Providing a forecast for the project's objectives and continued viability
Controlling any deviations from plan that would cause an exception
3.w: Lessons are reviewed and reported under the progress guidance and support the learn from experience principle, but seeking and passing on lessons is not one of the three elements of the progress purpose (monitor and compare, forecast, control deviations) (see manual 11.1, 11.2.3).

n.0: This IS part of the purpose of the progress practice (manual 11.1), so it cannot be the answer to a NOT question.
n.2: Forecasting the objectives and continued viability IS part of the purpose of the progress practice (manual 11.1).
n.3: Controlling deviations that cause an exception IS part of the purpose of the progress practice (manual 11.1).

3.q: According to PRINCE2 7, what is required to deliver organizational change successfully?
o: A change authority with its own change budget
A separate change project run after closure
A fixed set of interim states for every project
Effective leadership
3.w: PRINCE2 states that effective leadership is required to deliver the change from the current state to the target state (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: A change authority and change budget relate to approving changes to the baseline under the issues practice, not to leading organizational change (manual 10.2.4, 10.2.5).
n.1: The change is planned within the project through the change management approach; PRINCE2 does not call for a separate change project after closure (manual 3.2.1).
n.2: Interim states are used where needed: the business moves to the target state through any interim states, so there is no fixed set (manual 3.2.1).

3.q: Which person is NOT permitted to perform a project assurance role on a PRINCE2 project?
o: An external auditor engaged by the project board
A member of staff appointed from the wider business
A senior user checking the user interest personally
The project support officer working on the project
3.w: Project assurance roles cannot be assigned to the project manager, project team members or project support (see manual 6.2.4.7).

n.0: Assurance can be selected from an external party (manual 6.2.4.7).
n.1: Assurance can be appointed from the wider business (manual 6.2.4.7).
n.2: Board members can undertake assurance of their own area themselves (manual 6.2.4.7).

3.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
At a stage boundary, a change to the forecast benefits of the project is dealt with in the activity [?].
o: prepare exception plan
update the project plan
update the business case
request next stage
3.w: Update the business case reflects changes in the project and its environment, including forecast benefits, and updates the benefits management approach with the results of any benefits actions (see manual ch 18).

n.0: A change in the benefits forecast is handled when the business case is updated, not by an exception plan (manual ch 18).
n.1: The project plan holds products, timescales and costs; benefits are covered by the business case (manual ch 18).
n.3: Request next stage briefs the board; the benefits forecast has already been revised in the business case by then (manual ch 18).

3.q: How does PRINCE2 recommend that each risk is described?
o: In terms of its cause, the uncertain event, and the effect it would have on objectives
In terms of its probability, its proximity, and the response category chosen for it
In terms of the objective at risk, the risk owner, and the date it was first registered
In terms of the threat, the matching opportunity, and the overall risk exposure
3.w: Describing a risk by its cause (the source), event (the uncertain occurrence) and effect (the impact on objectives) makes it clear and comparable (see manual 9.2.1).

n.1: Probability, proximity and response category are assessed and recorded for a risk, but they do not describe what the risk is (manual 9.2.2, 9.5).
n.2: Owner and date are register details; the description itself sets out cause, event and effect (manual 9.2.1, 9.5).
n.3: A risk is either a threat or an opportunity; overall exposure is assessed across risks and is not part of a single risk's description (manual 9.1, 9.2).

3.q: Which statement describes a project in a commercial customer-supplier context?
o: The supplier works to the customer's business case, with none of its own
The project must sit in a programme so the contract is managed
The supplier's management team replaces the customer's project board
The supplier has its own business case for taking part
3.w: In a commercial context there are customer and supplier relationships, possibly under contracts, and the supplier has its own business case for its involvement; the project may also need to align with more than one management system (see manual 1.5).

n.0: Suppliers have their own justification for taking part, alongside the customer's business case (manual 1.5, 2.1).
n.1: A commercial project may be standalone or part of a programme or portfolio; a contract does not require a programme (manual 1.5, fig 1.2).
n.2: The supplier's interests are represented on the project board by the senior supplier; the board is not replaced (manual 6.2.1).

3.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
Co-creation is a specific form of [?] that involves users and key influencers in designing products and agreed ways of working.
o: quality assurance
delegation
governance
collaboration
3.w: PRINCE2 describes co-creation as a specific form of collaboration involving users and key influencers in design (see manual 3.3).

n.0: Quality assurance is an independent check, managed outside the project management team, that the project is meeting quality requirements; it is not joint design (manual 8.2.3).
n.1: Delegation passes authority down the levels of the project; co-creation is about designing things together (manual 3.3).
n.2: Governance is the framework of authority and control; co-creation is a form of collaboration (manual 3.3).

3.q: A project is nearing the end of its second delivery stage, with a third stage still to come. What should happen to the business case at this point?
o: The project manager prepares the outline business case for the board to approve
The business layer confirms all benefits and closes the benefits management approach
The senior supplier develops a new full business case for approval in initiation
The project manager updates it, and the board checks it before authorizing the next stage
3.w: At the end of each delivery stage the project manager maintains the business case (in managing a stage boundary) and the board checks it for continued justification before authorizing the next stage (see manual 5.2.1, 5.3.1).

n.0: The outline business case is prepared in starting up a project, not at the end of a delivery stage (manual 13.4.3).
n.1: Benefits are mainly confirmed after closure, and the benefits management approach is updated, not closed, at stage boundaries (manual 5.3.1, ch 18).
n.2: Initiation has already happened; the full business case was developed then, with the project manager responsible (manual 15.4.5).

3.q: When developing a business case, which three basic business options should be considered for any investment?
o: Build in-house, buy off the shelf, or contract a third party
Avoid the threat, reduce the threat, or accept the threat
Do the minimum, do more than the minimum, do the maximum
Do nothing differently, do the minimum, do more than the minimum
3.w: The three basic business options are do nothing differently, do the minimum and do more than the minimum; 'do nothing differently' is the baseline for quantifying the others (see manual 5.3.1).

n.0: These are choices made when selecting the project approach, not the three basic business options (manual 13.4.5).
n.1: These are risk responses, not business options for an investment (manual ch 9).
n.2: This leaves out the baseline option of doing nothing differently and adds a maximum option that is not one of the three (manual 5.3.1).

3.q: Which statement about who is involved in initiating a project is correct?
o: Team managers build early specialist products through managing product delivery
The business layer runs it and passes the completed PID to the project board
The project manager runs it, while the board directs it through directing a project
The board runs it day to day and the project manager provides project support
3.w: Initiating a project is a managing-level process run by the project manager; the board keeps control through directing a project, for example giving ongoing direction and then authorizing the project (see manual 12, fig 12.1, 15.3).

n.0: The process model shows no managing product delivery in the initiation stage; specialist delivery starts in later stages (manual 12, fig 12.1).
n.1: The business layer sits outside the project management team; the project manager assembles the PID and the board approves it (manual 15.4.6, 14.4.2).
n.3: The board manages by exception and does not run day-to-day work; the project manager runs initiation (manual 14.3, 15.3).

3.q: A retailer's project delivered a new stock app on time and to specification. Six months later, store staff still record stock on paper and the expected cut in waste has not appeared. What does this show about change management?
o: Benefits depend on people adopting new ways of working as well as on delivered outputs
The project should have raised an exception report when the app was handed over
The issue management approach failed to control changes to the app's specification
The senior supplier is responsible for realizing the planned reduction in waste
3.w: Outputs lead to benefits through outcomes, which are changes in how people work. Change management plans the move to the target state so that people adopt the new ways of working and benefits can be realized (see manual 3.2.1, fig 5.1).

n.1: The app was delivered on time and to specification, so no tolerance was forecast to be exceeded and no exception report was needed (manual 11.2.6).
n.2: The specification was met, so change control of the baseline was not the problem; the gap is in adoption by staff (manual 10.2.3, 3.2.1).
n.3: The senior user, not the senior supplier, specifies the benefits and is responsible for their realization after handover (manual 6.2.4).

3.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
In PRINCE2, project managers and team managers plan using [?], which can be improved with lessons and data from earlier work.
o: estimates
baselines
change budgets
product registers
3.w: Project managers and team managers always plan using estimates. Techniques include top-down, bottom-up, comparative, parametric, data analytics and expert consensus, and lessons help improve them (see manual 7.3.1.3, 7.7).

n.1: A baseline is an approved version of a plan or product; plans are built from estimates and then baselined on approval (manual 7.2.2.1, 7.3.1.3).
n.2: A change budget is an optional part of a plan's budget for approved changes; it is not the basis of planning (manual 7.3.1).
n.3: The product register records products and their status; planning is based on estimates (manual 4.3.2, 7.3.1.3).

3.q: Which is an objective of the 'closing a project' process?
o: To ensure the business can support the products after closure
To assure the board that all products in the stage plan are complete
To ensure work on products allocated to the team is authorized
To keep the risks and issues arising in the stage under control
3.w: Closing a project aims, among other things, to check user acceptance of the project product and ensure the business can support the products once the project has closed (see manual 19.2).

n.1: This is an objective of managing a stage boundary (manual 18.2).
n.2: This is an objective of managing product delivery (manual 17.2).
n.3: This is an objective of controlling a stage (manual 16.2).

3.q:
Which two statements about the later steps of the planning technique are correct?
1. The schedule is prepared before the products are defined, so that dates can be fixed early.
2. Documenting the plan is the first step, done before any estimates are prepared.
3. Analysing risks runs alongside the other steps, and a plan stays in draft until its risks are addressed.
4. The budget may include a risk budget and a change budget as well as the cost of the activities.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
1 and 4
3 and 4
3.w: Statements 3 and 4 are correct. Risk analysis runs alongside the planning steps, and the budget covers activity costs plus any risk budget, change budget and cost tolerances (see manual 7.3.1).

n.0: Statements 1 and 2 are both wrong. Statement 1 is wrong: the products are defined and analysed first, and the schedule is derived from them (manual 7.2.5, 7.3.1). Statement 2 is wrong: documenting the plan is the last step, after the budget has been prepared (manual 7.3.1).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: the products are defined and analysed first, and the schedule is derived from them (manual 7.2.5, 7.3.1). Statement 3 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 4.
n.2: Statement 1 is wrong: the products are defined and analysed first, and the schedule is derived from them (manual 7.2.5, 7.3.1). Statement 4 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.

3.q: Which statement best describes the main reporting lines used in the progress practice?
o: Team managers report work package progress directly to the project board in highlight reports
The PM reports stage progress to the business layer in checkpoint reports
Team managers report work package progress to the PM, who reports stage progress to the board
The project board reports stage progress to the PM in highlight reports
3.w: Checkpoint reports carry work package status from team managers to the project manager, and highlight reports carry stage status from the project manager to the project board (see manual 11.5, fig 11.2).

n.0: Team managers report to the project manager through checkpoint reports; the board is not involved in managing product delivery (manual 11.5, 17).
n.1: Checkpoint reports come from team managers to the project manager; stage progress goes to the board in highlight reports (manual 11.5).
n.3: Highlight reports flow from the project manager to the board, not the other way round (manual 11.5).

3.q: Which of the following is NOT an acceptable way to tailor PRINCE2 to a project?
o: Combining the project brief and business case on a small project
Deciding not to apply the 'manage by stages' principle on this project
Adding an agile coach role to support an iterative supplier team
Using the organization's own names for some management products
3.w: Principles are not tailored: all seven must be applied, so deciding not to apply manage by stages would mean the project is no longer a PRINCE2 project (manual ch 2, 2.7).

n.0: Small, low-value projects may merge the project brief and business case into one simple document, which is acceptable tailoring (manual 2.7, 5.4.5).
n.2: Roles can be added when tailoring, for example a coach to support an iterative way of working (manual 2.7).
n.3: Terminology can be tailored to use the organization's own terms (manual 2.7).

3.q: What is the purpose of the quality register?
o: To list all of the products required by a plan, together with their current status
To describe the quality techniques, standards and responsibilities for the whole project
To summarize all the quality management activities that are planned or have taken place
To set out the quality specifications and quality method for one specific product
3.w: The quality register summarizes all quality management activities that are planned or have taken place, and the project manager and project assurance use it to review progress (see manual 8.5).

n.0: Listing all products of a plan and their status is the purpose of the product register (manual 8.5).
n.1: The quality techniques, standards and responsibilities are described in the quality management approach (manual 8.5).
n.3: A product's quality specifications and quality method are set out in its product description (manual 8.5).

3.q: Which list gives the four types of plan used in PRINCE2?
o: Project plan, stage plan, work package plan and exception plan
Project plan, stage plan, team plan and exception plan
Project plan, initiation plan, delivery plan and closure plan
Business plan, project plan, stage plan and team plan
3.w: PRINCE2 uses four types of plan: the project plan, stage plans, team plans and exception plans (see manual 7.1.1).

n.0: There is no 'work package plan'; work is passed to teams in a work package description, and a team manager may produce a team plan (manual 7.1.1, 7.5).
n.2: These are not PRINCE2 plan types; initiation and delivery stages each have a stage plan, and closure is planned in the final stage plan (manual 7.1.1, 7.2.2.2).
n.3: A business plan belongs to the business, not the project, and this list leaves out the exception plan (manual 7.1.1).

3.q: A project team is split between two offices and several people working from home. Which action best follows PRINCE2's guidance on social cohesion?
o: Arrange regular co-location days for key people, focused on building key relationships
Rely on the team's informal networks to share information, as in a co-located team
Replace team meetings with written checkpoint reports to save people's time
Ask each office to run its work as a separate project with its own project board
3.w: Where teams are dispersed or hybrid, social cohesion needs deliberate methods, such as synchronized co-location days for key people focused on key relationships (see manual 3.3.3).

n.1: Organic sharing through informal networks is typical of co-located teams; a dispersed team needs deliberate methods (manual 3.3.3).
n.2: Checkpoint reports are progress controls from team managers to the project manager; they do not build trust and cohesion (manual 3.3.3, ch 11).
n.3: Splitting the work into separate projects does not address cohesion and would add governance; people should be brought together purposefully (manual 3.3.3).

3.q:
Which two statements about culture in PRINCE2 7 are correct?
1. Culture is defined in the project mandate and stays fixed for the project.
2. Non-compliance with project processes is best handled by escalating it to the business layer.
3. Each organization in the organizational ecosystem may have its own culture.
4. Behaviours and culture are hard to document and are best learned socially.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
3.w: Statement 3 is correct: the organizations in the organizational ecosystem each bring their own culture. Statement 4 is correct: behaviours, culture and relationships are hard to document and are best learned through social learning (see manual 3.1, 3.5.1).

n.0: Statements 1 and 2 are both wrong: culture evolves during a change, and non-compliance is a signal to gather and act on feedback, not to escalate to the business layer (manual 3.2.1, 3.2.3).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: PRINCE2 refers to an evolving culture, and the mandate is not where culture is defined (manual 3.2.1).
n.2: Statement 2 is wrong: persistent non-compliance is a leading indicator that ways of working need adapting through feedback (manual 3.2.3).

3.q: A supplier's team manager is slow to accept a work package. The project manager considers asking the executive to order the team manager to comply. Why is this unlikely to be effective?
o: The executive's role ends once the project has been authorized in directing a project
Work packages are authorized by the senior supplier rather than by the project manager
The team manager should accept work packages directly from the project board instead
The team manager does not report to the executive; a working relationship works better
3.w: Using the executive's authority over someone outside the executive's reporting line is unlikely to work; the project manager should build a working relationship and co-create the work package with the team manager (see manual 3.3.1, 16.4.1).

n.0: The executive remains accountable for the project until closure and continues to direct it (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: The project manager authorizes work packages in controlling a stage (manual 16.4.1).
n.2: Team managers take work packages from the project manager; the project board is not involved in managing product delivery (manual ch 17).

3.q: Before a team starts building a new online booking form, the project manager agrees with the users what the form is for, what it consists of and how its quality will be checked. Which principle is being applied?
o: Manage by exception
Focus on products
Learn from experience
Tailor to suit the project
3.w: Agreeing a product's purpose, composition and quality criteria before work starts is the focus on products principle, applied through a product description (manual 2.6).

n.0: Manage by exception sets tolerances for permitted variation; agreeing what the product is comes under focus on products (manual 2.5, 2.6).
n.2: Learn from experience concerns lessons; nothing in the situation involves lessons (manual 2.2).
n.3: Tailoring adapts the method to the project; defining one product's content and quality is focus on products (manual 2.7).

3.q: For a new online shop, the executive suggests recording 'a 10% rise in online sales within a year' as one of the user's quality expectations. Which statement is correct?
o: It is suitable as an expectation, because it is measurable and agreed with the users
It is a benefit the online shop should enable, not a quality expectation of the shop itself
It belongs among the acceptance criteria in the project product description instead
It belongs among the quality specifications in the shop's product description instead
3.w: A rise in sales is an outcome or benefit that the product should help to achieve; it says nothing about the quality of the product itself, so it is not a quality expectation, an acceptance criterion or a quality specification (see manual 8.1.1).

n.0: Being measurable does not make a benefit a quality expectation; expectations describe the quality of the project product (manual 8.1.1).
n.2: Acceptance criteria are measurable attributes of the project product the user can check before accepting it; a future sales rise is a benefit (manual 8.1.1, ch 5).
n.3: Quality specifications are measures of a product's own characteristics, not the business results it later enables (manual 8.1.1).

3.q: The project board reviews the end project report to decide whether the project can close. Which process and activity is the board using?
o: Closing a project: request project closure
Directing a project: authorize project closure
Managing a stage boundary: request next stage
Closing a project: confirm project acceptance
3.w: The project manager prepares the end project report in evaluate the project and requests closure; the board then reviews it and authorizes closure in directing a project (see manual 14.4.5, 19.4.4).

n.0: In request project closure the project manager asks the board to close; the decision is taken in directing a project (manual 19.4.5, 14.4.5).
n.2: This activity asks for the next stage to be authorized; it is not used at the end of the final stage (manual ch 18).
n.3: This activity hands products into operational use and confirms acceptance before closure is requested (manual 19.4.3).

3.q: In the risk practice, what is a risk owner?
o: The person nominated to own a specific agreed action that responds to a risk
The person who maintains the risk register and keeps its entries up to date
The person who sets the threshold beyond which a risk must be escalated
The person assigned to take responsibility for responding to a particular risk
3.w: A risk owner is the person assigned to take responsibility for responding to a risk; they may ask a risk action owner to carry out agreed actions (see manual 9.2).

n.0: This describes the risk action owner, also called the risk actionee, who carries out agreed actions for the risk owner (manual 9.2).
n.1: Maintaining the register is an administrative task usually given to project support; it does not make them responsible for responding to a risk (manual 9.5, appendix B).
n.2: Thresholds for risk are risk tolerances, set by the project board based on the business's risk appetite; that is not the risk owner's role (manual 9.2.1).

3.q: What should the roles and responsibilities assigned to people on a PRINCE2 project reflect?
o: The capability, authority and availability of the person doing the work
The standard job descriptions used by the person's home organization
The person's grade and seniority within the business layer
The responsibilities written into the person's employment contract
3.w: Roles and responsibilities should reflect the capability, authority and availability of the individual, considered through their key relationships (see manual 3.3.2).

n.1: Standard, generic role descriptions are unlikely to be effective; roles should fit the individual and their relationships (manual 3.3.2).
n.2: Grade and seniority are not the basis; it is not unusual for team members to be more senior than the project manager (manual 3.3, 3.3.2).
n.3: Employment contracts sit with the home organization; project roles are based on capability, authority and availability (manual 3.3.2).

3.q: Under the 'manage by exception' principle, which management levels set stage tolerances and work package tolerances?
o: Project board sets stage; project manager sets work package
Business layer sets stage; project board sets work package
Project manager sets stage; team manager sets work package
Project board sets stage; team manager sets work package
3.w: Authority is delegated level by level: the business layer sets project tolerances, the project board sets stage tolerances and the project manager sets work package tolerances (manual 11.2.1).

n.1: The business layer sets project tolerances, not stage tolerances, and the board does not set work package tolerances (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: The project manager works within stage tolerances set by the board and sets work package tolerances; team managers work within them (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: Team managers work within work package tolerances set by the project manager; they do not set them (manual 11.2.1).

3.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The [?] heading of a work package description records limits on the work, such as authorized working hours and any safety or security requirements.
o: references
constraints
techniques and procedures
agreement
3.w: The constraints heading of a work package description records limits such as authorized hours and safety or security requirements (see manual 7.5).

n.0: References link the work package to higher-level plans and documents; they do not set limits on the work (manual 7.5).
n.2: This heading records the methods to be used in producing the products, not limits such as working hours (manual 7.5).
n.3: The agreement heading records the initial authorization of the work and its final completion (manual 7.5).

3.q: One project board wants tighter control over a high-risk project. Another wants to reduce the demands its project makes on busy senior managers. How should the stage lengths of the two projects differ?
o: Shorter stages for the high-risk project; longer stages for the other
Longer stages for the high-risk project; shorter stages for the other
Equal stages for both, as stage length is fixed by the business layer
One long delivery stage for both, to keep decision points to a minimum
3.w: Stage length is a trade-off: shorter stages give more control, while longer stages reduce the burden on senior management (manual 2.4).

n.1: This reverses the trade-off: longer stages mean fewer decision points and less control (manual 2.4).
n.2: Stage length is chosen for each project, considering size, complexity and control needs; it is not fixed by the business layer (manual 2.4).
n.3: A single long delivery stage reduces control, which does not suit the high-risk project (manual 2.4).

3.q: Which statement BEST describes the 'temporary' characteristic of a project?
o: Once the change is in place, business as usual resumes and the project is no longer needed
Each project differs from others in some way, such as its team, customer, location or timeframe
People with different skills work together on a change that affects others outside the team
Projects bring threats and opportunities beyond those normally found in routine work
3.w: Projects are temporary: when the desired change has been implemented, business as usual resumes in its new form and the need for the project is removed (see manual 1.3).

n.1: This describes the 'unique' characteristic: every project differs in some way from others, even similar ones.
n.2: This describes the 'cross-functional' characteristic: different skills working together on a change that affects others.
n.3: This describes the 'uncertainty' characteristic: projects are riskier than business as usual.

4.q: When is the daily log first available for recording issues?
o: In starting up a project, before the issue register is set up in initiating a project
In initiating a project, at the same time as the issue register and the risk register
In controlling a stage, once the first work package has been authorized for delivery
In directing a project, once the project board has authorized initiation of the project
4.w: The daily log is set up in starting up a project, so early issues and risks can be noted before the issue register is created in initiating a project (see manual ch 13, ch 15, 11.5).

n.1: The registers are set up in initiating a project, but the daily log already exists from starting up a project (manual ch 13, ch 15).
n.2: The daily log is in use long before delivery starts; it is created in starting up a project (manual ch 13).
n.3: The daily log is created by the project manager in starting up a project, before the board authorizes initiation (manual ch 13, 14.4.1).

4.q:
Which two statements about the 'implement' step of the risk management technique are correct?
1. Planned responses are actioned and their effectiveness is reviewed.
2. The combined risk profile is compared with risk tolerance.
3. The risk owner and risk action owner for each risk are identified and agreed.
4. Business policies and standards are examined to shape the approach.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
4.w: In implement, planned responses are actioned and reviewed, with corrective action where needed, and the risk owner and risk action owner are identified and agreed for each risk (see manual 9.3.1.4).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: assessing the combined risk profile is part of the assess step (manual 9.3.1.2).
n.2: Both are wrong: statement 2 belongs to assess and statement 4 to identify, when context and objectives are defined (manual 9.3.1.1, 9.3.1.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: examining business policies and standards is part of defining context and objectives in identify (manual 9.3.1.1).

4.q: Board members of a joint customer-supplier project work in different regions. The project manager proposes reviewing highlight reports in short online calls rather than formal meetings. What does this show?
o: The board's responsibility for direction has been removed
'Manage by stages' is applied by changing the stage length
A business case change has occurred that needs an exception plan
Reporting is tailored in format and formality to suit the project
4.w: Tailoring makes project controls fit the project, typically by adjusting the frequency and formality of reports and reviews; holding highlight reviews online for a dispersed board is an example (see manual 2.7).

n.0: The board still directs the project; only the way it receives and discusses reports changes (manual 6.2.1).
n.1: Stage length is unchanged; the proposal concerns how reports are reviewed, which is a tailoring decision (manual 2.4, 2.7).
n.2: No business case change or tolerance breach is involved, so there is no need for an exception plan (manual ch 11).

4.q: A request for change would add a feature that users have asked for, at extra cost and with some new risk. How does the 'ensure continued business justification' principle guide the decision?
o: The extra benefit is weighed against the extra cost and risk of the change
The change is accepted if it falls within the project manager's tolerance
The change is rejected, as the business case cannot change once approved
The change is accepted if the senior user confirms the feature is wanted
4.w: Justification can evolve, but what is delivered must stay consistent with it, so a request for change is judged by weighing its extra benefit against its extra cost and risk (manual 2.1).

n.1: Tolerance decides who may approve, which is manage by exception; it does not show whether the change is justified (manual 2.5).
n.2: The business case is maintained and updated during the project, so it can change once approved (manual 2.1, 5.3.1).
n.3: User demand on its own does not justify a change; the benefit must be balanced against the cost and risk (manual 2.1).

4.q: A council sets up a project team for nine months to move its library catalogue online. When the new catalogue is in use, the team is disbanded and staff return to their usual jobs. Which characteristic of a project does this BEST illustrate?
o: Unique
Temporary
Uncertainty
Cross-functional
4.w: Projects are temporary: once the change is implemented, business as usual resumes in its new form and the need for the project ends, so the team is disbanded (see manual 1.3).

n.0: Unique is about how a project differs from other projects; the stem focuses on the project ending once its change is in place.
n.2: Uncertainty is about the extra threats and opportunities a project brings; the stem describes the team being disbanded at the end.
n.3: Cross-functional is about different skills working together; the stem does not describe the mix of skills, only that the team ends with the project.

4.q:
Which two statements about tailoring for suppliers and commercial relationships are correct?
1. A coach role may be added where teams combine PRINCE2 with an agile framework.
2. PRINCE2 is designed for use with linear-sequential delivery.
3. A commercial relationship can call for alignment with two or more quality systems.
4. A supplier's agile framework replaces the need for management stages.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
4.w: Statement 1 is correct: a coach can be added to guide teams combining PRINCE2 with a supplier's agile method. Statement 3 is correct: a commercial customer-supplier relationship may require alignment with two or more quality systems (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: PRINCE2 is not specific to any delivery method and can be tailored to iterative-incremental, linear-sequential or hybrid delivery (manual 1.1, 1.5.3).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: PRINCE2 is not tied to one delivery method, and manage by stages still applies with an agile supplier (manual 1.1, 2.4).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the 'manage by stages' principle applies whatever framework the supplier uses (manual 2.4).

4.q: Which statement about the project management team structure is correct?
o: It holds the authority to direct the project within the remit set by the business layer
It includes the business layer, because the business layer appoints the project executive
It is another name for the board of executive, senior user(s) and senior supplier(s)
It covers the board, project manager, team managers, and assurance and support roles
4.w: The project management team structure is composed of the project board, project manager, team managers, and the project assurance and project support roles (see manual 6.2.3).

n.0: PRINCE2 states that the project management team structure does not itself have authority to direct the project; the board does (manual 6.2.3, 6.2.1).
n.1: The business layer sits outside the project management team, even though it appoints the executive (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: The executive, senior users and senior suppliers make up the project board, which is only one part of the wider project management team structure (manual 6.2.3).

4.q: What triggers the 'prepare exception plan' activity in 'managing a stage boundary'?
o: A forecast that a work package will exceed its tolerances
A board request after it considers an exception report
A new issue raised by a team manager during the work
The need to plan the closure work for the final stage
4.w: Prepare exception plan is triggered when the project board, having considered an exception report, asks the project manager for an exception plan; the request is recorded in the project log (see manual ch 18).

n.0: Work package deviations are raised with the project manager and handled in controlling a stage (manual 17.4.2, 16.4.6).
n.2: New issues are captured and assessed in controlling a stage; they do not trigger an exception plan (manual 16.4.5).
n.3: Closure activities are planned in the final stage's plan, made in prepare next stage plan (manual ch 18).

4.q: Which feature of PRINCE2 means it can be applied to any project, of any scale, and used alongside specialist, industry-specific models?
o: Flexible
Proven
Outcome-focused
Universal
4.w: PRINCE2 is universal: it can be applied to any project of any scale and implemented alongside specialist, industry-specific models (see manual 1.6).

n.0: Flexible means the method can be tailored to the needs of the organizations involved, which is a different feature from applying to any project.
n.1: Proven means it is based on established and proven practice and governance.
n.2: Outcome-focused means participants stay focused on the project's viability against its business case objectives.

4.q: During which step of the organizational design and development technique would new team members be onboarded, for example through a site visit, an induction or a certification?
o: Design the project ecosystem
Understand the organizational ecosystem
Develop the project ecosystem
Manage ongoing changes to the project ecosystem
4.w: Developing the project ecosystem is ongoing work in response to changing needs, team members and relationships, and includes onboarding people through site visits, inductions or certification (see manual 6.3.1.3).

n.0: Designing the project ecosystem decides how to organize work and people: the people and resources needed, integrated working practices, behaviours and culture (manual 6.3.1.2).
n.1: Understanding the organizational ecosystem examines the existing structures and governance of the organizations involved (manual 6.3.1.1).
n.3: Managing ongoing changes concerns changing capabilities over the lifecycle, moving people on and off the project and a robust change management procedure (manual 6.3.1.4).

4.q: A regional director has asked for a new customer portal to be explored. What triggers the starting up a project process?
o: The project brief from the project manager
The initiation notice from the project board
The request to initiate a project from the executive
The project mandate from the business layer
4.w: Starting up a project is triggered by the project mandate, provided by the responsible authority in the business that is commissioning the project (see manual 13.3).

n.0: The project brief is an output of starting up a project, assembled by the project manager; it cannot be the trigger (manual 13.4).
n.1: The initiation notice comes from the board's authorize initiation activity and triggers initiating a project, not starting up (manual 14.4.1, 15.3).
n.2: The request to initiate is the final output of starting up a project and triggers directing a project (manual 13.4.8, 14.3).

4.q: A request for change is within the project manager's tolerances but needs a formal decision. Which management product describes the issue's impact on the project baseline, sets out ways to resolve it and recommends a decision?
o: Issue register
Exception report
Issue report
Highlight report
4.w: An issue report describes an issue's impacts on the project baseline, identifies ways to resolve it or address an off-specification, and recommends a decision. Where tolerance is not threatened, an issue report rather than an exception report is used (see manual 10.5).

n.0: The issue register records and tracks formal issues; it does not set out a full impact analysis and recommendation for one issue (manual 10.5).
n.1: An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance, which is not the case here (manual 11.5).
n.3: A highlight report summarizes stage status for the board at agreed intervals; it is not the vehicle for one issue's recommendation (manual 11.5).

4.q: Two analysts with identical qualifications are given similar tasks, but one works far more effectively when paired with a particular designer. How does PRINCE2 explain this?
o: People with the same capabilities may perform a role differently, depending on who they work with
The analysts' role descriptions were not approved by the project board before work began
Competence comes from qualifications, so the difference must come from the work package tolerances
The less effective analyst is a threat that should be recorded and owned in the risk register
4.w: PRINCE2 notes that people with the same capabilities and competencies often perform the same role differently, and the same person may perform differently depending on who they work with (see manual 3.3.2).

n.1: Approval of role descriptions does not explain why equally qualified people perform differently; PRINCE2 links this to individuals and their working relationships (manual 3.3.2).
n.2: Qualifications do not settle competence, and tolerances set limits on a work package; they do not explain differences between people (manual 3.3.2, 11.2.1).
n.3: The situation concerns how people work together, which PRINCE2 addresses through team building and roles, not by registering a colleague as a risk (manual 3.3.2).

4.q: Which management product defines the actions, reviews and controls that will be put in place to ensure the project's sustainability performance targets are achieved?
o: Benefits management approach
Sustainability management approach
Communication management approach
Change management approach
4.w: The sustainability management approach defines the actions, reviews and controls to ensure sustainability performance targets are achieved. It is part of the PID and supports the business case (see manual 5.5, 5.2.2).

n.0: The benefits management approach covers benefits actions and reviews, not sustainability performance targets (manual 5.5).
n.2: The communication management approach defines the means and frequency of communication with stakeholders, not sustainability targets (manual ch 3).
n.3: The change management approach concerns organizational transition, part of the people element (manual ch 3).

4.q: Which is NOT a feature of the PRINCE2 method?
o: It can be tailored to suit the organizations involved
It is designed for one industry and its engineering practices
It provides a common vocabulary for all participants
It is based on established and proven practice and governance
4.w: PRINCE2 is not specific to any industry, project type, delivery method or engineering practice; it is universal and works alongside specialist models (see manual 1.1 and 1.6).

n.0: This is a genuine feature: PRINCE2 is flexible and can be tailored to the organizations involved.
n.2: This is a genuine feature: common language and concepts give all participants a shared vocabulary.
n.3: This is a genuine feature: PRINCE2 is proven, based on established practice and governance.

4.q: What is the purpose of the risk register?
o: To keep a record of identified risks related to the project, including their status and history
To describe the procedures, techniques, standards and responsibilities for managing risk
To record informal issues and actions that the project manager needs to keep track of
To record the quality activities that are planned for products and the results of each
4.w: The risk register is part of the project log and records each identified threat and opportunity with its status and history (see manual 9.5).

n.1: This is the risk management approach, part of the PID (manual 9.5).
n.2: This describes the daily log (manual 11.5).
n.3: This describes the quality register (manual 8.5).

4.q: Team members on a project keep bypassing the agreed process for logging defects. According to PRINCE2 7, what does this persistent non-compliance suggest?
o: The agreed ways of working may no longer fit the emerging culture
A stage tolerance has been breached and must be escalated to the board
An off-specification has occurred and must go to the change authority
The team manager role should be combined with the project support role
4.w: PRINCE2 treats persistent non-compliance with project processes as a leading indicator that the agreed ways of working no longer match the emerging culture, so feedback should be gathered and acted on (see manual 3.2.3).

n.1: Not following a process is not, in itself, a forecast breach of stage tolerance, so there is nothing to escalate as an exception (manual 11.2.6).
n.2: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification; bypassing a process is a ways-of-working matter (manual 10.1, 3.2.3).
n.3: Combining roles is a tailoring decision about capacity and skills; it does not address a mismatch between processes and culture (manual 2.7, 3.2.3).

4.q: Which statement best describes how the 'ensure continued business justification' principle works together with the 'manage by stages' principle?
o: Business justification is checked once, at the end of the initiation stage
Business justification is checked by the board at each stage boundary
The length of each stage is set by the business case's payback period
Stage boundaries are used by the business layer to set stage tolerances
4.w: Decisions at each stage boundary include checking that the project is still justified before the board authorizes the next stage (manual tab 5.2, 5.3.1).

n.0: Justification is checked repeatedly, at the end of each stage and when assessing an exception plan, not just once (manual 5.3.1).
n.2: Stage length reflects control needs, size, complexity and external influences, not the payback period (manual 2.4).
n.3: Stage tolerances are set by the project board; the business layer sets project tolerances (manual 11.2.1).

4.q: In 'request project closure', what might the project manager recommend to the project board?
o: Extending the project until all benefits have been measured
Recognizing success and naming a strong supplier for future work
Moving the unspent project budget into the risk budget
Delaying acceptance until every open issue is resolved
4.w: Request project closure briefs the board on performance, confirms readiness to close and highlights concessions; it may recommend celebrating success and recognizing a high-performing supplier or team manager for future work (see manual 19.4.5).

n.0: Benefits continue to be reviewed after closure through the benefits management approach; the project is not extended for them (manual 19.2).
n.2: The risk budget funds risk responses during the project; closure does not move money into it (manual ch 9, 19.4.5).
n.3: Open issues and risks are handed on with follow-on action recommendations (manual 19.2).

4.q: In which process is the stage plan for the initiation stage created?
o: Initiating a project, alongside the project plan
Starting up a project, by the project manager
Managing a stage boundary, at the end of the first stage
Directing a project, by the project board
4.w: The initiation stage plan is created in starting up a project ('plan the initiation stage'). Every later stage plan is prepared near the end of the current stage, in managing a stage boundary (see manual 7.2.2.2).

n.0: Initiation cannot start until its stage plan is approved, so that plan is made earlier, in starting up a project; the project plan is the one created in initiation (manual 7.2.2.1, 7.2.2.2).
n.2: Managing a stage boundary prepares the plan for the next stage; the initiation stage plan exists before initiation begins (manual 7.2.2.2).
n.3: The board approves the initiation stage plan when it authorizes initiation; the project manager creates it in starting up a project (manual 7.2.2.2, 14.4.1).

4.q: The project board wants a regular summary of the status of the current stage, produced at intervals it has chosen. Which management product provides this?
o: Highlight report
Checkpoint report
End stage report
Exception report
4.w: The project manager produces highlight reports for the project board (and possibly other stakeholders), summarizing stage status at intervals defined by the board (see manual 11.5).

n.1: A checkpoint report gives work package status to the project manager, not stage status to the board (manual 11.5).
n.2: An end stage report is produced at the end of a stage, not at regular intervals during it (manual 11.5).
n.3: An exception report is raised when stage or project tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, not at regular intervals (manual 11.5).

4.q: Which term describes a prioritized list of measurable criteria that the project product must meet before the user will accept it?
o: User's quality expectations
Acceptance criteria
Quality specifications
Quality tolerance
4.w: Acceptance criteria are a prioritized list of measurable criteria the project product must meet before the user accepts it; they are recorded in the project product description (see manual 8.1.1).
