5.w: After an exception report, the board may request an exception plan. The project manager prepares it in managing a stage boundary, and the board approves it in directing a project, in authorize a stage or exception plan (see manual 18.3, 14.4.4).

n.1: Controlling a stage raises the exception report, but the exception plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary (manual 16.4.7, 18.3).
n.2: Controlling a stage is the project manager's process and cannot approve plans for the board (manual 14.4.4).
n.3: The board does not prepare plans; for a stage-level exception it approves the plan prepared by the project manager (manual 14.4.4, 18.3).

5.q: A request for change reaches the decide step of the issues technique. Which set lists typical decision choices available to the person or group with authority?
o: Avoid, reduce, transfer or share the matter with another party
Accept the matter, enhance it, exploit it or prepare a contingent plan
Escalate it to the business layer, close it, or record it as a lesson
Approve, reject, ask for an exception plan or request more information
5.w: Typical decisions on a request for change are to approve it, reject it, ask for an exception plan or request more information (see manual 10.3.1.4, tab 10.1).

n.0: Avoid, reduce, transfer and share are risk responses to threats, not decisions on a request for change (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.1: Accept, enhance, exploit and contingent plans are also risk responses, chosen in the risk technique (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.2: The project board escalates to the business layer only where project tolerance is threatened, and an unresolved request is not closed or turned into a lesson (manual 10.3.1.4, 11.3).

5.q: Which aspect of project performance helps the project management team understand who the project is for and what must be achieved to justify the investment?
o: Scope
Quality
Sustainability
Benefits
5.w: The benefits aspect asks who the project is for: the team must understand the project's purpose and what must be achieved to justify its investment (see manual 1.4).

n.0: Scope is about what the project will deliver, not who it is for or why the investment is justified.
n.1: Quality is about products being fit for purpose.
n.2: Sustainability is about the project's impact on its environment and the sustainability targets for its work and products.

5.q: How many organizational levels does PRINCE2 describe for a project, and how many of them make up the project management team?
o: Three levels, all of which make up the project management team
Four levels, all of which make up the project management team
Five levels, of which three make up the project management team
Four levels, of which three make up the project management team
5.w: There are four levels: the business layer (commissioning), directing, managing and delivering. The last three form the project management team; the business layer sits outside it (see manual 6.2, fig 6.2).

n.0: There are four levels, not three; the fourth, the business layer, sits outside the project management team (manual fig 6.2).
n.1: The business layer is one of the four levels but is not part of the project management team (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: PRINCE2 describes four levels, not five (manual fig 6.2).

5.q: A new team member asks what PRINCE2 means by the word 'issue'. Which definition should the project manager give?
o: An uncertain event that, should it occur, will affect the achievement of the project's objectives
An event relevant to the project that requires project management consideration
A situation where a deviation beyond the agreed tolerance levels can be forecast
A modification to an approved product that forms part of the project baseline
5.w: An issue is an event relevant to the project that requires project management consideration, and it can be raised by anyone at any time (see manual 10.1).

n.0: This defines a risk, which is uncertain; an issue is an event that needs consideration now (manual 9.1).
n.2: This defines an exception, which is handled through the progress practice (manual 11.1).
n.3: This defines a change; a change may arise from an issue, but the two terms are not the same (manual 10.1).

5.q: On a small, low-risk project, the board agrees that minor issues will be kept in a simple shared list reviewed at weekly team meetings, while requests for change still receive an issue report. Which principle is being applied?
o: Manage by stages
Focus on products
Tailor to suit the project
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
5.w: Adapting the formality of issue control and the form of management products to the project's size and risk is tailoring: controls are fitted to the project's scale, complexity and risk (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Manage by stages concerns planning and controlling the project stage by stage; the arrangement here adjusts how formal the issue controls are (manual 2.4).
n.1: Focus on products concerns defining and delivering products; the choice here is about the formality of controls (manual 2.6).
n.3: This principle concerns agreed roles and relationships; the arrangement here changes how formal the issue controls are (manual 2.3).

5.q: In the plans practice, who is responsible for providing the planning standards required by the business?
o: Project support
The business layer
Project assurance
The project manager
5.w: Among the planning areas of focus, the business layer provides the planning standards required by the business and sets project tolerances (see manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

n.0: Project support assists with compiling plans and maintaining planning tools; it does not set the business's planning standards (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).
n.2: Project assurance reviews stage and project progress against agreed tolerances; the standards come from the business layer (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).
n.3: The project manager prepares plans in line with the business's standards and decides how stages are applied (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

5.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
A project that is not part of a programme or portfolio and reports to a business unit is described as a [?] project.
o: linear
commercial
standalone
hybrid
5.w: A project may be standalone, reporting to a business unit, or part of a programme or portfolio (see manual 1.5 and fig 1.2).

n.0: Linear-sequential is a delivery approach, not a description of where the project sits in the organization (manual 1.5.3).
n.1: A commercial context is about customer and supplier relationships, which can apply whether or not the project sits in a programme (manual 1.5).
n.3: Hybrid is a delivery approach combining linear-sequential and iterative-incremental working, not an organizational context (manual 1.5.3).

5.q: As a delivery stage closes, the project manager gives the project board an end stage report so that it can decide whether to authorize the next stage. Which type of control is this, and why?
o: Time-driven, because stages have a fixed length set by the board
Time-driven, because it is a report from the PM to the board
Event-driven, because it is triggered by the end of a stage
Event-driven, because it is triggered by a forecast tolerance breach
5.w: The end stage report is an event-driven control: the event that triggers it is the end of a stage, at which the board decides whether to continue (see manual 11.2.2).

n.0: Stage length is chosen to suit the project rather than fixed, and the end stage report is classed as event-driven because the end of the stage triggers it (manual 2.4, 11.2.2).
n.1: Who sends a report does not decide its type: the highlight report also goes from the project manager to the board but is time-driven (manual 11.2.2).
n.3: A forecast breach of tolerance triggers an exception report, not an end stage report (manual 11.2.6).

5.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
When a gap in a team member's competence is identified, PRINCE2 suggests mitigations such as [?] the person or shifting responsibility for certain tasks to more appropriate people.
o: auditing
upskilling
escalating
rewarding
5.w: PRINCE2 says competency and capability gaps should be identified and mitigated, for example by upskilling or by shifting responsibility for certain tasks to more appropriate people (see manual 3.3.2).

n.0: Auditing checks compliance; it does not close a gap in someone's skills (manual 3.3.2).
n.2: Escalation is used when a decision could affect other areas or tolerances are threatened; it does not close a competency gap (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Rewards such as pay and career progression are often outside the project manager's remit and do not address a competency gap (manual 3.3).

5.q: A project manager from the IT department must lead finance and HR staff who report to other directors. Which approach reflects PRINCE2's guidance?
o: Ask the finance and HR directors to transfer their staff to the IT department for the project
Escalate to the project board each time a team member disagrees with an instruction
Use persuasion and influence, building key relationships with the staff and their directors
Treat the project's role descriptions as giving line authority over these staff members
5.w: When leading people beyond the project's direct authority, PRINCE2 favours leadership through persuading, influencing and co-creating, with a focus on key relationships (see manual 3.3, 3.3.1).

n.0: PRINCE2 expects project teams to work across organizational boundaries; moving staff between departments is not the guidance (manual 3.3).
n.1: Escalation is for decisions that could affect other areas of the project or threaten tolerances, not for everyday disagreements (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Role descriptions define project responsibilities; they do not create line authority over people who report elsewhere (manual 3.3.1).

5.q:
Which two statements are objectives of the 'managing a stage boundary' process?
1. To report progress to the board at the frequency agreed for highlight reports.
2. To review and, if necessary, update the project initiation documentation.
3. To authorize the start of the next stage on behalf of the project board.
4. To record lessons that can help later stages of this project or other projects.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
5.w: Statements 2 and 4 are correct. At a stage boundary the PID is reviewed and updated where needed, and lessons that can help later stages or other projects are recorded (see manual 18.2).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: highlight reporting is part of controlling a stage (manual 16.4.8). Statement 2 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 4.
n.1: Statements 1 and 3 are both wrong. Highlight reporting is part of controlling a stage (manual 16.4.8), and the next stage is authorized by the board in directing a project (manual 14.4.4).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: the project manager requests the next stage, and the board authorizes it in directing a project (manual 14.4.4). Statement 4 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 2.

5.q: During initiation, which objective of initiating a project is mainly addressed by agreeing the communication management approach?
o: How baselines will be established and controlled
How the required quality will be achieved
How risks will be identified, assessed and controlled
Who needs information, in what format and at what time
5.w: The communication management approach sets out how information will flow to and from stakeholders, which meets the initiation objective of understanding who needs information, in what format and when (see manual 15.2, 15.4.2).

n.0: How baselines are established and controlled is addressed through the issue management approach and change control (manual 15.2, 15.4.2).
n.1: How quality will be achieved is set out in the quality management approach (manual 15.2, 15.4.2).
n.2: How risks will be identified, assessed and controlled is set out in the risk management approach (manual 15.2, 15.4.2).

5.q: Where in the business case lifecycle is most of the work of confirming benefits carried out?
o: During initiation, when the project board approves the full business case
After the project has closed, in benefits reviews carried out by the business
At the end of starting up a project, when initiation is authorized
During each work package, when the checkpoint reports are reviewed
5.w: Confirming benefits mostly happens after closure through post-project benefits reviews by the business; some benefits may be confirmed during the project where products are released in stages. Confirmation continues outside the project lifecycle (see manual 5.2.1, fig 5.3, 5.3.1).

n.0: Approving the full business case authorizes the project; no benefits have been realized yet to confirm (manual 14.4.2, 5.3.1).
n.2: At that point the board checks the outline business case to authorize initiation; benefits are confirmed much later (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: Checkpoint reports give work package status to the project manager; they are not where benefits are confirmed (manual 11.5, 5.3.1).

5.q: At each stage boundary, a project board needs a sound basis for deciding whether to keep investing in the project. Which practice provides the mechanisms for that judgement, and why?
o: Quality, because it confirms that the products meet the users' requirements
Business case, because it judges whether the project remains worth the investment
Organizing, because it sets out who is accountable for each decision
Issues, because it assesses whether proposed changes are worth making
5.w: The business case practice exists to establish mechanisms to judge whether the project remains desirable, viable and achievable, supporting the board's decisions on continued investment (see manual 5.1).

n.0: The quality practice documents the user's requirements and how they will be met; it does not judge whether the investment is still worthwhile (manual 8.1).
n.2: The organizing practice establishes the structure of accountability and responsibilities, the 'who', not whether the investment is worthwhile (manual 6.1).
n.3: The issues practice assesses issues and controls changes to baselines; the judgement on continued investment in the whole project comes from the business case practice (manual 10.1, 5.1).

5.q: How is the project product description used when the project is being closed?
o: To confirm that the products meet the acceptance criteria
To pass the lessons from the project on to future projects
To set the benefits tolerances for the post-project benefits review
To record the final status of every product in the product register
5.w: The project product description holds the acceptance criteria and acceptance methods for the project, and is used during closure to confirm that the project product is acceptable (see manual 7.5).

n.1: Lessons are passed on through the lessons report, not the project product description (manual 11.5).
n.2: Benefits tolerances are held in the benefits management approach, not the project product description (manual 5.5).
n.3: Product status is kept in the product register within the project log; the project product description defines acceptance (manual 4.3.2, 7.5).

5.q: How does the business case develop during the initiating a project process?
o: The outline business case is developed into a full business case for board approval
The business case is created for the first time, based on the project mandate
The full business case is summarized into an outline version for the PID
The business case is passed to the business layer, which approves it before authorization
5.w: During initiation the outline business case from starting up is updated with costs and timescales from the project plan and the aggregated risks, giving the full business case that the board approves when it authorizes the project (see manual 15.4.5, 14.4.2).

n.1: The business case already exists in outline form, created in starting up a project (manual 13.4.3).
n.2: The direction is the reverse: the outline version from starting up is expanded into the full business case (manual 15.4.5).
n.3: The project board approves the full business case when it authorizes the project; it is not sent to the business layer for approval (manual 14.4.2).

5.q: How does the plans practice support the control of a project through the progress practice?
o: Plans record the actual cost and completion date of each product as it is handed over
Approved plans are the baseline that actual progress is compared with
Plans set the business's risk appetite that the board uses to judge progress
Plans hold the lessons log entries that are reviewed when each stage ends
5.w: Plans facilitate control: once approved, a plan is the baseline that the progress practice compares actual achievement with, so that deviations can be controlled (see manual 7.1, 11.1).

n.0: Actual progress is captured in progress reports and the product register, not in the plan itself (manual 11.5, 4.3.2).
n.2: Risk appetite is set by the business, not by a plan (manual 9.2.1).
n.3: The lessons log is part of the project log, not a plan (manual 4.3.2).

6.q: Which principle requires a project to have a justifiable reason to start, with that reason remaining valid and being revalidated throughout the project's life?
o: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Ensure continued business justification
Focus on products
Manage by exception
6.w: Ensure continued business justification requires a justifiable reason to start the project, which must stay valid and be revalidated throughout; if it lapses, the project should be stopped (manual 2.1).

n.0: Defining roles, responsibilities and relationships makes sure the business, user and supplier interests are represented; it does not require a reason for the investment (manual 2.3).
n.2: Focus on products is about defining and delivering products to agreed quality, not about the reason for the investment (manual 2.6).
n.3: Manage by exception sets tolerances to delegate authority between levels; it does not require a justifiable reason for the project (manual 2.5).

6.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
In starting up a project, the [?] activity decides how the work will be tackled, for example in-house or by third parties, and which delivery method will be used.
o: select the project approach
assemble the project brief
prepare the outline business case
plan the initiation stage
6.w: Select the project approach decides how the work of the project will be approached, including in-house or external delivery, build or buy, and the delivery method (see manual 13.4.5).

n.1: Assemble the project brief brings the starting up products together; the approach it contains is decided in select the project approach (manual 13.4).
n.2: Prepare the outline business case sets out the justification and creates the project product description, not the delivery approach (manual 13.4.3).
n.3: Plan the initiation stage plans the work of initiation, not how the whole project's work will be delivered (manual 13.4.7).

6.q: A project manager encourages a decision about a minor product feature to be made by the team member who understands it best, and asks for it to be escalated if it could affect other teams. Which principle is being applied?
o: Manage by exception
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Learn from experience
Focus on products
6.w: PRINCE2 7 applies manage by exception to people: decisions are made at the most local level where the knowledge resides, and escalated when they could affect other areas (manual 3.5.1).

n.1: The action is about where a decision is made and when it is escalated, which PRINCE2 links to manage by exception rather than to defining roles (manual 3.5.1).
n.2: No lessons are being sought or shared; the action concerns the level at which a decision is made (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: The feature is a product, but the action concerns who decides and when to escalate, not defining the product (manual 3.5.1).

6.q: Which statement best explains how the 'focus on products' principle supports change control?
o: Changes are approved by the team manager who builds the product
Agreed product definitions give a baseline for judging changes
Products cannot be changed once their descriptions are written
Changes to products are deferred to the final stage for review
6.w: A product focus is the basis of planning, quality, scope and change control: with products clearly defined and agreed, a proposed change can be judged against that baseline (manual 2.6).

n.0: Team managers build products; changes are decided by the board or a change authority, not by the team manager (manual ch 10).
n.2: Agreed products can be changed through issue and change control; the definitions make change visible rather than forbidden (manual 2.6, ch 10).
n.3: Requests for change are handled as they arise through the issues practice, not saved for the final stage (manual ch 10).

6.q: What does the stakeholder analysis identify in PRINCE2?
o: The roles that will approve each request for change and the limits on their authority
Who is impacted by the outcome or the delivery, and who can influence success or failure
The current, interim and target states and the activities that support each transition
The products to be delivered, their quality criteria and the people who will review them
6.w: The stakeholder analysis in the communication management approach identifies who is impacted by the outcome or the delivery process, and who can influence the project's success or failure (see manual 3.4).

n.0: Who approves requests for change, and within what limits, is set out in the issue management approach (manual 10.2.4, 10.5).
n.2: States and enabling activities are described in the change management approach (manual 3.2.1).
n.3: Products, their quality criteria and reviewers are set out in product descriptions and the quality management approach (manual 8.5).

6.q:
Which two statements about the features and benefits of PRINCE2 are true?
1. PRINCE2 is designed for one industry and its engineering practices.
2. PRINCE2 is designed to work with PeopleCert's guides on programme, portfolio and risk management.
3. PRINCE2 replaces the specialist techniques used to design and build products.
4. PRINCE2 promotes learning and continual improvement across the organization.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
6.w: Statement 2 describes PRINCE2 being part of an integrated suite of methods, and statement 4 describes increased organizational maturity (see manual 1.6).

n.0: Statement 2 is true, but statement 1 is false: PRINCE2 is not specific to any industry or engineering practice.
n.1: Both are false: PRINCE2 is not industry-specific, and it works alongside specialist techniques rather than replacing them.
n.3: Statement 4 is true, but statement 3 is false: PRINCE2 is used alongside specialist, industry-specific models rather than replacing them.

6.q: Which statement correctly describes the request project authorization activity?
o: The project manager asks the board for authority to deliver the project, with or without a formal meeting
The executive asks the business layer to approve the project brief and the outline business case
The project manager asks the board to approve the initiation stage plan before initiation starts
The project manager asks team managers to accept the work packages for the first delivery stage
6.w: Request project authorization is the last activity of initiating a project: the project manager contacts the board to request authority to deliver the project, which may be done with or without a formal meeting (see manual 15.4.7).

n.1: The project brief and outline business case were approved by the board in authorize initiation, not by the business layer (manual 14.4.1).
n.2: The initiation stage plan was approved before initiation began, in authorize initiation (manual 14.4.1).
n.3: Work packages are agreed with team managers in controlling a stage after the board has authorized the project and the stage (manual 16.1, 14.4.4).

6.q: A threat might arise in nine months' time, but if it occurred it would stop all work within hours. Which statement correctly describes this threat?
o: It has a high proximity, as its impact would arrive within hours
It has a low probability, as it may not occur for nine months
It is not near in time, but it has a high velocity
It has a low impact, as the project has time to prepare for it
6.w: Nine months away describes its proximity (not near). Stopping work within hours of occurring describes a high velocity, so a contingent plan may be needed well in advance (see manual 9.2).

n.0: Proximity is how near in time the risk might occur (nine months here); the speed of the impact is velocity (manual 9.2).
n.1: Timing does not set probability; how likely the threat is to occur is a separate estimate (manual 9.2).
n.3: Impact is the effect on objectives if it occurs; halting all work is a severe effect whatever the timing (manual 9.2).

6.q: Which delivery approach typically defines products in detail up front, with stages following one another, such as design, then build, then test?
o: Iterative-incremental
Hybrid
Agile
Linear-sequential
6.w: In a linear-sequential approach, work moves through a sequence of stages and products are defined in detail at the outset (see manual 1.5.3 and 7.3.1.1.3).

n.0: Iterative-incremental work evolves products through repeated cycles, refining criteria as it goes rather than fixing detail up front.
n.1: Hybrid mixes linear and iterative work; the description is of a purely sequential approach.
n.2: Agile ways of working are iterative-incremental and refine products in cycles, not in one sequence defined up front.

6.q: Which step of the organizational design and development technique involves determining the people and resources needed and implementing integrated working practices?
o: Develop the project ecosystem
Design the project ecosystem
Understand the organizational ecosystem
Transition the project into the organizational ecosystem
6.w: Designing the project ecosystem concerns how to organize work and people: determining people and resources, implementing integrated working practices and developing project behaviours and culture, shaped by the WBS and the commercial management approach (see manual 6.3.1.2).

n.0: Developing the project ecosystem is the ongoing development that follows the design, such as onboarding and skills assessment (manual 6.3.1.3).
n.2: Understanding the organizational ecosystem looks at the existing organizations before any project design is done (manual 6.3.1.1).
n.3: Transitioning the project hands products, people and learning back to the business at closure (manual fig 6.5).

6.q: On a small project with one delivery team, which roles may the project manager also perform?
o: Team manager and project support
Executive and team manager
Project assurance and project support
Project assurance and team manager
6.w: Depending on the project's scale, complexity, skills and capacity, the project manager may also perform the team manager and project support roles (see manual 6.2.4).

n.1: The executive role cannot be combined with the project manager role, however small the project (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Project assurance cannot be done by the project manager or project support, and must be kept separate from support (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Team manager is acceptable, but project assurance must be independent of the project manager (manual 6.2.4).

6.q:
Which two statements about the project log are correct?
1. The project log is baselined when the project is authorized and put under change control.
2. The project log holds the daily log, lessons log and the issue, risk, quality and product registers.
3. The project log is passed to the business after closure so that its registers stay open.
4. The project log is started in starting up a project and completed during initiation.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
6.w: Statements 2 and 4 are correct. The project log is the dynamic record holding the daily log, lessons log and the issue, risk, quality and product registers; it is set up in starting up a project and completed in initiation (see manual 4.3.2).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: it is the PID that is baselined and placed under change control; the project log is a dynamic record (manual 4.3.1, 15.4.6). Statement 2 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 4.
n.1: Statements 1 and 3 are both wrong. The PID, not the project log, is baselined (manual 15.4.6), and the project log is closed in closing a project (manual 19.4.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: the project log is closed in closing a project (manual 19.4.1). Statement 4 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 2.

6.q: Which feature of PRINCE2 keeps project participants focused on whether the project remains viable in relation to its business case objectives?
o: Proven
Outcome-focused
Flexible
Common language and concepts
6.w: PRINCE2 is outcome-focused: it keeps participants focused on the viability of the project against its business case objectives (see manual 1.6).

n.0: Proven means it is based on established practice and governance, not that it keeps attention on viability.
n.2: Flexible means the method can be tailored to the organizations involved.
n.3: Common language and concepts is about a shared vocabulary, not a focus on viability.

6.q: Which statement describes quality control in PRINCE2?
o: Independently checking that the project's quality control measures are appropriate for the business
Monitoring specific products and their development activities to see whether they comply with standards
Capturing the quality specifications and writing the product descriptions for the stage
Transferring ownership of the project product to the project board on behalf of the users
6.w: Quality control consists of the procedures that monitor specific products and the activities that develop them, to check they comply with the relevant standards and to minimize causes of unsatisfactory performance (see manual 8.2.2).

n.0: Independently checking that the quality control measures are appropriate is quality assurance, carried out outside the project management team (manual 8.2.3).
n.2: Capturing quality specifications and writing product descriptions is quality planning (manual 8.2.1).
n.3: Transferring ownership of the project product is project acceptance, the final part of the quality technique (manual 8.3.1.3).

6.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

Stakeholder engagement starts by identifying the stakeholders and the key [?] who can shape whether the change succeeds.
o: risk owners
change authorities
influencers
suppliers
6.w: PRINCE2 stakeholder engagement involves identifying stakeholders and key influencers, then building relationships with them (see manual 3.2.2).

n.0: Risk owners manage specific risks under the risk practice; they are not the people stakeholder engagement seeks out (manual ch 9).
n.1: A change authority approves requests for change within delegated limits under the issues practice (manual 10.2.4).
n.3: Suppliers are one stakeholder group; the term PRINCE2 uses for people who can shape the change is key influencers (manual 3.2.2).

6.q: In the quality management technique, what does project acceptance typically achieve?
o: It transfers ownership of the project product from the users to the supplier
It confirms that the quality management approach can be approved by the board
It records the planned dates of quality checks in the quality register
It transfers ownership of the project product to the project board for the users
6.w: Acceptance of the project product typically transfers ownership or responsibility from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the user (see manual 8.3.1.3).

n.0: The transfer runs the other way: from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the users (manual 8.3.1.3).
n.1: The quality management approach is approved by the board during initiation, long before project acceptance (manual 15.4.2, tab 14.3).
n.2: Recording planned dates of quality checks belongs to quality planning and control through the quality register, not to acceptance (manual 8.3.1.2, 8.5).

6.q: A team manager finds that a records database already built for the project can also be used by a second department with no extra work, giving that department benefits nobody had expected. Which type of issue is this?
o: Business opportunity
Request for change
Off-specification
Event external to the project
6.w: A business opportunity is an issue representing unanticipated positive consequences for the project or the user organization, as with the unexpected extra use of the database (see manual 10.1).

n.1: No change to an approved product is being proposed; the database can be reused as it is (manual 10.2.3).
n.2: The database is not failing its quality specifications; the event is positive (manual 10.2.3).
n.3: The discovery comes from the project's own work on the database, not from an event outside the project (manual 10.1).

6.q: In which process is the communication management approach first created, alongside the other management approaches?
o: Starting up a project
Initiating a project
Controlling a stage
Managing a stage boundary
6.w: The management approaches, including the communication management approach, are created in initiating a project during 'agree the management approaches', and are then reviewed at stage boundaries and at closure (see manual 15.4.2, 3.4).

n.0: Starting up a project produces the project brief and initiation stage plan; the management approaches are agreed in initiation (manual ch 13, 15.4.2).
n.2: Controlling a stage uses the approach, for example for the frequency of highlight reports, but does not first create it (manual 16.4.8).
n.3: Managing a stage boundary reviews and updates the approaches; it is not where they are first created (manual ch 18).

6.q: Which is an objective of the 'managing a stage boundary' process?
o: To give the project manager accurate progress information at an agreed frequency
To check that the users accept the project product before closure
To keep the risks and issues that arise in the stage under control
To assure the board that all products in the stage plan are complete and approved
6.w: Managing a stage boundary aims to assure the board that all products in the current stage plan have been completed and approved, among its other objectives (see manual 18.2).

n.0: This is an objective of managing product delivery, where checkpoint reports go to the project manager (manual 17.2).
n.1: This is an objective of closing a project (manual 19.2).
n.2: This is an objective of controlling a stage (manual 16.2).

6.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

Gathering and acting on [?] helps keep the project's defined ways of working aligned with how people actually work.
o: checkpoint reports
quality records
exception reports
feedback
6.w: PRINCE2 recommends gathering and acting on feedback so that the defined ways of working stay aligned with the way people really work (see manual 3.2.3).

n.0: Checkpoint reports give the project manager the status of a work package; they are not the mechanism PRINCE2 names for aligning ways of working with culture (manual ch 11).
n.1: Quality records are evidence that quality activities were carried out on products (manual ch 8).
n.2: Exception reports warn the board of a forecast breach of tolerance (manual 11.2.6).

6.q: Which activity is an example of leadership rather than management, as PRINCE2 describes them?
o: Instructing a team member to carry out a task using the agreed procedure
Confirming that work was carried out in line with the agreed ways of working
Seeking regular feedback so that team members stay aligned with the objectives
Recording the current status of each product in the product register
6.w: Seeking regular feedback to keep team members aligned with the project's objectives is part of the PRINCE2 description of leadership (see manual 3.3).

n.0: Instructing the execution of a task in line with agreed ways of working is the definition of management (manual 3.3).
n.1: Checking that tasks follow the agreed ways of working is management control, not leadership (manual 3.3).
n.3: Maintaining the product register is an administrative task, typically done by project support, not an act of leadership (manual 6.2.4).

6.q: A new payroll system is delivered on time and within budget, but it calculates some deductions wrongly and cannot be used as specified. Which aspect of project performance has the project failed to meet?
o: Scope
Quality
Benefits
Risk
6.w: The quality aspect is about products being fit for purpose: finishing on time and within budget is of little value if what is delivered does not work as specified (see manual 1.4).

n.0: Scope is about what the project will deliver; the payroll system was delivered, but it does not work as specified, which is a quality failure.
n.2: Benefits may later suffer, but the aspect describing a product that does not work as specified is quality.
n.3: Risk is about limits on the plan's aggregated risks; a product failing to meet its specification is a quality shortfall.

6.q:
Which two statements about PRINCE2 roles are correct?

1. The executive can delegate accountability for the project's success to the project manager.
2. On a small project, the project manager may also perform the team manager role.
3. The senior user is accountable for the approach taken to capture user requirements.
4. The senior supplier is responsible for the business case and continued business justification.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
6.w: The project manager may also perform the team manager role depending on scale and capacity (statement 2), and the senior user is accountable for the approach to capturing user requirements (statement 3) (see manual 6.2.4.2, 6.2.4.5).

n.0: Statement 1 is false: the executive's accountability cannot be delegated (manual 6.2.4.1).
n.1: Statements 1 and 4 are both false: executive accountability cannot be delegated, and the business case belongs to the executive (manual 6.2.4.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is false: the executive, not the senior supplier, is responsible for the business case (manual 6.2.4.1).

6.q: A water company's project board expects many minor requests for change during the next stage and does not want to meet for each one. Which arrangement is consistent with PRINCE2?
o: Delegate approval of minor changes to a change authority, with defined limits and a change budget
Ask project support to approve minor changes, as support already administers the issue register
Delegate approval of all changes to project assurance, as assurance is independent of the manager
Ask the business layer to approve each request for change so that the board keeps its independence
6.w: The board may delegate approval of requests for change to a change authority (or the project manager) within defined limits, ideally with a change budget, and reviews this at each stage boundary (see manual 10.2.4, 10.2.5).

n.1: Project support provides administration for the project manager; it is not given authority to approve changes (manual 6.2.4.8, 10.2.4).
n.2: Project assurance advises and monitors on behalf of the board members; approving changes is a delegated change authority role (manual 6.2.4.7, 10.2.4).
n.3: The business layer deals with project-level matters such as project tolerances; routine requests for change are handled by the board or its delegated change authority (manual fig 6.2, 10.2.4).

6.q: A project board approves an exception plan in response to a forecast breach of stage tolerance. What happens to the plans for the current stage?
o: The exception plan is added to the affected team plan for that work
The exception plan becomes the project plan for the rest of the project
The exception plan replaces the stage plan, and a revised stage begins
The exception plan is filed and the original stage plan continues
6.w: When approved, the exception plan replaces the stage plan; its approval marks a stage boundary and a revised stage begins (for example stage 2 becomes stage 2a) (see manual 11.3.1).

n.0: Exception plans are never used to replace a team plan; a stage-level exception plan replaces the stage plan (manual 11.3.1).
n.1: A stage-level exception plan replaces the stage plan, not the project plan (manual 11.3.1).
n.3: Once approved, the exception plan takes the place of the stage plan; the original plan does not continue (manual 11.3.1).

6.q:
Which two statements about the 'learn from experience' principle are correct?
1. Lessons should be drawn from successes as well as from mistakes.
2. Lessons are gathered at closure rather than during the project.
3. Lessons are kept within the project rather than given to others.
4. Lessons should be shared so that other projects can apply them.
o: 1 and 4
1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
6.w: Statement 1 is correct: the principle covers learning from both mistakes and successes. Statement 4 is correct: lessons are shared for others to apply (manual 2.2).

n.1: Statement 2 is wrong: lessons are sought before the project, throughout it and at closure, not left to the end (manual 2.2).
n.2: Statements 2 and 3 are both wrong: lessons are gathered throughout the project and are passed on to others (manual 2.2).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: the principle expects lessons to be shared with others, for example through a lessons report (manual 2.2).

6.q: A project manager is starting a stage with a newly formed team that has no experience of PRINCE2. What does PRINCE2 guidance suggest about the frequency of progress reporting?
o: Report less often at first so that the new team can concentrate on building the products
Report more often at first and reduce the frequency as confidence in the team grows
Keep the reporting frequency fixed for the whole project as stated in the project mandate
Replace checkpoint reports with end stage reports until the team has gained experience
6.w: Reporting frequency should reflect the level of control required; an inexperienced team usually needs more frequent reporting, which can be relaxed as confidence grows (see manual 11.2.4).

n.0: PRINCE2 suggests the reverse: an inexperienced team needs more frequent reporting until confidence grows (manual 11.2.4).
n.2: Reporting frequency reflects the level of control needed and can be adjusted; it is agreed between management levels, not fixed in the mandate (manual 11.2.4).
n.3: End stage reports are event-driven reports to the board and cannot replace the regular checkpoint reports on work packages (manual 11.2.2, 11.5).

6.q: According to PRINCE2, what is the main aim of co-creating products and agreed ways of working?
o: To reduce the number of management products that the project needs
To transfer accountability for the products from the executive to the users
To ensure they are adopted by the project and organizational ecosystems
To let the supplier fix the project's scope before initiation begins
6.w: Co-creation involves users and key influencers in design so that the resulting products and ways of working are adopted by the project and organizational ecosystems (see manual 3.3).

n.0: Reducing or merging management products is a matter for tailoring, not the aim of co-creation (manual 2.7).
n.1: The executive's accountability cannot be delegated, and co-creation does not move it (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Co-creation brings users and key influencers into design; it does not hand scope decisions to the supplier (manual 3.3).

6.q: During which process is the change management approach created?
o: Starting up a project
Initiating a project
Managing a stage boundary
Directing a project
6.w: All nine management approaches, including the change management approach, are created in initiating a project, in the 'agree the management approaches' activity (see manual 15.4.2).

n.0: Starting up a project produces the project brief and initiation stage plan; the management approaches come later, in initiation (manual ch 13, 15.4.2).
n.2: Managing a stage boundary reviews and, if needed, updates the management approaches; it does not first create them (manual ch 18).
n.3: In directing a project the board approves the PID, including the approaches, in 'authorize the project'; it does not create them (manual ch 14).

6.q: Which statement about choosing risk responses is correct?
o: Avoidance should be chosen for each threat where possible, as it gives the project the lowest exposure
Threats and opportunities use identical response types, so one response list covers both of them
The best response depends on the situation and type of risk, and threats and opportunities can differ
Accept is reserved for opportunities, as each threat needs definite action from the risk owner
6.w: PRINCE2 says the best response depends on the particular situation and type of risk, and it gives different response types for threats and opportunities (see manual 9.2.3.1, table 9.1).

n.0: Avoiding every threat can be costly or impossible; the choice depends on the situation and type of risk (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.1: Some responses are specific: avoid and reduce for threats, exploit and enhance for opportunities (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.3: Accept applies to threats as well as opportunities; taking the chance and monitoring can be the right choice (manual 9.2.3.1).

6.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
The [?] step of the business case technique assesses whether the intended benefits have been realized, or will be, and is carried out mostly after the project has closed.
o: check
maintain
confirm
develop
6.w: The confirm step assesses whether intended benefits have been (or will be) realized; much of it happens in post-project benefits reviews carried out by the business (see manual 5.3.1).

n.0: Check assesses whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable at key decision points within the project (manual 5.3.1).
n.1: Maintain updates the business case at each stage end with progress data and forecasts (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: Develop creates the outline and then the full business case before and during initiation (manual 5.3.1).

6.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
In the plans practice, the [?] defines the tolerances for each stage and approves the stage plans.
o: senior user
project manager
executive
business layer
6.w: Among the planning areas of focus, the executive defines tolerances for each stage and approves stage plans (see manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

n.0: The senior user makes sure plans remain consistent with the user perspective; stage tolerances are defined by the executive (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).
n.1: The project manager prepares stage plans and sets work package tolerances; the executive defines stage tolerances (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).
n.3: The business layer sets tolerances for the project as a whole, not for each stage (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

6.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
A [?] is a measurable decline resulting from an outcome that the investing organization perceives as negative, and which detracts from one or more business objectives.
o: risk effect
dis-benefit
off-specification
output
6.w: A dis-benefit is the measurable decline resulting from an outcome perceived as negative by the investing organization, detracting from business objectives. Dis-benefits are identified and managed in the business case (see manual 5.1).

n.0: A risk effect is the impact an uncertain risk event would have on objectives; a dis-benefit is an expected, measurable decline caused by an outcome (manual 9.1, 5.1).
n.2: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications; it is a type of issue, not a decline caused by an outcome (manual 10.1).
n.3: An output is the deliverable of an activity, not a measurable decline (manual 5.1).

6.q: Under which heading of the business case is the period over which the project will run, and the period over which benefits will be realized, recorded?
o: Reasons
Expected benefits
Costs
Time
6.w: The 'time' heading covers both the period over which the project runs and the period over which the benefits will be realized (see manual 5.5).

n.0: The reasons heading explains why the project is needed and how it enables business objectives (manual 5.5).
n.1: Expected benefits are stated in measurable terms against the situation before the project; the periods involved are recorded under time (manual 5.5).
n.2: The costs heading covers project costs and ongoing operations and maintenance costs with their funding (manual 5.5).

6.q: Why must project support be kept separate from project assurance?
o: Because project support is funded from the change budget, while assurance is funded from the risk budget
Because project support reports to the business layer, while assurance reports to the project manager
Because project support works for the project manager, so combining them would weaken independent assurance
Because project support is an optional role, while assurance has to be carried out by external auditors
6.w: Project support is the project manager's responsibility, whereas assurance monitors the project independently of the project manager on behalf of the board, so keeping them apart maintains that independence (see manual 6.2.4.7, 6.2.4.8).

n.0: The change and risk budgets fund approved changes and risk responses; they are not why support and assurance are separated (manual 7.3.1, 10.2.5).
n.1: This reverses the lines: support is the project manager's responsibility, and assurance acts for the board members (manual 6.2.4.7, 6.2.4.8).
n.3: Assurance can be done by board members or people from the wider business as well as external parties; the reason for separation is independence (manual 6.2.4.7).

6.q: When does the project board approve the tailoring agreed for the project?
o: When authorizing initiation at the end of starting up
When giving ongoing direction during a delivery stage
When authorizing closure in the final stage
When authorizing the project and approving the PID
6.w: Tailoring decisions are recorded in the PID, which is assembled in initiating a project and approved by the board when it authorizes the project (see manual 2.7 and 15.4.6).

n.0: Authorizing initiation approves the project brief and initiation stage plan; the tailoring is agreed later, during initiation (manual ch 14, 15.4.1).
n.1: Giving ongoing direction responds to reports, requests and issues during a stage; approval of the PID and its tailoring comes when the board authorizes the project (manual ch 14).
n.2: Authorizing closure confirms the project can close; tailoring has to be approved before delivery begins (manual ch 19).

6.q: During a delivery stage, the project manager forecasts that the stage will exceed its cost tolerance. Which process does 'controlling a stage' send this to?
o: Managing product delivery, so the team manager can re-plan
Managing a stage boundary, to draw up an exception plan first
Closing a project, as the business case may no longer be viable
Directing a project, as the board set the stage tolerances
6.w: When stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, controlling a stage escalates it with an exception report to the project board in directing a project. The board set the stage tolerances, so the decision is the board's (see manual 16.3, 16.4.7).

n.0: Managing product delivery works to work package tolerances set by the project manager; a forecast breach of stage tolerance goes to the board (manual 16.4.7, 17.2).
n.1: An exception plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary only after the board has seen the exception report and asked for one (manual ch 18, 14.4.3).
n.2: A forecast cost overrun is an exception for the board to decide on; premature closure happens only if the board orders it (manual 16.4.7, 19.3).

6.q: Why is it important to understand which of a project's constraints take precedence when planning?
o: It guides the choice of approach and how much tolerance is set for each aspect
It decides which role approves the project plan in directing a project
It lets the project manager change the business case targets without approval
It determines how many team plans each team manager must produce
6.w: Understanding which constraints take precedence is crucial to choosing the right approaches and setting tolerances, for example a tight time tolerance where a fixed date matters most (see manual 7.2.4).

n.1: The project board approves the project plan when it authorizes the project, whatever the constraints (manual 7.2.2.1).
n.2: The project manager cannot change approved targets; deviations beyond tolerance are escalated (manual 7.2.4).
n.3: Team plans are optional; the reason for understanding constraints is to guide the approach and tolerances, not to fix how many team plans exist (manual 7.2.2.3, 7.2.4).

6.q: Which situation may require a project to align its processes, practices and documents with two or more quality systems?
o: A project manager who is new to the business
A commercial customer-supplier relationship
A single internal team in one location
Updating the business case at stage boundaries
6.w: A commercial customer-supplier relationship is an influence that gives cause to tailor: the project may need to align its processes, practices and documentation with both parties' quality systems (see manual 2.7).

n.0: A new project manager may affect team capability, but it does not create a second quality system to align with (manual 2.7).
n.2: A single internal team in one location has one organization's quality system, so there is no second system to align with (manual 2.7).
n.3: Updating the business case at stage boundaries is normal practice in managing a stage boundary, not an influence that needs alignment of quality systems (manual ch 18).

6.q: A team manager resolves a minor scheduling clash within the team's work package because the team has the relevant knowledge, the solution stays within tolerance and no other area is affected. Which principle does this apply?
o: Manage by exception, as decisions sit at the most local level holding the knowledge
Manage by stages, as the decision is made within the current management stage
Focus on products, as the work package defines the products to be delivered
Learn from experience, as the team is drawing on lessons from earlier projects
6.w: The people element applies manage by exception by keeping decisions at the most local level where the knowledge to make and own them resides, escalating when other areas could be affected (see manual 3.5.1).

n.1: Manage by stages concerns planning and decision points at stage boundaries, and reviewing relationships there; the decision here is about where it is made (manual 3.5.1).
n.2: Focus on products is about defining and co-creating products; the situation concerns the level at which a decision is taken (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Nothing in the situation involves earlier lessons; the point is that the decision is made locally within tolerance (manual 3.5.1).

6.q: Before drafting the project brief, a project manager reads the lessons reports from two similar projects and talks to their project managers about what went wrong. Which principle is being applied?
o: Learn from experience
Manage by stages
Focus on products
Ensure continued business justification
6.w: Seeking lessons from previous similar projects before the project begins is learn from experience, applied in starting up a project through 'assess previous lessons' (manual 2.2, 13.4.2).

n.1: Nothing here concerns stage planning or decision points; the PM is gathering lessons (manual 2.4).
n.2: The PM is not defining products or quality criteria; reviewing past lessons is learn from experience (manual 2.6).
n.3: The PM is not testing whether the project is worth doing; the action is gathering lessons from earlier projects (manual 2.1).

6.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes quality assurance from project assurance?
o: Quality assurance is the senior user's responsibility; project assurance is the executive's
Quality assurance checks the business case; project assurance checks the specialist products
Quality assurance is independent of the project management team; project assurance of the project manager
Quality assurance is carried out by project support; project assurance by the business's quality office
6.w: Quality assurance is independent of the whole project management team, while project assurance is the board's responsibility and is independent of the project manager but not of the project (see manual 8.2.3).

n.0: Project assurance is shared by all board members for their own interests, and quality assurance is not a board role at all (manual 8.2.3, ch 6).
n.1: Quality assurance concerns the appropriateness of quality control measures, and project assurance covers business, user and supplier interests, not just products (manual 8.2.3, ch 6).
n.3: Project support cannot provide either form of assurance, and project assurance is done on behalf of the project board (manual 8.2.3, ch 6).

6.q: PRINCE2 includes three principal categories of stakeholder in the governance and management arrangements of every project. Which are these three project interests?
o: Business, programme and customer
Business, user and supplier
Directing, managing and delivering
Executive, sponsor and supplier
6.w: The three project interests are business, user and supplier, and all three are represented in the project management team through the project board (see manual 6.2.1, fig 6.1).

n.0: Programme and customer are not PRINCE2 project interests; 'customer' reflects older customer/supplier wording rather than the three v7 interests (manual 6.2.1).
n.2: Directing, managing and delivering are three of the four organizational levels, not the stakeholder interests (manual fig 6.2).
n.3: Sponsor is not a PRINCE2 role or interest, and the executive is a role that represents the business interest (manual 6.2.4).

6.q: A delivered brochure uses a slightly different shade of the brand colour from the one specified. The board decides that this is acceptable and that no rework is needed. What is this decision called?
o: Approving a request for change
Extending the stage tolerance
Reducing the project scope
Granting a concession
6.w: A concession is an off-specification that is accepted without corrective action; granting one is a decision option for an off-specification (see manual 10.3.1.4, tab 10.1).

n.0: A request for change proposes altering the baseline; here a product already falls short of its specification and is accepted as it is (manual 10.2.3).
n.1: Tolerances relate to forecast deviations beyond plan limits; accepting a product that misses its specification is not a tolerance change (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Nothing is removed from the scope; the product is still delivered and accepted despite the shortfall (manual 10.3.1.4).

6.q: A project has an initiation stage followed by three delivery stages, and no exceptions occur. How many stage plans will the project manager prepare in managing a stage boundary?
o: Four stage plans
Two stage plans
One stage plan
Three stage plans
6.w: The initiation stage plan is made in starting up a project. Each of the three delivery stages has its stage plan prepared near the end of the stage before it, in managing a stage boundary, giving three (see manual 7.2.2.2).

n.0: Four counts the initiation stage plan, which is made in starting up a project, not in managing a stage boundary (manual 7.2.2.2).
n.1: Two misses the plan for the first delivery stage, which is prepared at the end of the initiation stage (manual 7.2.2.2).
n.2: One would apply to a project with a single delivery stage; here each of the three delivery stages needs a stage plan (manual 7.2.2.2).

6.q:
Which two statements about the project initiation documentation (PID) are correct?
1. It is assembled during initiating a project and used to gain authorization for the project.
2. It is created in starting up a project to give a firm foundation for initiation.
3. The version used to gain authorization is baselined and later compared with actual performance.
4. It holds the daily log and lessons log so that they can be reviewed at each stage end.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
2 and 4
1 and 3
6.w: Statement 1 is correct: the PID is assembled in initiating a project from the products created or updated there, and is used to gain authorization. Statement 3 is correct: the authorized version is baselined and later used to compare performance, for example when evaluating the project (see manual 4.3.1, 15.4.6).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the product created in starting up a project as the foundation for initiation is the project brief, not the PID (manual 5.5).
n.1: Statement 2 is wrong: the project brief, not the PID, is created in starting up a project; the PID is assembled in initiation (manual 5.5, 4.3.1).
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: the project brief is created in starting up a project, and the daily log and lessons log are held in the project log, not the PID (manual 4.3.2).

6.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
When the project manager forecasts that the stage will go beyond its tolerances, the activity [?] is used to send an exception report to the project board.
o: escalate issues and risks
take corrective action
capture issues and risks
evaluate stage status
6.w: Escalate issues and risks is used when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded: the project manager sends an exception report to the board so it can decide how to respond (see manual 16.4.7).

n.1: Corrective action is used for deviations the project manager can resolve within the stage tolerances (manual 16.4.6).
n.2: This activity registers and assesses new issues and risks before a course of action is chosen; it does not escalate them (manual 16.4.5).
n.3: This activity compares actual with planned progress and may reveal the problem, but escalation is a separate activity (manual 16.4.4).

6.q: A retail company aligns a project review with the close of its accounting year so the board can confirm funding for the next year. Which type of control is this review?
o: A time-driven control, as it recurs once every year
An event-driven control, triggered by an organizational event
A time-driven control, set at the frequency in the work package
An event-driven control, triggered by a forecast tolerance breach
6.w: Event-driven controls occur when a specific event happens, such as the end of a stage, completion of the PID, an exception report or an organizational event such as the end of the financial year (see manual 11.2.2).

n.0: Although it recurs, the review is triggered by a specific organizational event, the end of the financial year, which PRINCE2 classes as event-driven (manual 11.2.2).
n.2: Frequencies in a work package apply to checkpoint reports from the team manager, not to a board review linked to the accounting year (manual 11.2.2).
n.3: The review is triggered by the end of the accounting year, not by a forecast breach of tolerance, which would lead to an exception report (manual 11.2.2, 11.2.6).

6.q: Once the delivery approach is decided, which step of the planning technique identifies the delivery activities for each product and groups them for allocation to teams?
o: Preparing the schedule
Organizing work packages
Preparing estimates
Documenting the plan
6.w: After the products are defined and analysed and the delivery approach is decided, the delivery activities for each product are identified and grouped into work packages (see manual 7.3.1.2).

n.0: Scheduling sets the sequence and duration of work packages once they have been organized (manual 7.3.1.4).
n.2: Estimating works out the effort, time and cost of the work; grouping activities into work packages is a separate step (manual 7.3.1.3).
n.3: Documenting the plan is the final step, recording the narrative such as assumptions and controls (manual 7.3.1).

6.q: What is the purpose of a work package description?
o: To describe the project's major products and how they will be accepted when the project closes
To record every product of a plan and its current status so that progress can be tracked
To describe how one or more products will be produced and to pass responsibility for the work formally to a team
To set out the major products of the whole project and when, how and at what cost they will be delivered
6.w: A work package description describes how one or more products will be produced and delivered, and is used to pass responsibility for that work formally to a team manager or team member (see manual 7.5).

n.0: This describes the project product description, which covers the whole project and its acceptance (manual 7.5).
n.1: This describes the product register, which is held in the project log (manual 4.3.2).
n.3: This describes the project plan, the high-level plan for the whole project (manual 7.2.2.1).

6.q: In the prepare the full business case activity, what information is used to update the outline business case?
o: Actual costs from the first delivery stage and the first end stage report
Benefits figures from the project mandate and lessons from the lessons log
Time and costs from the project plan and aggregated risks from the project log
Progress figures from the checkpoint reports produced by team managers
6.w: The outline business case is refined into the full business case using the timescales and costs from the project plan and the aggregated risks from the project log. The executive is accountable and the project manager responsible (see manual 15.4.5).

n.0: The first delivery stage has not started during initiation, so there are no actual stage costs or end stage report yet (manual 12, 15.4.5).
n.1: The mandate fed the outline business case in starting up; the full version is built from the project plan and the aggregated risks (manual 13.4.3, 15.4.5).
n.3: Checkpoint reports come from team managers during delivery stages, after initiation has finished (manual 17.1, 15.4.5).

6.q: How does PRINCE2 describe decision bias in its guidance on risk culture?
o: As a failing that a mature risk culture removes from the project's decision-making
As a concern for the business layer rather than for the project management team
As natural and largely positive, though it can sometimes lead to less effective decisions
As a problem that affects how threats are judged but not how opportunities are judged
6.w: Decision bias is natural and largely positive, because it lets people make rapid decisions every day; sometimes, though, it leads to less effective decision-making (see manual 9.2.4).

n.0: Bias is natural and mostly helpful; the guidance is to understand it, not to remove it (manual 9.2.4).
n.1: Decision bias affects decisions at every level of the project, so the project management team needs to understand it (manual 9.2.4).
n.3: Bias can affect any risk decision; loss aversion, for example, can stop people pursuing a gain (manual 9.2.4).

6.q: Which statement best describes how the project board works during the directing a project process?
o: It authorizes work packages directly with the team managers
It prepares the next stage plan towards the end of each stage
It writes highlight reports for the business layer at agreed intervals
It manages by exception and delegates day-to-day management
6.w: In directing a project the board manages by exception: it makes the key decisions and exercises overall control but does not carry out day-to-day management, which is delegated to the project manager (see manual 14.1, 14.3).

n.0: Work packages are authorized by the project manager in controlling a stage; the board is not involved in managing product delivery (manual 14.3, 16.1).
n.1: The project manager prepares the next stage plan in managing a stage boundary; the board approves it in directing a project (manual 18.1, 14.4.4).
n.2: Highlight reports are written by the project manager for the board, not by the board for the business layer (manual 16.1, 11.5).

6.q: The digital and data management approach supports the progress practice. In which management product is the digital and data management approach included?
o: The project brief from starting up a project
The end project report produced at closure
The project mandate from the business layer
The project initiation documentation
6.w: The digital and data management approach is one of the nine management approaches agreed in initiating a project and held in the project initiation documentation (see manual 11.5, 15).

n.0: The project brief is assembled in starting up; the management approaches are agreed later, in initiating a project, and form part of the PID (manual 15).
n.1: The end project report reviews performance at closure; it does not contain the management approaches (manual 11.5).
n.2: The project mandate is provided by the business layer to trigger starting up; it does not contain PRINCE2 management approaches (manual 13).

6.q: A delivered product will not meet one of its quality specifications. How should the project manager handle this issue?
o: Informally in the daily log, because it was raised verbally by the team manager
Formally, recording it in the issue register as an off-specification
As a risk in the risk register, because its impact has not yet been measured
As an entry in the lessons log, to be reviewed when the project is closed
6.w: An off-specification is a discrepancy between the baseline and the delivered product and must go through change control, so it is handled formally in the issue register (see manual 10.2.3, 10.5).

n.0: Issues can be raised through informal channels, but how it was raised does not make it informal; an off-specification needs formal change control (manual 10.3.1.1, 10.2.3).
n.2: The shortfall already exists, so it is an issue, not an uncertain risk (manual 9.1, 10.1).
n.3: A lesson may be drawn later, but the off-specification must be resolved now through change control (manual 10.2.3).

6.q:
Which two statements about aligning the business case to business objectives and tolerances are correct?
1. Benefits tolerance is agreed with team managers in each work package description.
2. ESG goals replace the business objectives recorded in the business case.
3. The project's sustainability performance targets should reference the organization's ESG goals.
4. The sustainability management approach supports the business case.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
6.w: Statement 3 is correct: sustainability performance targets and tolerances should reference and contribute to the organization's ESG goals. Statement 4 is correct: the sustainability management approach supports the business case (see manual 5.2.2).

n.0: Statements 1 and 2 are both wrong: work package descriptions carry scope, cost and time tolerances only, and ESG goals may form part of the business objectives rather than replacing them (manual 11.2.1, 5.2.2).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: benefits tolerance is documented in the benefits management approach, not in work package descriptions (manual 5.2.2, 11.2.1).
n.2: Statement 2 is wrong: business objectives may include ESG goals; ESG goals do not replace them (manual 5.2.2).

6.q: A draft risk register entry reads: 'The supplier is already two weeks late with the design.' Why is this not a well-formed risk?
o: It names a supplier, and a risk must be described without reference to any party outside the project
It does not state a probability, and each risk description must start with its probability
It is a threat, and threats are recorded in a separate register from opportunities
It describes something that has already happened, so it is an issue or a cause rather than an uncertain event
6.w: A risk is uncertain. A situation that is already true is an issue, or it may be the cause of a risk, for example a late design that may delay testing (see manual 9.1, 9.2.1).

n.0: Risk descriptions may refer to external parties; the problem is that the event has already happened (manual 9.2.1).
n.1: Probability is assessed and recorded separately; the description sets out cause, event and effect (manual 9.2.1, 9.2.2).
n.2: Threats and opportunities are both recorded in the risk register (manual 9.5).

6.q: Which integrated element describes aspects of project management that must be applied consistently and throughout the project lifecycle?
o: Processes
Principles
People
Practices
6.w: The seven practices describe essential aspects of project management, such as business case, plans and risk, that must be applied consistently throughout the lifecycle so that the processes are effective (see manual 1.2 and 4.1).

n.0: The processes describe the lifecycle activities; the aspects of project management applied throughout them are the practices.
n.1: The principles are the guiding obligations that determine whether a project is genuinely PRINCE2.
n.2: The people element covers the needs, capabilities, motivations and relationships of those involved.

6.q: Why should delegated change authority be accompanied by a change budget?
o: So that the change authority can extend stage tolerances without referring to the board
So that the changes the change authority approves can be funded and then implemented
So that the responses planned for threats can be paid for without escalating them
So that the project manager can add new products without recording them as issues
6.w: Delegated authority should come with an appropriate change budget; applying the change budget is what allows approved changes to be funded and therefore implemented (see manual 10.2.5).

n.0: A change budget funds approved changes; it does not let anyone extend the tolerances that the board sets (manual 10.2.5, 11.2.1).
n.2: Funding responses to threats is the purpose of a risk budget, not a change budget (manual 9.2).
n.3: New products still go through change control and are recorded; the budget funds approved changes rather than bypassing the procedure (manual 10.2.3).

6.q:
Which two statements about quality terms are correct?

1. An outcome such as 'more customers return each year' is a user's quality expectation.
2. Acceptance criteria are a prioritized list of measurable criteria.
3. Quality specifications are found in product descriptions.
4. A requirement is any need, whether or not it is documented in a management product.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
6.w: Statement 2 is the definition of acceptance criteria and statement 3 is correct because each product's quality specifications are held in its product description (see manual 8.1.1, 8.5).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: an outcome or benefit is not a quality expectation of the project product (manual 8.1.1).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong (an outcome is not a quality expectation), and statement 4 is wrong because a requirement is a need or expectation documented in an approved management product (manual 8.1.1).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct but statement 4 is wrong: in PRINCE2 a requirement is documented in an approved management product (manual 8.1.1).

7.q: Which of the three project interests covers the people who will use, operate or maintain the project's products, or who will be affected by them?
o: User
Business
Supplier
Corporate
7.w: The user interest covers those who will use, operate, maintain or be impacted by the products; they help define the requirements and check they are met (see manual 6.2.1).

n.1: The business interest is about meeting a business need and remaining justified as value for money (manual 6.2.1).
n.2: The supplier interest is about those with the skills and knowledge to deliver the products (manual 6.2.1).
n.3: 'Corporate' comes from the older 'corporate, programme management or the customer' level, now the business layer; it is not one of the three interests (manual fig 6.2).

7.q: A risk is written as: 'Because the venue has a single access road, the road may be closed by roadworks, which would delay equipment delivery by two days.' Which part is the risk event?
o: The venue having a single access road
The two-day delay to equipment delivery
The supplier that will deliver the equipment
The possible closure of the road by roadworks
7.w: The event is the uncertain occurrence: the road may be closed. The single access road is the cause, and the two-day delay is the effect (see manual 9.2.1).

n.0: This is a current fact that gives rise to the risk, so it is the cause, not the uncertain event (manual 9.2.1).
n.1: This is what would happen to objectives if the event occurred, so it is the effect (manual 9.2.1).
n.2: The supplier is not part of the cause, event and effect described; the event is the possible road closure (manual 9.2.1).

7.q: A board member asks which management product explains how the organization's staff will move from the old way of working to the new one. Which product should the project manager point to?
o: Issue management approach
Change management approach
Issue register
Project product description
7.w: Moving staff from the current to the target way of working is change management, planned in the change management approach (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: The issue management approach covers capturing issues and controlling changes to the baseline, not the organizational transition (manual 10.5).
n.2: The issue register records formal issues and their status; it does not plan how staff will move to new ways of working (manual 10.5).
n.3: The project product description defines the project's main product, quality expectations and acceptance criteria, not the transition of staff (manual 8.5).

7.q:
Which two statements about the types of control in PRINCE2 are correct?

1. Highlight reports are an event-driven control.
2. Checkpoint reports are a time-driven control.
3. Completion of the project initiation documentation is a time-driven control.
4. Creating an exception report is an event-driven control.
o: 2 and 4
1 and 2
1 and 3
3 and 4
7.w: Checkpoint reports occur at a frequency set in the work package, so they are time-driven (2); creating an exception report is triggered by a forecast breach, so it is event-driven (4) (see manual 11.2.2).

n.1: Statement 2 is correct, but highlight reports are produced at intervals set by the board, so they are time-driven (manual 11.2.2).
n.2: Both are wrong: highlight reports are time-driven, and completion of the PID is an event, so it is event-driven (manual 11.2.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is correct, but completing the PID is a specific event, which makes it event-driven (manual 11.2.2).

7.q: At which organizational level is the project mandate provided and the executive identified?
o: Directing (the project board)
Business layer (commissioning)
Managing (the project manager)
Delivering (the team managers)
7.w: The commissioning party in the business layer provides the project mandate, identifies the executive and defines the project-level tolerances within which the board works (see manual 6.2, fig 6.2).

n.0: The project board directs the project; it does not exist until the executive has been identified by the business layer (manual fig 6.2, 13.4.1).
n.2: The project manager is appointed alongside the executive in starting up a project; the mandate comes from above the project (manual 13.3).
n.3: Team managers deliver products within constraints set by the project manager; they do not commission the project (manual fig 6.2).

7.q: Where are the activities for closing the project planned?
o: In the stage plan for the final stage
