In a separate closure stage plan approved at the last stage boundary
In a team plan produced by project support
In an exception plan prepared at the end of the final stage
7.w: Closing a project is not a separate stage. Its activities are planned in, and carried out within, the final stage, so they appear in the final stage plan (see manual 7.2.2.2).

n.1: There is no closure stage; closing a project happens within the final stage (manual 7.2.2.2).
n.2: Team plans are produced by team managers for work packages, and closure is planned by the project manager (manual 7.2.2.3).
n.3: Exception plans respond to exceptions; they are not how planned closure is arranged (manual 7.2.2.4).

7.q: A delivered product differs from the approved version in the project baseline. How should this discrepancy be handled?
o: Recorded as a lesson and left in place, because the product has already been delivered
Recorded as a new threat in the risk register so that it can be monitored in later stages
Corrected by the team manager as routine work, with the baseline left as it is
Treated as an off-specification and taken through the change control procedure
7.w: An off-specification is a discrepancy between the approved baseline and the delivered products, and it must be addressed through the change control procedure (see manual 10.2.3).

n.0: A lesson may be learned, but the discrepancy itself is an off-specification that must go through change control (manual 10.2.3).
n.1: The discrepancy already exists, so it is an issue rather than an uncertain future event for the risk register (manual 9.1, 10.2.3).
n.2: Off-specifications go through change control and a decision by the right authority, rather than being fixed as routine team work (manual 10.2.3, 10.2.4).

7.q: When, by whom and in which process is an end stage report normally produced?
o: At regular intervals in a stage, by the project manager, in controlling a stage
Near the end of a stage, by the project manager, in managing a stage boundary
At the end of each work package, by the team manager, in managing product delivery
At the end of the project, by the project manager, in closing a project
7.w: The project manager prepares the end stage report as close as possible to the end of each stage, in the 'evaluate the stage' activity of managing a stage boundary (see manual 11.5, 18).

n.0: Regular reports during a stage are highlight reports, produced in controlling a stage (manual 11.5, 16.4.8).
n.2: Team managers report on work packages through checkpoint reports and notify completion to the project manager; they do not produce end stage reports (manual 11.5, 17).
n.3: The report produced at the end of the project in closing a project is the end project report (manual 11.5, 19.4.4).

7.q: Which management products does a team manager produce in the 'managing product delivery' process?
o: Checkpoint reports and, if needed, a team plan
Work package descriptions and highlight reports
Exception reports and the issue register
End stage reports and lessons reports
7.w: In managing product delivery the team manager may produce a team plan when accepting a work package and sends checkpoint reports to the project manager (see manual 17.4.1, 17.4.3).

n.1: Both are produced by the project manager in controlling a stage (manual 16.4.1, 16.4.8).
n.2: Exception reports come from the project manager, and the issue register is maintained for the project manager, updated with team input (manual 16.4.7, 17.7).
n.3: These are prepared by the project manager in managing a stage boundary or closing a project (manual ch 18, 19.4.4).

7.q: What does PRINCE2 say that co-creating products with the business, user and supplier communities helps to achieve?
o: It removes the need for quality reviews, as users have already seen the products
It lets the senior supplier accept the completed products on behalf of the users
It moves responsibility for realizing benefits from the senior user to the supplier
It improves the products' adoption into the business and reduces handover risks
7.w: Co-creating products, with agreed product descriptions, unites the different perspectives of the business, user and supplier communities, improving development and adoption and reducing handover risks (see manual 3.5.1).

n.0: Products still go through the quality control methods in their product descriptions; involvement in design does not replace quality checks (manual 8.2.2).
n.1: Acceptance is given by or on behalf of the users, not by the supplier that built the products (manual 8.3.1.3).
n.2: The senior user remains accountable for specifying the benefits and responsible for their continued realization (manual 6.2.4.2).

7.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

The project board is the ultimate authority for requests for change and off-specifications, but it may delegate their approval, within agreed limits, to a [?].
o: team manager
project assurance
project support
change authority
7.w: A change authority is a person or group to whom the project board delegates approval of requests for change and off-specifications, within limits and usually with a change budget (see manual 10.2.4, 10.2.5).

n.0: Team managers implement agreed work within their work packages; PRINCE2 names the change authority (or the project manager) as the delegate for approving changes (manual 10.2.4).
n.1: Project assurance gives the board members independent advice and monitoring; it is not a body that approves changes (manual 6.2.4.7).
n.2: Project support administers the issue and change procedure for the project manager; it does not approve changes (manual 6.2.4.8).

7.q: Which activity forms part of the develop step of the business case technique?
o: Comparing the benefits realized with the forecast benefits in a post-project benefits review
Comparing the costs of developing, operating and maintaining the products with the value of benefits
Updating the business case with progress data at the end of each delivery stage
Reviewing the business case when the project board is assessing an exception plan
7.w: Developing the business case includes options analysis and investment appraisal, comparing the costs of developing, operating and maintaining the products with the value of the benefits over a period (see manual 5.3.1).

n.0: Assessing realized benefits after closure is the confirm step (manual 5.3.1).
n.2: Updating with progress data at each stage end is the maintain step (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: The board's review when assessing an exception plan is part of the check step (manual 5.3.1).

7.q: Who typically performs quality assurance for a PRINCE2 project?
o: A business or programme function that is independent of the project management team
The members of the project board, acting as project assurance for their own interests
Project support, as part of maintaining the quality register and quality records
The team managers, as part of carrying out the quality checks in each work package
7.w: Quality assurance is performed independently of the project management team, typically by a business or programme function such as part of the business's quality management system (see manual 8.2.3).

n.1: Board members are accountable for project assurance, which is independent of the project manager but part of the project; quality assurance sits outside the project management team (manual 8.2.3).
n.2: Project support is part of the project management team and administers quality records; it cannot provide independent quality assurance (manual 8.2.3, ch 6).
n.3: Team managers carry out quality control within work packages; quality assurance is independent of the project management team they belong to (manual 8.2.2, 8.2.3).

7.q: When is the outline business case developed, and what is it developed from?
o: In initiating a project, using the project plan
In the first delivery stage, using the PID
In closing a project, using the end project report
In starting up a project, using the project mandate
7.w: The project mandate triggers starting up a project and is used to develop the initial justification, documented in the outline business case within the project brief (see manual 5.2.1, 5.3.1, 13.4.3).

n.0: Initiation uses the project plan's time and cost figures to turn the outline into the full business case; the outline already exists by then (manual 15.4.5).
n.1: By the first delivery stage the full business case has been approved as part of the PID; the outline version comes much earlier (manual 5.2.1).
n.2: Closing a project updates the business case with actual costs and benefits; it does not develop the outline version (manual ch 19).

7.q:
Which two are among the seven aspects of project performance in PRINCE2 7?
1. Stakeholders
2. Sustainability
3. Resources
4. Benefits
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
7.w: Sustainability and benefits are both aspects of performance. The full set is benefits, costs, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk (see manual 1.4).

n.0: Sustainability is an aspect, but stakeholders are not; stakeholders are addressed through the people element.
n.1: Neither stakeholders nor resources is one of the seven aspects of performance.
n.3: Benefits is an aspect, but resources are not; resources are planned within the plans practice.

7.q: A project manager uses actual figures from a similar earlier project to sharpen the estimates in a stage plan. Which principle is the plans practice supporting?
o: Ensure continued business justification
Focus on products
Learn from experience
Tailor to suit the project
7.w: Using lessons and past data to improve estimates is how the plans practice supports the learn from experience principle (see manual 7.7 tab 7.2).

n.0: Business justification is supported by aligning plan targets with the business case; the use of past figures here is learning from experience (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).
n.1: Focus on products is supported by starting planning from the products; this example is about improving estimates with experience (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).
n.3: Tailoring adjusts the formality and detail of plans; drawing on past figures is learning from experience (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).

7.q: Which integrated element consists of the guiding obligations and good practices that determine whether a project is genuinely being managed using PRINCE2?
o: Practices
Principles
Processes
Project context
7.w: The seven principles are the guiding obligations and good practices that decide whether a project is genuinely a PRINCE2 project; unless all are applied, it is not (see manual 1.2).

n.0: The practices describe aspects of project management that must be applied consistently throughout the lifecycle; they do not decide whether a project is genuinely PRINCE2.
n.2: The processes provide the activities to direct, manage and deliver the project from start-up to closure.
n.3: The project context is the setting the method is applied in, such as the organizational and commercial context, delivery method and scale.

7.q: How does the people element apply the 'focus on products' principle?
o: By making decisions at the most local level where the knowledge to make them is held
By reviewing at each stage boundary how people interact with the wider organization
By co-creating products with the business, user and supplier communities to aid adoption
By sharing knowledge hidden in the project ecosystem through social learning
7.w: Co-creating products, with agreed product descriptions, with the business, user and supplier communities unites their perspectives, improves development and adoption and reduces handover risks: this is how the people element applies focus on products (see manual 3.5.1).

n.0: Deciding at the most local level where the knowledge resides is how the people element applies manage by exception (manual 3.5.1).
n.1: Using stage boundaries to review how people interact is how the people element applies manage by stages (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Drawing out hidden knowledge through social learning is how the people element applies learn from experience (manual 3.5.1).

7.q: On a construction project using two external contractors, which role is accountable for the quality of the products the suppliers deliver and for their technical integrity?
o: Senior user
Senior supplier
Project executive
Team manager
7.w: The senior supplier represents the suppliers on the project board and is accountable for the quality of products delivered by suppliers and their technical integrity (see manual ch 6, tab 8.2).

n.0: The senior user represents the users, specifying their requirements and benefits; the senior user does not answer for supplier quality (manual ch 6).
n.2: The executive owns the business case and is ultimately accountable for the project, but supplier product quality is the senior supplier's accountability (manual ch 6).
n.3: A team manager produces products to specification within a work package, but is not a board role and is not accountable for supplier quality overall (manual ch 6).

7.q: A team manager forecasts that their work package will exceed its cost tolerance, although the stage as a whole is still within its tolerances. How should the team manager handle this?
o: Raise it with the project manager as an issue
Send an exception report to the project board
Prepare an exception plan for the project manager to approve
Agree new work package tolerances with the senior supplier
7.w: A team manager works within the work package tolerances set by the project manager and escalates a forecast work package breach to the project manager as an issue, which the project manager handles in controlling a stage (see manual 11.2.1, 11.2.6).

n.1: Exception reports are raised by the project manager when stage or project tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, not by a team manager for a work package (manual 11.2.6).
n.2: Exception plans are prepared by the project manager in managing a stage boundary for stage or project breaches (manual 11.3.1).
n.3: Work package tolerances are set by the project manager, so the senior supplier cannot change them (manual 11.2.1).

7.q:
Which two statements about the integrated elements of PRINCE2 7 are true?
1. There are four integrated elements.
2. Tailoring to the project environment is one of the integrated elements.
3. People is one of the integrated elements.
4. The project context is one of the integrated elements.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
7.w: PRINCE2 7 has five integrated elements, two of which are people and the project context (see manual 1.2).

n.0: Both are false: PRINCE2 7 has five elements, and tailoring is covered by the principle tailor to suit the project rather than being an element.
n.1: Statement 3 is true, but statement 1 is false: PRINCE2 7 has five integrated elements, not four.
n.2: Statement 4 is true, but statement 2 is false: tailoring is covered by the principle tailor to suit the project, not an element.

7.q: Which of the following is an objective of the initiating a project process?
o: Appointment of the individuals who will carry out the work of initiation
Common understanding of how and when products are delivered and at what cost
An effective connection between the business layer and the project
Confirmation that the business can support the products after closure
7.w: Initiating a project aims for a common understanding of, among other things, how and when the project's products will be delivered and at what cost (see manual 15.2).

n.0: Appointing the people who will do the work of initiation is an objective of starting up a project (manual 13.2).
n.2: Giving the business layer an effective connection to the project is an objective of directing a project (manual 14.2).
n.3: Ensuring the business can support the products after the project closes is an objective of closing a project (manual 19.2).

7.q: What happens in the 'accept a work package' activity of 'managing product delivery'?
o: The project manager checks that each completed product has the required approval
The team manager agrees the work, reporting and constraints with the project manager
The team manager sends a checkpoint report to show progress on the work
The project board reviews and approves the work package before the team starts work
7.w: In accept a work package the team manager agrees with the project manager what is to be delivered, the reporting requirements, constraints and procedures, and whether the work is achievable, then agrees to deliver it (see manual 17.4.1).

n.0: Checking that completed products are approved happens in receive completed work package in controlling a stage (manual 16.4.3).
n.2: Checkpoint reporting happens once work is under way, in execute and evaluate a work package (manual 17.4.3).
n.3: The project manager authorizes work packages; the board is not involved in managing product delivery (manual 16.4.1, 17.3).

7.q:
Which two statements describe leadership as PRINCE2 defines it?
1. Persuading, influencing and co-creating, with a focus on key relationships.
2. Instructing the execution of tasks in line with agreed ways of working.
3. Motivating people to achieve the project's objectives.
4. Setting tolerances for each work package on behalf of the project board.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
7.w: Statements 1 and 3 are both parts of the PRINCE2 description of leadership: motivating people towards the objectives, and persuading, influencing and co-creating with a focus on key relationships (see manual 3.3).

n.0: Statement 2 is the definition of management, not leadership (manual 3.3).
n.2: Statement 2 defines management, and statement 4 is a control the project manager uses to manage by exception, not part of the definition of leadership (manual 3.3, 11.2.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is a management control: the project manager sets work package tolerances, which is not part of the definition of leadership (manual 11.2.1).

7.q: During starting up a project, the project manager consults the executive, senior user and senior supplier about what the project will deliver. In which activity is the project product description created?
o: Assemble the project brief
Prepare the outline business case
Select the project approach
Appoint the project management team
7.w: In prepare the outline business case the project manager consults the senior user, senior supplier and executive to define what the project will deliver, and creates the project product description (see manual 13.4.3).

n.0: Assemble the project brief brings together products already created, including the project product description, rather than creating it (manual 13.4).
n.2: Select the project approach decides how the work will be approached, such as build or buy and the delivery method (manual 13.4.5).
n.3: Appoint the project management team puts the board and other key roles in place; it does not define the project's main product (manual 13.4.4).

7.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

Because only the near future can be planned in detail, PRINCE2 combines a high-level project plan with a detailed [?] for the current management stage.
o: team plan
stage plan
exception plan
work package
7.w: The planning horizon limits detailed planning, so manage by stages pairs a high-level project plan with a detailed stage plan for the current stage (manual 2.4).

n.0: Team plans are optional plans for a team's work, not the detailed plan for the whole current stage (manual ch 7).
n.2: An exception plan is produced when tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, not as the normal detailed stage plan (manual ch 7).
n.3: A work package is a set of information for a team manager, not a plan for the stage (manual ch 7).

7.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
The [?] is assembled in 'initiating a project' and, together with the current stage plan, forms the contract between the project manager and the project board.
o: project brief
project product description
project initiation documentation
communication management approach
7.w: The PID gives the direction and scope of the project and, with the current stage plan, forms the contract between the project manager and the board. It is assembled in initiating a project (see manual 4.3.1, 15.4.6).

n.0: The project brief is assembled in starting up a project and is superseded by the PID (manual 13.4, 4.3.1).
n.1: The project product description is created in starting up a project and is one input to the PID, not the contract itself (manual 13.4.3).
n.3: This approach is one part of the PID; on its own it does not form the contract with the board (manual 4.3.1).

7.q: A new team member says she is unsure what is expected of her and what she can expect from others in the team. Which principle has been applied poorly?
o: Manage by stages, as her work has not been planned stage by stage
Focus on products, as her products have no agreed quality criteria
Learn from experience, as lessons from past teams were not shared
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, as roles are unclear
7.w: The principle aims to make sure the right people are involved and that each knows what is expected of them and what they can expect from others (manual 2.3).

n.0: Nothing in the situation concerns stage planning; manage by stages is about planning and deciding stage by stage, not who does what (manual 2.4).
n.1: The situation says nothing about quality criteria; the gap is unclear expectations between people, which focus on products does not address (manual 2.6).
n.2: The situation is not about lessons from past teams; it is about not knowing what is expected and what to expect from others (manual 2.2, 2.3).

7.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. Change, temporary teams, cross-functional working and the uniqueness of each project create [?], so projects bring threats and opportunities over and above those of business as usual.
o: uncertainty
governance
tolerance
sustainability
7.w: Uncertainty is the fifth characteristic: the other four introduce threats and opportunities beyond those typically met in business as usual, which makes projects riskier (see manual 1.3).

n.1: Governance is how a project is directed and controlled; it is a response to project risk, not the characteristic that describes it.
n.2: Tolerance is the permitted deviation from a plan's targets under manage by exception, not one of the five characteristics of a project.
n.3: Sustainability is one of the seven aspects of project performance, not one of the five characteristics that distinguish projects from business as usual.

7.q: When is the quality management approach created, and who approves it?
o: During starting up a project, and the business layer approves it with the project mandate
During initiating a project, and quality assurance approves it on behalf of the business
During initiating a project, and the project board approves it in directing a project
During the first delivery stage, and the senior supplier approves it for the suppliers
7.w: The quality management approach is agreed in initiating a project (agree the management approaches) and approved by the project board in directing a project (see manual 15.4.2, tab 14.3).

n.0: Starting up a project produces the project product description, not the management approaches, and the business layer does not approve them (manual ch 13, 15.4.2).
n.1: Quality assurance is independent of the project management team; the board, not quality assurance, approves the project's management approaches (manual 8.2.3, tab 14.3).
n.3: The approach must exist before delivery starts, as part of the project initiation documentation the board approves when it authorizes the project (manual 15.4.2, tab 14.3).

7.q: In the plans practice, which role reviews stage and project progress against the agreed tolerances?
o: Project assurance
Project support
The team manager
The senior supplier
7.w: Project assurance reviews stage and project progress against agreed tolerances on behalf of the project board (see manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

n.1: Project support assists the project manager with compiling plans and planning tools; reviewing progress against tolerances is an assurance task (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).
n.2: The team manager prepares schedules for each work package and reports on work package progress; it does not review the stage or project (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).
n.3: The senior supplier makes sure plans are consistent with the supplier perspective and commits supplier resources (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

7.q: Site engineers must complete a new online checklist before each customer visit. They find it slow, and many now phone bookings through to the office instead. What should the project manager do, in line with PRINCE2 7 guidance on culture?
o: Announce that bookings phoned through to the office will no longer be accepted
Record each phoned booking as an off-specification in the issue register
Use the engineers' feedback to review and simplify the checklist
Ask the project board to replace the engineers who keep phoning bookings
7.w: Persistent workarounds show the defined ways of working do not fit how people actually work. PRINCE2 7 recommends gathering and acting on feedback so the ways of working stay aligned with the culture (see manual 3.2.3).

n.0: Enforcing the process without understanding the reason ignores the leading indicator; PRINCE2 asks the project to act on the feedback instead (manual 3.2.3).
n.1: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications; phoned bookings are a ways-of-working matter (manual 10.1).
n.3: Replacing people does not address why the agreed ways of working no longer fit; acting on feedback does (manual 3.2.3).

7.q: Which process refines the outline business case into the full business case, ready for the project board to approve when it authorizes the project?
o: Initiating a project
Starting up a project
Managing a stage boundary
Directing a project
7.w: In initiating a project, the activity 'prepare the full business case' updates the outline business case with time and costs from the project plan and the aggregated risks; the board approves it when authorizing the project (see manual 5.2.1, 15.4.5).

n.1: Starting up a project produces the outline business case; the full version is prepared during initiation (manual 13.4.3, 15.4.5).
n.2: Managing a stage boundary updates an existing business case at the end of each stage; it does not create the full version (manual ch 18).
n.3: Directing a project is where the board approves the business case; the project manager prepares it in initiating a project (manual 14.4.2, 15.4.5).

7.q: Which role is responsible for ensuring that the project and its management approaches are aligned with the business's environmental, social and governance (ESG) commitments?
o: Team manager
Project support
Project board
Change authority
7.w: The project board's responsibilities include ensuring business strategy is reflected in the business case and that the project and its management approaches align with the business's ESG commitments (see manual 6.2.4).

n.0: The team manager delivers products within work package tolerances and looks after the team's approach; ESG alignment of the project is a board responsibility (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: Project support provides administration and maintains registers; it does not set the project's direction on ESG (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: A change authority approves requests for change within delegated limits; it is not responsible for ESG alignment (manual 6.2.4).

7.q:
Which two statements about risk responses are correct?
1. Exploit makes an opportunity certain to happen.
2. Enhance removes the uncertainty from an opportunity.
3. A reduce response can leave a residual risk.
4. Share passes the whole financial impact of a risk to an insurer.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
7.w: Statement 1 describes exploit, which makes the situation certain. Statement 3 is right because reducing a threat rather than removing it leaves residual risk (see manual 9.2.3.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: enhance changes probability or impact but leaves the opportunity uncertain; making it certain is exploit (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: passing financial impact to an insurer is transfer; share is a pain and gain arrangement with a partner (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.3: Statement 2 is wrong: removing the uncertainty from an opportunity is exploit, not enhance (manual 9.2.3.1).

7.q:
Which two statements are objectives of the 'controlling a stage' process?
1. To keep the risks and issues that arise during the stage under control.
2. To prepare the next stage plan so the board can decide whether to continue.
3. To make sure the stage's agreed products meet quality expectations and are accepted.
4. To give the authority for the project product to be delivered.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
7.w: Statements 1 and 3 are objectives of controlling a stage: risks and issues are controlled, and the stage's agreed products meet their quality expectations and are accepted (see manual 16.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the next stage plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary (manual 18.2). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong. The next stage plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary (manual 18.2), and authority to deliver the project product is an objective of directing a project (manual 14.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: giving authority to deliver the project product is an objective of directing a project (manual 14.2). Statement 3 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 1.

7.q: A project manager sets up a robust change management procedure so that the effect of decisions on different parts of the project ecosystem is considered before they are made. Which step of the organizational design and development technique is being applied?
o: Step 3: develop the project ecosystem
Step 4: manage ongoing changes to the project ecosystem
Step 5: transition the project into the organizational ecosystem
Step 1: understand the organizational ecosystem
7.w: In managing ongoing changes to the project ecosystem, the project manager ensures a robust change management procedure so that impacts on different areas of the project ecosystem are considered in decision-making (see manual 6.3.1.4).

n.0: Developing the project ecosystem covers onboarding, skills assessment and similar development activities, not the change management procedure (manual 6.3.1.3).
n.2: Transition takes place at closure, when products, people and learning return to the business (manual fig 6.5).
n.3: Understanding the organizational ecosystem examines existing structures and governance before the project is designed (manual 6.3.1.1).

7.q: Which statement describes project support in PRINCE2?
o: Administrative and advisory services that are the project manager's responsibility and can be delegated
Independent monitoring of all aspects of the project's performance on behalf of the project board members
Approval of requests for change and off-specifications within limits and a budget delegated by the board
A business function, independent of the project, that checks the organization's quality system is followed
7.w: Project support provides services such as administration, facilitating meetings and workshops, tool advice and planning support. It is the project manager's responsibility and can be delegated, for example to a project office or team members (see manual 6.2.4.8).

n.1: Independent monitoring on behalf of the board members is project assurance, not project support (manual 6.2.4.7).
n.2: Approving changes within delegated limits and a change budget is the change authority role (manual 10.2.4).
n.3: A business function independent of the project management team that checks the quality system is quality assurance, a quality practice concept (manual 8.2.3).

7.q: Which statement about the organizational context of a PRINCE2 project is correct?
o: PRINCE2 assumes the project sits within a programme that sets its objectives
PRINCE2 does not assume any particular organizational context for the project
PRINCE2 assumes the customer and the supplier belong to the same organization
PRINCE2 assumes the project reports directly to the organization's portfolio office
7.w: The PRINCE2 method does not assume any specific organizational context: a project may be standalone, part of a programme or portfolio, or delivered in a commercial customer and supplier relationship (see manual 1.5).

n.0: A project may be part of a programme, but it may equally be standalone or in a portfolio; PRINCE2 does not assume a programme.
n.2: PRINCE2 explicitly allows for commercial contexts where the customer and supplier are separate organizations with their own business cases.
n.3: A standalone project may report to its business unit's management structure rather than a portfolio office; no single reporting line is assumed.

7.q: What is a change budget?
o: Money set aside to fund the planned responses to specific threats and opportunities
The cost tolerance allowed for a stage before an exception has to be raised
Money or authorized constraints set aside to cover the cost of approved changes
The total cost of the project, as shown in the investment appraisal of the business case
7.w: A change budget is money, or a set of authorized constraints, set aside in a plan to cover changes, allocated by those with delegated authority so that authorized changes can be delivered (see manual 10.2.5).

n.0: Money for responses to threats and opportunities is the risk budget, not the change budget (manual 9.2).
n.1: Cost tolerance is the permitted deviation in cost before escalation; it is not a fund for approved changes (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: The project's total cost appears in the business case; the change budget is a separate amount reserved for approved changes (manual 5.5, 10.2.5).

7.q: Which management product in the PID establishes a controlled, two-way flow of information to engage stakeholders?
o: Communication management approach
Change management approach
Sustainability management approach
Benefits management approach
7.w: The communication management approach supports engagement with stakeholders by establishing a controlled and bidirectional flow of information (see manual 3.4).

n.1: The change management approach sets out the target organizational state and how the business will transition to it (manual 3.2.1).
n.2: The sustainability management approach defines the actions, reviews and controls that ensure the project's sustainability targets are achieved (manual ch 5).
n.3: The benefits management approach defines the actions to ensure outcomes are achieved and benefits are confirmed (manual ch 5).

7.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
A PRINCE2 project is tailored to suit its environment, size, complexity, importance, [?], team capability and level of risk.
o: funding source
business case
stage plan
delivery method
7.w: Delivery method is one of the seven factors named by the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, alongside environment, size, complexity, importance, team capability and level of risk (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Where the funding comes from is not one of the seven named tailoring factors; securing funding is an executive responsibility (manual 2.7, 6.2.4).
n.1: The business case is a management product that is itself tailored in format and detail; it is not one of the named factors (manual 2.7, 5.4.5).
n.2: A stage plan is a management product created for each stage; it is not one of the named tailoring factors (manual 2.7).

7.q: What is recorded under the 'agreement' heading of a work package description?
o: The terms of the contract agreed with an external supplier for the work
The acceptance criteria for the project agreed with the senior user
The stage tolerances agreed between the executive and the project manager
A record of the initial authorization of the work and of its final completion
7.w: The agreement heading of a work package description records the initial authorization of the work and its final completion (see manual 7.5).

n.0: Supplier contracts are dealt with through the commercial management approach, not the agreement heading of a work package (manual 7.5).
n.1: The project's acceptance criteria are in the project product description (manual 7.5).
n.2: Stage tolerances belong in the stage plan; a work package carries its own scope, cost and time tolerances (manual 7.6 tab 7.1, 11.2.1).

7.q: Under the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle, which three primary stakeholder interests must be represented in the project management team?
o: Business, user and supplier
Sponsor, customer and contractor
Executive, project manager and team
Strategic, operational and technical
7.w: Every project has three primary stakeholder interests, business, user and supplier, and all three must be represented in the project management team, as reflected in the project board (manual 2.3).

n.1: Sponsor, customer and contractor are general terms; PRINCE2 names the business, user and supplier interests (manual 2.3).
n.2: These are roles or levels within the project, not the three stakeholder interests the principle requires (manual 2.3).
n.3: These are not PRINCE2 stakeholder interests; the three are business, user and supplier (manual 2.3).

7.q:
Which two statements about the 'ensure continued business justification' principle are correct?
1. The justification is usually documented in a business case.
2. The justification is fixed once the project is authorized.
3. Suppliers also need their own justification for taking part.
4. It applies to commercial projects but not to compulsory ones.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
7.w: Statement 1 is correct: justification is usually documented in a business case. Statement 3 is correct: every party, including suppliers, needs a balance of benefits, costs and risks to justify its involvement (manual 2.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the justification can change during the project, and what the project delivers must stay consistent with it (manual 2.1).
n.1: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: justification can change, and compulsory projects still justify the option chosen (manual 2.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: compulsory projects still need justification of the chosen option (manual 2.1).

7.q: An approved change to a baselined product has been made. What should happen to the baseline for that product?
o: The original version stays current and the change is noted in the daily log
A new version becomes the baseline and the superseded version is archived
The baseline is frozen until the next stage boundary, when the change is applied
The issue report describing the change replaces the product in the baseline
7.w: Each approved change creates a new baselined version. Records of change are kept and superseded versions are archived, which is configuration control (see manual 10.2.1, 10.3.1.5).

n.0: Once an approved change is implemented, the affected product and baseline are updated; keeping the old version as current would defeat change control (manual 10.3.1.5).
n.2: Approved changes are implemented when decided, through work packages, not held until the next stage boundary (manual 10.3.1.5).
n.3: The issue report describes the issue and recommends a decision; it does not become part of the product baseline (manual 10.5).

7.q: Why is the version of the PID that is used to gain project authorization baselined and placed under change control?
o: So that actual performance can later be compared with what was originally agreed
So that the daily log and registers can be stored in it and updated every day
So that the business layer can reuse it as the project mandate for later projects
So that the project brief can be prepared from it in starting up a project
7.w: The authorized PID is baselined so that it can be compared with actual performance later; for example, the end project report reviews performance against the baselined PID. Changes after that go through change control (see manual 4.3.1, 15.4.6, 19.4.4).

n.1: The logs and registers are dynamic records in the project log; the PID is a baselined set of products, not a daily record (manual 4.3.2).
n.2: The project mandate comes from the business layer before starting up a project; it is not created from a baselined PID (manual 13.3).
n.3: The project brief is created in starting up a project, before the PID exists; the PID supersedes the brief, not the other way round (manual 5.5).

7.q: A project's product is central to the organization's strategy, and failure would be highly visible. How is this MOST likely to affect tailoring?
o: Some principles may be dropped so decisions are taken faster
Controls are likely to be more formal, given the project's importance
The business layer is likely to take over directing the project
Fewer management products are needed, as senior support is strong
7.w: Importance is one of the tailoring factors, and project controls such as the formality of reports and reviews are fitted to the project's importance; a highly important project is likely to need more formal control (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Principles are never tailored away, whatever the pressure for speed; all seven must be applied (manual ch 2).
n.2: The business layer sets project-level tolerances and decides on project-level exceptions; the project board still directs the project (fig 6.2).
n.3: Strong senior support does not reduce the products needed; an important project is more likely to need fuller control (manual 2.7).

7.q: A project board is agreeing tolerances for the next stage. Which set of items are all aspects for which PRINCE2 7 allows tolerances to be set?
o: Time, cost, scope and stakeholders
Time, cost, scope and sustainability
Quality, risk, benefits and resources
Benefits, risk, quality and communication
7.w: PRINCE2 7 recognizes tolerances for seven aspects of performance: time, cost, scope, quality, benefits, risk and sustainability, the last being new in this edition (see manual 11.2.1).

n.0: Stakeholders are not a tolerance aspect; the seven are time, cost, scope, quality, benefits, risk and sustainability (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Resources are not one of the seven tolerance aspects; the other three items are (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: Communication is planned through the communication management approach and is not a tolerance aspect (manual 11.2.1).

7.q: A team estimates the effort for each work item by privately voting with cards and discussing differences until they agree. Which kind of estimating technique is this?
o: Parametric, applying known rates to measured units
Expert consensus, agreeing an estimate as a group
Top-down, splitting an overall figure across the parts
Comparative, using similar past work as a reference
7.w: Planning poker, like the Delphi technique, is an expert consensus approach to estimating, one of the techniques used in the preparing estimates step (see manual 7.3.1.3).

n.0: Parametric estimating applies known rates or measures to the size of the work, not group voting (manual 7.3.1.3).
n.2: Top-down estimating starts from an overall figure and splits it across the parts; it is not a voting method (manual 7.3.1.3).
n.3: Comparative estimating uses similar past work as the reference, not repeated rounds of voting (manual 7.3.1.3).

7.q: During initiation, the project manager documents how the organization's standard project method will be adapted to suit this project, and the board agrees it. Which initiating a project activity is this?
o: Agree the management approaches
Establish project controls
Assemble the project initiation documentation
Agree the tailoring requirements
7.w: In agree the tailoring requirements the project decides how PRINCE2, or the business's own standard method, will be tailored to internal and external factors, and that tailoring is documented and agreed (see manual 15.4.1).

n.0: Agree the management approaches defines the nine approaches, such as risk and quality, rather than how the method as a whole is tailored (manual 15.4.2).
n.1: Establish project controls agrees the board's level of control and the mechanisms for it, not the tailoring of the method (manual 15.4.3).
n.2: Assemble the PID brings together and cross-checks products already prepared, including the tailoring decisions; it does not define them (manual 15.4.6).

7.q: A project manager sends the board an exception report forecasting that stage cost tolerance will be exceeded. In which directing a project activity does the board respond to the exception report?
o: Give ongoing direction
Authorize a stage or exception plan
Authorize the project
Authorize project closure
7.w: The board responds to exception reports in give ongoing direction, for example by asking for an exception plan. Any exception plan is later approved in authorize a stage or exception plan (see manual 14.4.3, 14.4.4).

n.1: Authorize a stage or exception plan is used once an exception plan has been prepared; the first response to the report, such as requesting that plan, is given in give ongoing direction (manual 14.4.3, 14.4.4).
n.2: Authorize the project is the decision at the end of initiation to proceed with the rest of the project; it is not used to respond to a stage exception (manual 14.4.2).
n.3: Authorize project closure confirms that the project can close at the end of the final stage; an exception report is handled through give ongoing direction (manual 14.4.5, 14.4.3).

7.q: While tailoring the method, a project manager notes that most of the project team have no experience of the delivery method being used. Which tailoring factor is she considering?
o: Team capability
Project importance
Project environment
Project size
7.w: Team capability is one of the seven tailoring factors; the experience and skills of the team affect how controls such as reporting should be set (see manual 2.7).

n.1: Importance concerns how significant the project is to the organization, not how experienced the team is (manual 2.7).
n.2: Environment concerns the setting the project runs in, such as the organization, regulation or commercial context, not the team's own experience (manual 2.7).
n.3: Size concerns the scale of the project, not the experience of the people doing the work (manual 2.7).

7.q:
Which two statements about stakeholder engagement in PRINCE2 7 are correct?
1. Stakeholders are limited to people who hold a formal role in the project.
2. Regular meetings and working groups help build shared understanding across interfaces.
3. Stakeholder engagement is complete once the project initiation documentation is approved.
4. Stage boundaries are a useful point to review key relationships and influencers.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
7.w: Statement 2 is correct: regular meetings and working groups build shared understanding of perspectives across interfaces. Statement 4 is correct: stages often mark a change in influencers and key relationships, so they are good points to review them (see manual 3.2.2, 3.5.1).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: stakeholders include anyone who can affect or is affected by the project, many of whom have no formal role (manual 3.2.2).
n.1: Statements 1 and 3 are both wrong: stakeholders go well beyond formal roles, and engagement continues as relationships change (manual 3.2.2).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: relationships change over time, so engagement carries on throughout the project (manual 3.2.2).

7.q: What does risk velocity describe?
o: How near in time a risk might occur during the project
How quickly a risk would have an impact on objectives should it occur
The estimated chance that a risk will occur in the current stage
The rate at which new risks are added to the risk register
7.w: Risk velocity, a concept added in PRINCE2 7, is how quickly a risk would affect objectives once it occurs (see manual 9.2).

n.0: This is risk proximity: when the risk might happen, not how fast its effect would follow (manual 9.2).
n.2: This is risk probability, the estimated likelihood or frequency of occurrence (manual 9.2).
n.3: Velocity is a property of a single risk's impact after it occurs, not a count of new risks (manual 9.2).

7.q: Partway through a project, the board reviews whether the expected benefits still justify the remaining costs and risks before it approves the next stage plan. Which principle is the board applying by making this check?
o: Manage by exception
Learn from experience
Ensure continued business justification
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
7.w: Checking that benefits still justify the remaining costs and risks applies ensure continued business justification, which requires the justification to be revalidated throughout (manual 2.1, tab 5.2).

n.0: No tolerance is being set or breached; the board is checking whether the project is still worth doing (manual 2.5).
n.1: The board is not seeking lessons; it is revalidating the business justification (manual 2.2).
n.3: No roles or relationships are being defined; the check concerns the project's justification (manual 2.3).

7.q: The project board delegates to a change authority the approval of changes up to an agreed cost, and anything above that limit is referred back to the board. Which principle does this aspect of the issues practice support?
o: Manage by exception
Ensure continued business justification
Focus on products
Tailor to suit the project
7.w: Delegating authority for changes within defined limits, with matters beyond those limits escalated, applies manage by exception: limits of delegated authority with escalation when they would be exceeded (see manual 2.5, 10.2.4).

n.1: Business justification concerns whether the change is worth its costs and risks, not the limits on who may approve it (manual 2.1).
n.2: Focus on products concerns defining and delivering products; the limits of approval authority are a manage by exception mechanism (manual 2.6).
n.3: Tailoring adapts the method to the project; setting delegated limits with escalation is the core of manage by exception (manual 2.5, 2.7).

7.q:
Which two statements about assurance are correct?

1. Quality assurance is the responsibility of the project board.
2. Project assurance is independent of the project manager but not of the project.
3. Quality assurance is performed independently of the project management team.
4. Project support can carry out project assurance on behalf of the project board.
o: 1 and 4
2 and 3
1 and 2
3 and 4
7.w: Statement 2 is correct because project assurance is the board's responsibility and is independent of the project manager, not of the project; statement 3 is correct because quality assurance sits outside the project management team (see manual 8.2.3).

n.0: Both are wrong: project assurance (not quality assurance) is the board's responsibility, and project support can never carry out project assurance (manual 8.2.3, ch 6).
n.2: Statement 2 is correct but statement 1 confuses quality assurance with project assurance (manual 8.2.3).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct but statement 4 is wrong: project support must be kept separate from project assurance (manual ch 6).

7.q: A supplier proposes replacing the material specified in a baselined product description with a cheaper alternative. How is this handled in PRINCE2 7?
o: Through the change management approach, as it changes the project
Through the communication management approach, as users must be told
Through the benefits management approach, as cost affects benefits
Through the issues practice, as a request for change to a baseline
7.w: A proposal to change a baselined product is a request for change, an issue type handled by change control within the issues practice (see manual 10.1, 10.2.3).

n.0: The change management approach plans the organizational transition; changes to baselined products go through change control in the issues practice (manual 3.2.1, 10.2.3).
n.1: Communication may follow a decision, but the request itself must be captured and assessed through change control (manual 10.2.3).
n.2: The benefits management approach covers achieving outcomes and confirming benefits; a proposed change to a baselined product is a request for change (manual 5.5, 10.1).

7.q: What is the correct order of the first four steps of the PRINCE2 risk management technique?
o: Identify, assess, plan, implement
Identify, plan, assess, implement
Assess, identify, plan, implement
Identify, assess, implement, plan
7.w: The technique runs identify, assess, plan and implement in sequence, with communicate running alongside all four (see manual 9.3.1, figure 9.2).

n.1: Risks must be assessed and prioritized before responses are planned (manual 9.3.1).
n.2: A risk cannot be assessed until it has been identified (manual 9.3.1).
n.3: Responses are planned before they are implemented (manual 9.3.1).

8.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The person nominated to own agreed actions to respond to a risk, also known as the risk actionee, is the [?].
o: risk action owner
risk owner
issue owner
project assurance
8.w: The risk action owner (risk actionee) owns the agreed actions taken in response to a risk, on behalf of the risk owner (see manual 9.2).

n.1: The risk owner is responsible for responding to the risk as a whole and may nominate a risk action owner for specific actions (manual 9.2).
n.2: An issue owner manages an issue that has already arisen; the term for owning agreed risk actions is risk action owner (manual 9.2, 10.2).
n.3: Project assurance reviews how the project is run for the board; it is not the named owner of agreed risk actions (manual 6.2.4.7, 9.2).

8.q: Which statement best reflects how PRINCE2 treats opportunities?
o: They are managed with the same discipline as threats and are recorded in the risk register
They are recorded in the issue register as business opportunities as soon as they are identified
They are passed to the business layer, as they affect benefits rather than project objectives
They are noted in the daily log, while threats are entered in the risk register
8.w: Opportunities are risks with a positive effect on objectives, so they go through the same technique as threats and are recorded in the risk register (see manual 9.1, 9.5).

n.1: An uncertain future opportunity is a risk and belongs in the risk register; a business opportunity issue is an event that has already arisen (manual 9.5, 10.2).
n.2: Opportunities are managed by the project's risk practice; they are defined by their positive effect on objectives (manual 9.1).
n.3: Both threats and opportunities are recorded in the risk register; the daily log is for informal issues and notes (manual 9.5).

8.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

The quality management approach forms part of the project [?] documentation and describes the quality techniques, standards and responsibilities to be applied.
o: assurance
completion
mandate
initiation
8.w: The quality management approach is one of the management approaches agreed in initiating a project and held in the project initiation documentation (see manual 8.5, 15.4.2).

n.0: Project assurance is a board responsibility carried out by people, not a set of documents; the approaches sit in the project initiation documentation (manual 8.2.3, 15.4.2).
n.1: Documents produced at completion, such as the end project report, review performance at the end; the approach is set at the start (manual ch 19).
n.2: The project mandate comes from the business layer to trigger starting up a project; it does not contain the management approaches (manual ch 13).

8.q: A bank's project will introduce a new loan system. Which of these people is affected by the project but does not work within the project team?
o: The team manager building the loan screens
The senior user representing the lending department
A branch adviser who will process loans on the new system
The project support officer maintaining the registers
8.w: A branch adviser who will use the new system is affected by the project's outputs but holds no role in the project team, so is one of the people affected by the project rather than working within it (see manual 3.1, 3.3.1).

n.0: A team manager holds a role at the delivering level, so works within the project team (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: The senior user is a project board member, so works within the project team even though they represent the users (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Project support is a role in the project management team, so this person works within the project (manual 6.2.4).

8.q: A project to build a new depot will affect local residents, and a trade union represents staff who will work there. How does the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle treat these groups?
o: As stakeholders with whom the project should build relationships
As members of the project board representing the user interest
As outside the project's concern, as they are not part of the business
As suppliers, as they influence how the products will be delivered
8.w: Stakeholders can be inside or outside the business, including trade unions and communities, and the project management team builds relationships with them (manual 2.3).

n.1: Being affected by a project does not make a group a board member; the board represents the business, user and supplier interests through its roles (manual 2.3).
n.2: External groups such as unions and communities are stakeholders the principle expects the project to engage (manual 2.3).
n.3: Suppliers provide expertise, people and resources; residents and a union are stakeholders, not suppliers (manual 2.3).

8.q:
Which two statements about the management products of the plans practice are correct?
1. The project product description is written in starting up a project.
2. The 'references' heading of a work package description links the work to higher-level plans and documents.
3. A work package description may set benefits tolerances for the products it covers.
4. The project product description replaces the individual product descriptions in a stage plan.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
8.w: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The project product description is written in starting up a project, and a work package description includes references to higher-level plans and documents (see manual 7.3.1.1, 7.5).

n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: a work package description carries scope, cost and time tolerances; benefits tolerances are not set at work package level (manual 11.2.1). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 2.
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: stage plans use product descriptions for their products; the project product description is for the project plan only (manual 7.3.1.1). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 2.
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: a work package description carries scope, cost and time tolerances; benefits tolerances are not set at work package level (manual 11.2.1). Statement 2 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 1.

8.q: Which statement about stakeholder relationships is correct, according to PRINCE2 7?
o: They are fixed once the stakeholder analysis has been approved in the PID
They change over time, so engagement continues as the project progresses
They are managed by the business layer rather than the project management team
They are important during initiation and are left to the business after stage one
8.w: Relationships with stakeholders change over time, so engagement is ongoing, with ways of working set up so that all impacted areas stay involved as the project progresses (see manual 3.2.2).

n.0: Approving the PID does not freeze relationships; PRINCE2 expects them to change and the approaches to be reviewed at stage boundaries (manual 3.2.2, tab 6.5).
n.2: The project management team builds relationships with internal and external stakeholders; the board manages the interface with the organizational ecosystem (manual 2.3, 6.2.4).
n.3: Stakeholder engagement continues throughout the project; stages often mark changes in influencers and key relationships (manual 3.5.1).

8.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

In PRINCE2, monitoring and reporting are mainly time-driven, whereas [?], in the sense of decision-making, is event-driven.
o: forecasting
control
assurance
planning
8.w: PRINCE2 explains that monitoring and reporting are time-based, while control, meaning decision-making, is event-based; both are needed in every stage (see manual 11.2.2).

n.0: Forecasting is part of each progress review and looks forward; it is not the decision-making that PRINCE2 describes as event-driven (manual 11.2.5).
n.2: Assurance is the board's responsibility for checking the project independently of the project manager; it is not the decision-making described here (manual 6.2).
n.3: Planning belongs to the plans practice; the event-driven element of progress is control, meaning decisions (manual 11.2.2).

8.q: Which statement describes the purpose of the 'managing product delivery' process?
o: To control the link between the project manager and the team manager for specialist work
To assign and monitor work and take corrective action to keep the stage within tolerance
To let the board stay accountable while delegating day-to-day management
To set solid foundations before significant resources are committed
8.w: Managing product delivery controls the link between the project manager and the team manager by agreeing the requirements for acceptance, execution, reporting and delivery of specialist products (see manual 17.1).

n.1: This is the purpose of controlling a stage, the project manager's process for running the stage (manual 16.1).
n.2: This is the purpose of directing a project, the project board's process; the board is not involved in managing product delivery (manual 14.1).
n.3: This is the purpose of initiating a project, which runs in the initiation stage (manual 15.1).

8.q: During the second delivery stage, a competitor launches a similar service and the forecast benefits fall so far that they no longer outweigh the remaining costs and risks. What does the 'ensure continued business justification' principle require?
o: The project should be stopped, as it no longer has a valid justification
The project should continue, as its business case was approved at initiation
The current stage should be extended so extra scope can recover the benefits
The project manager should close the project without involving the board
8.w: If the justification is no longer valid, the principle says the project should be stopped; stopping a project that is no longer viable is not a failure (manual 2.1).

n.1: Approval at initiation is not enough: justification must remain valid throughout the project, so it cannot rest on the original approval (manual 2.1).
n.2: Extending the stage to add scope ignores that the benefits no longer justify the investment; the principle points to stopping (manual 2.1).
n.3: Premature closure is triggered by the project board, not decided by the project manager alone; the PM then prepares the closure (manual ch 19).

8.q: Which list contains three of the management approaches agreed during initiating a project?
o: Benefits, configuration management, and quality
Change control, risk, and communication
Stakeholder engagement, quality, and risk
Benefits, commercial, and digital and data
8.w: The nine management approaches are benefits, change, commercial, communication, digital and data, issue, quality, risk and sustainability, so benefits, commercial, and digital and data are all among them (see manual 15.4.2).

n.0: There is no configuration management approach in PRINCE2 7; control of changes to baselined products, including version control, is covered by the issue management approach (manual 15.4.2, 10.5).
n.1: There is no change control approach in PRINCE2 7: change control sits in the issue management approach, and the change management approach covers organizational change (manual 15.4.2).
n.2: There is no stakeholder engagement approach; stakeholder communication is covered by the communication management approach (manual 15.4.2).

8.q: Why is the 'do nothing differently' option considered first when developing a business case?
o: It is the option the project board is expected to prefer when the budget is tight
It is the option recorded under the expected dis-benefits heading of the business case
It is the option chosen when the project is compulsory under legislation or regulation
It is the baseline against which the costs and benefits of the other options are measured
8.w: 'Do nothing differently' is the starting point: the difference between it and the other options shows what the investment would buy, so it is the baseline for quantifying them (see manual 5.3.1).

n.0: No option is preferred by default; the options are compared to find the best overall value (manual 5.2.3, 5.3.1).
n.1: Doing nothing differently is a business option used for comparison, not a dis-benefit (manual 5.1, 5.3.1).
n.2: Compulsory projects still compare options and justify the chosen one; doing nothing differently is the baseline (manual 2.1, 5.2.3).

8.q: A project manager uses the planning technique to prepare the plan for stage 3. Which step of defining and analysing the products is NOT carried out for this plan?
o: Creating the product breakdown structure
Writing the project product description
Writing product descriptions
Creating the product flow diagram
8.w: The project product description is written for the project plan only. For a stage plan, the project manager creates a product breakdown structure, writes product descriptions and creates a product flow diagram (see manual 7.3.1.1).

n.0: Each plan has its own product breakdown structure of the products it will produce (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.2: Product descriptions are written for products at all levels of plan, including stage plans (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.3: The planning technique, including the product flow diagram, is repeated for each stage plan (manual 7.3.1.1).

8.q:
Which two statements about the activities of 'closing a project' are correct?
1. In 'request project closure', the project manager authorizes closure and notifies the business layer.
2. In 'confirm project acceptance', the team manager raises an exception report if products are rejected.
3. In 'prepare planned closure', the project manager updates the project plan with actuals from the final stage.
4. In 'evaluate the project', the project manager produces a lessons report and the end project report.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
8.w: Statements 3 and 4 are correct. Prepare planned closure updates the project plan with actuals, and evaluate the project produces the lessons report and end project report (see manual 19.4.1, 19.4.4).

n.0: Statements 1 and 2 are both wrong. The board authorizes closure and notifies the business layer (manual 14.4.5), and team managers do not raise exception reports (manual 16.4.7).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: the project manager requests closure and the board authorizes it (manual 19.4.5, 14.4.5). Statement 3 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 4.
n.2: Statement 2 is wrong: exception reports are raised by the project manager to the board (manual 16.4.7). Statement 4 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.

8.q: In which step of the business case technique does the project manager, at the end of each stage, update the business case with products delivered, costs, benefits realized and the latest forecasts?
o: The develop step
The maintain step
The confirm step
The check step
8.w: In the maintain step, at the end of each stage the project manager updates the business case with progress data and the latest forecasts of benefits and performance targets (see manual 5.3.1).

n.0: Develop produces the outline business case in starting up a project and the full business case in initiation (manual 5.3.1).
n.2: Confirm assesses whether intended benefits have been, or will be, realized, mostly after closure (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: Check is the assessment of whether the business case still shows a justified project; updating it with progress data is the maintain step (manual 5.3.1).

8.q: How does PRINCE2 define an output?
o: The result of change, normally affecting real-world behaviour
The measurable improvement that results from an outcome
The tangible or intangible deliverable of an activity
The completed set of products needed to deliver an outcome
8.w: An output is the tangible or intangible deliverable of an activity; in PRINCE2 outputs are the products the project delivers (see manual 5.1).

n.0: This defines an outcome, which arises when outputs are put to use (manual 5.1).
n.1: This defines a benefit (manual 5.1).
n.3: This defines a capability, the completed set of project outputs required to deliver an outcome (manual 5.1).

8.q: According to PRINCE2 7, how well a change is implemented, and therefore how well the project performs, depends on which factors?
o: The number of stages and the level of detail in each stage plan
The size of the change budget and the limits of delegated authority
The format of reports and the frequency of highlight reporting
The team's capabilities, its relationships and the people impacted
8.w: PRINCE2 7 explains that the success of the change, and so the project's performance, depends on the capabilities of the project team, the strength of their relationships and the people impacted by the change (see manual ch 3 introduction).

n.0: The number of stages and planning detail are decided through the plans practice and manage by stages; they are not what PRINCE2 names as driving how well change lands (manual ch 7).
n.1: The change budget and delegated authority govern approval of changes to the baseline under the issues practice (manual 10.2.4, 10.2.5).
n.2: Report formats and frequency are progress controls that can be tailored; they are not the people factors PRINCE2 links to successful change (manual 11.2.4).

8.q: In PRINCE2, the work breakdown structure forms a link between which two things?
o: The business case and the benefits management approach
The product breakdown structure and the work packages
The project mandate and the project brief for the project
The risk register and the issue register in the project log
8.w: The WBS links the product breakdown structure (what is to be produced) to the work packages (how the work is allocated and delivered) (see manual 6.2.5).

n.0: The business case and benefits management approach are linked through the business case practice, not by the WBS (manual 5.5).
n.2: The project brief is built from the mandate in starting up a project; the WBS is not involved (manual 13.4).
n.3: The risk and issue registers are records in the project log; the WBS is a hierarchy of work (manual 4.3.2, 6.2.5).

8.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
In the [?] activity, the board checks that post-project benefits reviews are planned and sends a closure notification to the business layer.
o: give ongoing direction
authorize project closure
authorize the project
authorize a stage or exception plan
8.w: In authorize project closure the board confirms that the project can close, ensures post-project benefits reviews are planned to cover the products in operational use, and notifies the business layer (see manual 14.4.5).

n.0: Give ongoing direction gives guidance during the project; it does not confirm closure or issue the closure notification (manual 14.4.3).
n.2: Authorize the project is the decision to proceed at the end of initiation, not the end of the project (manual 14.4.2).
n.3: Authorize a stage or exception plan approves the next stage or an exception plan; it is not used to close the project (manual 14.4.4).

8.q: Which statement BEST describes project management as PRINCE2 7 uses the term?
o: A temporary organization created to deliver business products under an agreed business case
Applying methods, tools, techniques and competencies to a project so it meets its objectives
Running the repeatable, ongoing operations that keep an organization's services available
Selecting and balancing an organization's whole set of change investments against its strategy
8.w: Project management is the application of methods, tools, techniques and competencies to a project so that it achieves its objectives (see manual ch 1 and the glossary). The project is the temporary organization; project management is what is done to direct and control it.

n.0: This is the definition of a project, not of project management; the question asks about the management activity applied to the project.
n.2: Running repeatable, ongoing operations is business as usual, which a project changes rather than manages.
n.3: Balancing an organization's whole set of change investments against strategy is portfolio management, not the management of a single project.

8.q: Which statement about delegating authority for changes is correct?
o: Delegation lets the change authority carry out the changes it approves within its own team
Once delegated, change authority stays fixed for the whole project and is not revisited
The board decides whether to delegate, and the delegation is reviewed at stage boundaries
The business layer appoints the change authority when it issues the project mandate
8.w: The project board decides whether to delegate authority for changes and to whom; the arrangement is reviewed at each stage boundary or when tolerances change (see manual 10.2.4).

n.0: Delegation concerns approving changes, not implementing them; implementation is done by the project manager through work packages (manual 10.2.4, 10.3.1.5).
n.1: Delegated change authority is reviewed at stage boundaries or when tolerances change (manual 10.2.4).
n.3: Delegating change authority is a project board decision recorded in the issue management approach, not something set in the mandate (manual 10.2.4, 10.5).

8.q: Which statement explains the difference between people within a project and people affected by it?
o: People within the project are employees of the business; affected people are external to it
People within the project hold roles in the project team; affected people may have no formal role
People within the project are the users; affected people are the suppliers and their staff
People within the project sit on the board; affected people are the team managers and teams
8.w: People within the project hold roles in the project team, while people affected by it may sit anywhere in the organizational ecosystem and may hold no formal role (see manual 3.1, 3.3.1).

n.0: Affected people can be inside the business, for example staff who integrate the new products into their area, and project team members can come from external suppliers (manual 3.3.1).
n.2: Users and suppliers can both be within the project (senior user, senior supplier, team members) and both can also be affected by it (manual 6.2.1).
n.3: Team managers and team members work within the project at the delivering level; they are not just affected by it (manual 6.2).

8.q: Which elements make up the PRINCE2 quality management technique?
o: Quality planning, quality control and quality assurance
Quality planning, quality control and project acceptance
Quality expectations, acceptance criteria and quality specifications
Quality review, quality audit and quality certification
8.w: The quality management technique has three parts: quality planning, quality control and project acceptance (see manual 8.3.1).

n.0: Quality planning, quality control and quality assurance are the three areas of guidance for effective quality management; the technique ends with project acceptance, not quality assurance (manual 8.2, 8.3.1).
n.2: Quality expectations, acceptance criteria and quality specifications are key quality concepts, not the steps of the technique (manual 8.1.1).
n.3: Reviews and audits are examples of quality methods or assurance activities, not the elements of the PRINCE2 technique (manual 8.3.1).

8.q: When an exception plan is prepared, what does PRINCE2 say about producing an end stage report?
o: It is replaced by a final highlight report
The team manager writes it for the stage
It is merged into the exception report
It is prepared only if the board requires one
8.w: In evaluate the stage the end stage report is normally produced at each stage end, but when an exception plan is being prepared it is produced if the board asks for it (see manual ch 18).

n.0: Highlight reports are regular reports in controlling a stage; they do not replace the end stage report (manual 16.4.8).
n.1: The end stage report is prepared by the project manager in evaluate the stage (manual ch 18).
n.2: The exception report was sent from controlling a stage before the exception plan was requested (manual 16.4.7).

8.q: A project manager forecasts that the current stage will finish two weeks later than planned, but this is still within the stage's time tolerance. What should the project manager do?
o: Take corrective action within the stage, without raising an exception report
Raise an exception report so that the project board can decide on the delay
Ask the business layer to extend the project tolerances to cover the delay
Prepare an exception plan in the managing a stage boundary process
8.w: If the project manager can resolve an issue within stage tolerance, no exception report is needed; the project manager takes corrective action in controlling a stage (see manual 11.2.6, 16.4.6).

n.1: An exception report is needed when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded; a delay within tolerance is the project manager's to manage (manual 11.2.6).
n.2: Project tolerances are not threatened by a delay that is within stage tolerance, and the project manager does not deal directly with the business layer on this (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: An exception plan is prepared when the board requests one after an exception report; none is needed for a deviation within tolerance (manual 11.3.1).

8.q: Which statement describes a 'thin client' delivery model in the commercial management approach?
o: Most of the work, including much of the project management, is carried out by suppliers
Most of the work is carried out by the business, with suppliers giving specialist input
The work is split evenly between the business and one external supplier under a joint contract
The supplier's director takes the executive role so that the supplier owns the business case
8.w: Delivery models range from thin client, where suppliers do most of the work including much of the project management, to thick client, where the business does most of the work (see manual 6.3.2.1, 6.5).

n.1: Most of the work being done by the business describes a thick client model (manual 6.3.2.1).
n.2: Thin and thick client describe how much work suppliers do rather than the business; an even split is not the definition of thin client (manual 6.3.2.1).
n.3: The executive represents the business interest and owns the business case; the delivery model does not change who holds that role (manual 6.2.4.1).

8.q: To keep a small project lean, the finance director proposes being both executive and project manager. Why is this unacceptable?
o: Because the executive must come from outside the business
Because a small project is directed by the business layer
Because the senior user appoints the project manager
Because executive and project manager roles must stay separate
