8.w: Roles can be combined to suit a small project, but the rules still apply: the executive role cannot be combined with the project manager role (see manual 2.7 and 6.2.4).

n.0: The executive is usually a senior person from the business who can secure funding; there is no requirement for an outsider (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: The business layer sits outside the project; even a small project is directed by its project board (fig 6.2, 6.2.1).
n.2: The executive appoints the rest of the project management team, with the business layer accountable; the senior user does not appoint the project manager (manual 6.2.4).

8.q: PRINCE2 assumes no particular organizational context. Which parties does it describe as typically involved in a project?
o: Users, suppliers and business decision-makers
Sponsors, contractors and external regulators
Programme managers, auditors and end users
Shareholders, customers and team members
8.w: The typical parties are the users who specify the outputs they need, the suppliers who provide resources and expertise, and the business decision-makers who make sure the investment is and stays justified (see manual 1.5).

n.1: PRINCE2 has no sponsor role, and regulators are stakeholders rather than one of the three typical parties (manual 1.5, 6.2.4).
n.2: Users are a typical party, but programme managers and auditors are not the other two; the typical parties are users, suppliers and business decision-makers (manual 1.5).
n.3: Shareholders and team members are not the typical parties named; the business, user and supplier interests are represented on the project board (manual 1.5, 6.2.1).

8.q: A key server used by the project team fails overnight, and work on two products has stopped this morning. Which type of issue has an immediate and negative impact such as this?
o: Concern
Problem
Off-specification
Request for change
8.w: A problem is an issue with an immediate and negative impact on the project, such as work stopping because a server has failed (see manual 10.1).

n.0: A concern is an issue whose timing and impact still need to be assessed; here the impact is already immediate and known (manual 10.1).
n.2: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications; the failed server is not a product failing its specification (manual 10.2.3).
n.3: Nobody is proposing a change to a baseline; the event is a failure that has already happened (manual 10.2.3).

8.q: In PRINCE2's figure of the five integrated elements, which element is shown as the foundation on which practices, people and processes rest?
o: People
Processes
Principles
Project context
8.w: Figure 1.1 shows the principles as the foundation, with practices, people and processes built on them, all within the project context (see manual 1.2).

n.0: People are shown at the centre, above the principles, not as the foundation.
n.1: Processes are one of the three elements built on the principles.
n.3: The project context surrounds all the other elements; it is not shown as the foundation they rest on.

8.q: How might the project plan for an iterative-incremental project arrange its delivery stages?
o: As a single delivery stage, because acceptance criteria cannot change once initiation is complete
As delivery stages with no initiation stage, because the product backlog replaces the project initiation documentation
As several delivery stages in which quality and acceptance criteria are refined alongside the products using a product backlog
As one management stage per iteration, each authorized by a team manager instead of the board
8.w: For an iterative-incremental project, the project plan may provide several delivery stages, with quality and acceptance criteria refined in parallel with developing the products through a product backlog (see manual 7.2.3).

n.0: Iterative-incremental projects refine acceptance criteria during delivery, and they may use several delivery stages (manual 7.2.3).
n.1: Every PRINCE2 project has an initiation stage that produces the project initiation documentation (manual 7.2.3, 4.3.1).
n.3: Management stages are authorized by the project board in directing a project, not by team managers (manual 7.2.3).

8.q: Which statement about team plans is correct?
o: They are required for every work package and are approved in directing a project
They are produced by the project manager to control each management stage
They are replaced by an exception plan when work package tolerances are exceeded
They are optional and are produced by a team manager for one or more work packages
8.w: A team plan is produced by a team manager to organize and control the work of a team on one or more work packages. Team plans are optional in PRINCE2 (see manual 7.2.2.3).

n.0: Team plans are optional, and the project board does not direct work at team level (manual 7.2.2.3).
n.1: The project manager controls a stage using the stage plan; team plans are produced by team managers (manual 7.2.2.2, 7.2.2.3).
n.2: Exception plans replace stage or project plans, not team plans; work package deviations are handled by the project manager (manual 7.2.2.4).

8.q: In which type of team does PRINCE2 say that information tends to be shared organically through formal and informal networks?
o: A virtual team whose members work from their homes
A co-located team working together at the same site
A hybrid team that meets in person once a month
A remote team spread across several time zones
8.w: In co-located teams, information tends to flow organically through formal and informal networks; virtual, remote and hybrid teams need more deliberate methods (see manual 3.3.3, 3.4).

n.0: Virtual teams do not share information organically in the same way; social cohesion has to be built more deliberately (manual 3.3.3).
n.2: Hybrid working is one of the arrangements where cohesion needs deliberate effort, such as synchronized co-location days (manual 3.3.3).
n.3: Remote teams at a distance from each other need deliberate methods to build cohesion and share information (manual 3.3.3).

8.q: In PRINCE2, what are the user's quality expectations?
o: The measures applied by those doing quality control and the levels each finished product must reach
The permissible deviation in a product's quality before the deviation must be escalated
A need or expectation that has been documented in an approved management product
A statement about the quality expected from the project product, recorded in the project product description
8.w: The user's quality expectations are a statement about the quality expected from the project product; they are captured in the project product description and are typically high-level (see manual 8.1.1, 8.2.1.1).

n.0: Measures applied in quality control, with the levels to be met, are quality specifications, held in product descriptions (manual 8.1.1).
n.1: The permissible deviation in quality before escalation is quality tolerance (manual 8.2.1.2).
n.2: A need or expectation documented in an approved management product is the general definition of a requirement (manual 8.1.1).

8.q: The project board agrees that the current stage may cost up to 5% more than planned before the project manager must escalate to the board. Which principle is being applied?
o: Manage by stages
Manage by exception
Ensure continued business justification
Tailor to suit the project
8.w: Setting a cost tolerance for the stage, within which the PM can act without escalating, is manage by exception (manual 2.5).

n.0: Manage by stages provides the stage itself, but setting the permitted variation before escalation is manage by exception (manual 2.4, 2.5).
n.2: The board is not judging whether the project is still worthwhile; it is setting delegated limits (manual 2.1).
n.3: Tailoring adapts the method; setting a tolerance for a stage is manage by exception (manual 2.7).

8.q:
Which two statements about managing a stage boundary in the PRINCE2 lifecycle are correct?
1. It is first used towards the end of the initiation stage.
2. It is used at the end of the final stage to prepare for closure.
3. It can be used during a stage to prepare an exception plan.
4. It is carried out by the project board at the directing level.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
8.w: Statement 1 is correct: managing a stage boundary is first used near the end of initiation to plan the first delivery stage. Statement 3 is correct: it is also used whenever the board asks for an exception plan (see manual chapter 12, fig 12.1, and 18.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: managing a stage boundary is not used at the end of the final stage; closing a project is carried out within the final stage instead (manual 12).
n.2: Both statements are wrong: managing a stage boundary is not used at the end of the final stage, and it is run by the project manager at the managing level, not by the board (manual 12, 18.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the project manager carries out managing a stage boundary; the board then decides in directing a project (manual 12, 14.4).

8.q: Which list gives the five integrated elements of PRINCE2 7?
o: Principles, people, practices, processes and the project context
Principles, themes, processes, people and tailoring to the environment
Principles, people, practices, processes and the business layer
Principles, roles, practices, processes and the project context
8.w: The five integrated elements are principles, people, practices, processes and the project context (see manual 1.2, figure 1.1).

n.1: Themes and tailoring to the project environment belong to the 2017 model of four elements; PRINCE2 7 uses practices and the project context.
n.2: The business layer is the level of the organization that commissions the project, not one of the integrated elements; the fifth element is the project context.
n.3: Roles are covered within the organizing practice and the people element; 'roles' is not itself an integrated element, whereas people is.

8.q: Which PRINCE2 role description includes monitoring and supporting social cohesion within the project ecosystem?
o: Project support
Team manager
Project assurance
Project board
8.w: The project board's role description includes focusing on the safety and well-being of the project team and monitoring and supporting social cohesion within the project ecosystem (see manual 6.2.4).

n.0: Project support provides administrative services such as registers, meetings and version control (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: The team manager's description covers relationships within the team and the safety and well-being of team members, not cohesion across the whole project ecosystem (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Project assurance gives the board independent assurance in the business, user and supplier areas (manual 6.2.4).

8.q: During delivery, a team adds several extra features that are not in any agreed product description because it believes users will like them. Which principle is this team weakening?
o: Learn from experience
Manage by stages
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Focus on products
8.w: Focus on products means doing no more work than needed to deliver the agreed products; adding unagreed features is scope creep, which the principle is meant to control (manual 2.6).

n.0: Learn from experience concerns seeking and sharing lessons; the problem here is work beyond the agreed products (manual 2.2).
n.1: Manage by stages concerns stage-by-stage planning and decisions; the team is going beyond its agreed products (manual 2.4).
n.2: The team's roles are not the issue; it is delivering products that were never defined or agreed (manual 2.6).

8.q: Why does PRINCE2 expect both event-driven and time-driven controls to be used in every stage?
o: Time-driven controls apply in the initiation stage, while event-driven controls apply in the delivery stages
Event-driven controls are used by team managers, while time-driven controls are used by the business layer
Time-driven controls replace event-driven controls once the project team has gained experience
Periodic reports keep each level informed, while key decisions are taken when events such as a stage end occur
8.w: Time-driven monitoring and reporting (highlight and checkpoint reports) keep people informed between decisions, while event-driven control (for example at the end of a stage or on an exception) is where decisions are taken; both are needed in every stage (see manual 11.2.2).

n.0: Both types of control are needed in every stage, including initiation and delivery stages; they are not split by stage (manual 11.2.2).
n.1: The two types differ by what triggers them, not by who uses them; for example the project manager produces both highlight and exception reports (manual 11.2.2).
n.2: Experience can reduce how often reports are needed, but it does not remove the event-driven decision points (manual 11.2.2, 11.2.4).

8.q: Which list gives the three delivery approaches named in PRINCE2 7?
o: Predictive-sequential, adaptive-iterative and blended
Linear-phased, agile-incremental and combined
Linear-sequential, iterative-incremental and hybrid
Waterfall-sequential, Scrum-iterative and mixed
8.w: PRINCE2 7 names three delivery approaches: linear-sequential, iterative-incremental and hybrid (see manual 1.5.3).

n.0: These are not PRINCE2 7 terms; the method uses linear-sequential, iterative-incremental and hybrid.
n.1: These are not PRINCE2 7 terms; agile ways of working fall under the iterative-incremental approach.
n.3: Waterfall and Scrum are general industry terms, not the delivery approaches PRINCE2 7 names.

8.q:
Which two statements about when PRINCE2 plans are produced are correct?
1. The project plan is created in initiating a project and baselined when the project board approves it.
2. An exception plan is prepared in controlling a stage as soon as an exception report is sent.
3. Team plans are prepared for every work package and are approved by the executive.
4. Each stage plan after initiation is prepared near the end of the stage before it.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
8.w: Statements 1 and 4 are correct. The project plan is created in initiating a project and baselined on approval by the board; each later stage plan is prepared near the end of the current stage, close to when its work happens (see manual 7.2.2.1, 7.2.2.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the exception report is raised in controlling a stage, but the exception plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary if the board decides to address the exception (manual 7.2.2.4). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 4.
n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: team plans are optional and are produced by team managers (manual 7.2.2.3). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 4.
n.3: Statements 2 and 3 are both wrong. Statement 2 is wrong: the exception report is raised in controlling a stage, but the exception plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary if the board decides to address the exception (manual 7.2.2.4). Statement 3 is wrong: team plans are optional and are produced by team managers (manual 7.2.2.3).

8.q: Which statement describes the purpose of the commercial management approach?
o: To describe how the project will communicate with its stakeholders, including its suppliers
To set out who is in the project management team and how its members will work together
To describe how the benefits will be measured and reviewed, including after the project closes
To describe how commercial agreements will be secured, serviced and maintained for the project
8.w: The commercial management approach sets out the procedures, techniques, standards and responsibilities for securing, servicing and maintaining the project's commercial agreements, covering market engagement, procurement and contract management (see manual 6.5).

n.0: How the project communicates with stakeholders is set out in the communication management approach (manual 3.4).
n.1: Who is involved and how they will work together is the project management team structure (manual 6.5).
n.2: Measuring and reviewing benefits is covered by the benefits management approach (manual 5.5).

8.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The outcomes and benefits of a project need to align with the organization's business objectives, which may include [?] goals set by the organization.
o: environmental, social and governance
planning, estimating and scheduling
supplier, contractor and procurement
stage, work package and checkpoint
8.w: Outcomes and benefits must align with and contribute to business objectives, which may include environmental, social and governance (ESG) goals; sustainability targets should reference those goals (see manual 5.2.2).

n.1: Planning, estimating and scheduling belong to the plans practice; the business objectives referred to here may include ESG goals (manual 7.1, 5.2.2).
n.2: Supplier and procurement arrangements are part of commercial management; the alignment described is with ESG goals (manual ch 6, 5.2.2).
n.3: Stages, work packages and checkpoints are levels of plan, delegation and reporting, not types of business objective (manual 11.2.1, 5.2.2).

8.q: Why does the project management team periodically compare the status of products with the versions the board approved?
o: To find any discrepancies between what has been authorized and what actually exists
To release the change budget so that approved changes can be funded and delivered
To decide which change authority should be appointed for the next delivery stage
To confirm that the benefits in the business case have been realized as forecast
8.w: Periodically verifying that the actual status of products reflects their authorized state reveals discrepancies; it is part of the baselines guidance and helps the team understand product status (see manual 10.2.1).

n.1: The change budget is what enables approved changes to be funded; checking product status does not release it (manual 10.2.5).
n.2: The project board decides on delegating change authority, reviewing it at stage boundaries; a status check does not make that decision (manual 10.2.4).
n.3: Benefits are reviewed through the benefits management approach, not by checking product versions against their authorized state (manual 5.5).

8.q: In which 'managing a stage boundary' activity are the actuals from the finishing stage and the forecasts for the next stage added to the project plan?
o: Update the project plan
Prepare next stage plan
Update the business case
Evaluate the stage
8.w: Update the project plan brings in actual progress from the finishing stage and forecasts from the next stage plan or exception plan, and the revised costs and dates feed the business case (see manual ch 18).

n.1: This activity produces the detailed plan for the next stage; the project plan is then updated to reflect it (manual ch 18).
n.2: The business case takes its revised costs and dates from the updated project plan; it does not update the plan (manual ch 18).
n.3: This activity reviews the stage's performance in the end stage report (manual ch 18).

8.q: Which challenge is PRINCE2's principle of ensuring continued business justification designed to address?
o: Teams working in different locations finding it hard to build relationships
Projects carrying on after they have stopped being worth the investment
Specialist products being built with unsuitable engineering techniques
Project staff being unsure what common project terms actually mean
8.w: A PRINCE2 project must have business justification to start and to continue; if it is no longer justified it should be stopped. This tackles the common problem of projects continuing with few real benefits (see manual 1.4 and 2.1).

n.0: Building relationships across dispersed teams is addressed by the people element and the define roles, responsibilities and relationships principle.
n.2: PRINCE2 works alongside specialist, industry-specific models; it does not set the engineering techniques used to build products.
n.3: A shared vocabulary is a benefit of PRINCE2's common language and concepts, not of the business justification principle.

8.q: The project board has just approved the project brief and the initiation stage plan. What triggers the initiating a project process?
o: The project mandate from the business layer
The request to initiate from the project manager
The project authorization notice from the board
The initiation notice from authorize initiation
8.w: Initiating a project is triggered by the initiation notice the board issues in the authorize initiation activity of directing a project (see manual 15.3, 14.4.1).

n.0: The project mandate triggers starting up a project, which comes before the board's decision to initiate (manual 13.3).
n.1: The request to initiate is the project manager's request to the board; the board must authorize initiation before initiation starts (manual 13.4.8, 14.4.1).
n.2: The project authorization notice comes at the end of initiation, when the board authorizes the project (manual 14.4.2).

8.q: Which statement defines the work breakdown structure (WBS) in PRINCE2?
o: A hierarchy of all the products to be produced during a plan, from the major products downwards
A diagram showing the sequence in which products are developed and the dependencies between them
A chart showing the roles in the project management team and the lines of authority between them
A hierarchy of all the work to be done in a project, linking the product breakdown to the work packages
8.w: The WBS is a hierarchy of all the work to be done during a project, forming the link between the product breakdown structure and the work packages (see manual 6.2.5).

n.0: A hierarchy of all the products of a plan is the product breakdown structure, created in the plans practice's planning technique (manual 7.3.1).
n.1: A diagram of product sequence and dependencies is the product flow diagram (manual 7.3.1).
n.2: A chart of roles and lines of authority belongs in the project management team structure (manual 6.5).

8.q: Why does PRINCE2 expect a forecast breach of tolerance to be escalated as soon as it is identified?
o: So the project manager can widen the stage tolerances in good time
So the next level of management can decide while there is still time to act
So the team manager can approve an exception plan before the stage ends
So the business layer can take over the project board's role for the stage
8.w: Escalating as soon as a breach is forecast alerts the next level of management early, while there are still options to respond, which is the point of managing by exception (see manual 2.5, 11.2.6).

n.0: Stage tolerances are set by the board; the project manager cannot widen them (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Exception plans are prepared by the project manager and approved by the board, not by a team manager (manual 11.3.1).
n.3: Escalation lets the next level decide on the exception; it does not transfer the board's role to the business layer (manual 11.2.6).

8.q: Which pairing of a lifecycle point with the business case work done there is correct?
o: End of initiation: the board checks the outline business case to authorize the first stage
End of each delivery stage: the project manager confirms benefits with the business layer
End of starting up a project: the board checks the outline business case to authorize initiation
After closure: the project board checks the updated business case before closing the project
8.w: The board checks the outline business case at the end of starting up a project when deciding to authorize initiation, then checks the full business case at the end of initiation (see manual 5.3.1, 14.4.1).

n.0: At the end of initiation the board checks the full business case when authorizing the project, not the outline version (manual 5.3.1, 14.4.2).
n.1: At each stage end the project manager maintains the business case and the board checks it; benefits confirmation is mainly post-project (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: Checking happens within the project; after closure the business confirms benefits, and the board has already authorized closure (manual 5.2.1, 14.4.5).

8.q: In a risk workshop, the team spends most of its time on a minor supplier delay due next week, because it is soon, and gives little attention to a serious regulatory threat six months away. Which bias is most likely affecting them?
o: Optimism bias
Proximity bias
Groupthink
Loss aversion
8.w: Proximity bias is a mindset in which situations closer in time seem riskier and more important than those further in the future (see manual 9.2.4).

n.0: Optimism bias discounts risk on the assumption of success; here the team's attention follows how soon each risk is (manual 9.2.4).
n.2: Groupthink is about keeping group cohesion rather than voicing other views; nothing suggests people are suppressing disagreement (manual 9.2.4).
n.3: Loss aversion values avoiding loss over gains; the team's focus here is driven by nearness in time (manual 9.2.4).

8.q: Midway through a stage, a key relationship in the project changes when one team manager is replaced by another. What does PRINCE2 suggest about the affected roles and responsibilities?
o: They stay as agreed in the PID until the end of the project
They are passed unchanged to the new team manager by project support
They are taken on by the executive until the next stage boundary is reached
They are reviewed against the changed relationship and updated as needed
8.w: Roles and responsibilities are viewed through the lens of key relationships and should be reviewed and updated when those relationships shift (see manual 3.3.2).

n.0: Freezing roles until closure ignores the guidance to review roles whenever key relationships shift (manual 3.3.2).
n.1: Project support provides administration; handing roles over unchanged ignores the new person's capability, authority and availability (manual 3.3.2, 6.2.4).
n.2: The executive directs the project and does not take over a team manager's delivery responsibilities (manual 6.2.4).

8.q: A supplier wants to use its in-house iterative-incremental framework with agile approaches. To avoid confusion, what might the project manager propose?
o: Replacing the project board with the supplier's product owner
Adding a coach to help teams combine PRINCE2 with that framework
Removing stage boundaries so the supplier can work continuously
Asking the supplier to switch to linear-sequential delivery
8.w: Where a supplier uses its own iterative-incremental, agile framework, the project manager might propose adding a coach role to guide teams in working effectively with the combination of PRINCE2 and that framework (see manual 2.7).

n.0: The project board directs the project and is accountable to the business; tailoring for a supplier's framework does not remove it (manual 6.2.1).
n.2: Manage by stages is a principle and cannot be tailored away; an iterative-incremental project still has an initiation stage and delivery stages (manual 2.4, 2.7).
n.3: PRINCE2 is not specific to a delivery method; the aim is to tailor the method to the supplier's approach, not to force a different one (manual 1.1, 2.7).

8.q:
Which two statements about the purpose of the risk practice are correct?
1. It identifies, assesses and controls uncertainty that would affect the project's objectives.
2. It collects issues and controls changes to the project's baseline.
3. It improves the ability of the project to succeed.
4. It makes sure that every threat is removed before a stage is authorized.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
8.w: Statement 1 is the core of the purpose, and statement 3 is its result: controlling uncertainty improves the project's ability to succeed (see manual 9.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is the purpose of the issues practice, not the risk practice (manual 10.1).
n.2: Statement 2 describes the issues practice, and statement 4 is wrong because threats cannot all be removed; many are reduced, accepted or covered by contingent plans (manual 9.1, 9.2.3.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the practice does not require every threat to be removed before a stage is authorized, and removal is not possible for many threats (manual 9.2.3.1).

8.q: According to PRINCE2, what does an effective project team require?
o: People who share the same professional background and working style
Team members drawn from one organization so that reporting lines are kept simple
A diverse set of capabilities, competencies and perspectives matching the project's needs
The most senior people available from each of the business, user and supplier areas
8.w: PRINCE2 says an effective team needs a diverse set of capabilities, competencies and perspectives that match what the project requires (see manual 3.3.2).

n.0: A shared background and style works against the diversity of capabilities and perspectives that PRINCE2 says effective teams need (manual 3.3.2).
n.1: Project teams typically work across organizational boundaries; the guidance is to match diverse capabilities to the project's needs, not to draw from one organization (manual 3.3, 3.3.2).
n.3: Seniority is not the test: roles should reflect capability, authority and availability, matched to the project's needs (manual 3.3.2).

8.q: Which statement describes the delivering level in the PRINCE2 organizational structure?
o: It provides the project mandate and sets the tolerances within which the project board works
It directs the project within the constraints that have been set by the commissioning party
It manages and makes decisions on its element of the work within constraints set by the project manager
It manages the whole project day to day within the constraints established by the project board
8.w: Team managers and team members at the delivering level manage and make decisions on their element of the project within the constraints set by the project manager, co-creating with others where needed (see manual 6.2, fig 6.2).

n.0: Providing the mandate and setting project-level tolerances is the business layer (manual fig 6.2).
n.1: Directing within the constraints set by the commissioning party is the directing level, the project board (manual fig 6.2).
n.3: Day-to-day management of the whole project is the managing level, the project manager (manual fig 6.2).

8.q: A trainee project manager is listing the steps of the PRINCE2 issues technique for an exam revision card. Which is NOT one of the steps of the issues technique?
o: Recommend
Identify
Implement
Decide
8.w: Identify is the first step of the risk technique. The issues technique has five steps: capture, assess, recommend, decide and implement (see manual 10.3.1, 9.3.1).

n.0: Recommend is the third step of the issues technique, where options are evaluated and a recommendation made (manual 10.3.1.3).
n.2: Implement is the fifth step, where corrective action is taken and records and baselines updated (manual 10.3.1.5).
n.3: Decide is the fourth step, where the person or group with authority makes the decision (manual 10.3.1.4).

8.q: During quality planning, why should the project product description identify all of the project's major products?
o: So that requirements outside the approved scope do not creep into the lower-level product descriptions
So that the team manager can agree a quality tolerance for each product in the work package description
So that the quality register can show the result of each quality check before the products are built
So that quality assurance can approve each major product before the project board accepts it
8.w: By identifying all the major products in the project product description, the project prevents requirements that are outside the approved scope from appearing in product descriptions (see manual 8.2.1.1).

n.1: A work package description carries scope, cost and time tolerances only; quality tolerance is not agreed there (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: The quality register records checks that are planned or have taken place; it does not show results before products exist (manual 8.5).
n.3: Quality assurance gives independent confidence in the quality control measures; it does not approve individual products before acceptance (manual 8.2.3).

8.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

Under the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle, the project management team builds relationships with and between internal and [?] stakeholders.
o: senior
external
commissioning
operational
8.w: The principle says the project management team initiates and builds relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (manual 2.3).

n.0: The principle covers stakeholders inside and outside the business, not a seniority group (manual 2.3).
n.2: The commissioning organization is the business layer, which is internal; the pairing in the principle is internal and external (manual 2.3).
n.3: Operational staff are one internal group; the principle refers to internal and external stakeholders (manual 2.3).

9.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

Quality tolerances support the principle of manage by [?], because a product's quality may vary within agreed limits before the deviation has to be escalated.
o: exception
stages
objectives
results
9.w: Quality is one of the seven aspects for which tolerances are set; working within tolerance and escalating forecast breaches is manage by exception (see manual 2.5, 8.2.1.2).

n.1: Manage by stages concerns stage-by-stage planning and control with decision points, not the limits of delegated authority (manual 2.4).
n.2: 'Manage by objectives' is not a PRINCE2 principle; tolerances apply manage by exception (manual 2.5).
n.3: 'Manage by results' is not a PRINCE2 principle; tolerances apply manage by exception (manual 2.5).

9.q: A hospital project brings together nurses, software developers and estates staff to introduce a new patient check-in system that will alter how reception teams across the site work. Which characteristic of a project does this BEST illustrate?
o: The project is unique
The project is cross-functional
The project is temporary
The project carries uncertainty
9.w: Cross-functional means people with different skills working together, on a temporary basis, to introduce a change that affects others outside the team (see manual 1.3). Here clinical, technical and estates staff combine on a change that affects reception teams.

n.0: Unique means each project differs in some way, such as its team, customer or location; the stem stresses the mix of skills and the people affected, not how this project differs from others.
n.2: Temporary means the need for the project ends once the change is in place; nothing in the stem describes the project ending.
n.3: Uncertainty refers to the extra threats and opportunities projects bring; the stem describes who is working together, not risk.

9.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The issues practice supports the '[?]' principle, because change control is based on clearly defined products and the approved versions held in the baseline.
o: focus on products
manage by stages
learn from experience
define roles, responsibilities and relationships
9.w: Focus on products underpins change control: product definitions and baselined versions make it clear what is being changed (see manual 2.6, 10.1).

n.1: Manage by stages provides stage-by-stage planning and decision points; it is not what change control of product versions rests on (manual 2.4).
n.2: Learn from experience concerns lessons; the link described here is with defined products and their baselined versions (manual 2.2).
n.3: This principle concerns roles and relationships in the project management team, not the products that change control is based on (manual 2.3).

9.q:
Which two statements about reporting progress in PRINCE2 are correct?

1. The intervals for highlight reports are defined by the project board.
2. The frequency of checkpoint reports is defined in the work package.
3. Changing the formality of progress reports is not a permitted form of tailoring.
4. Lessons are reported to the project board through checkpoint reports.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
9.w: Highlight reports are produced at intervals defined by the project board (1), and checkpoint reports at the frequency defined in the work package (2) (see manual 11.5).

n.0: Statement 1 is correct, but adjusting the frequency and formality of reports is a recognized form of tailoring (manual 2.7).
n.2: Statement 2 is correct, but checkpoint reports go from the team manager to the project manager, not to the board (manual 11.5).
n.3: Both are wrong: report formality can be tailored, and checkpoint reports are sent to the project manager, not the board (manual 2.7, 11.5).

9.q: An auditor from a manufacturer's central quality office, acting for the company's quality management system rather than for the project board, confirms that a project's planned inspections and tests are suitable. Which activity is this?
o: Quality assurance
Project assurance
Quality control
Quality planning
9.w: An independent check, from outside the project management team and on behalf of the business's quality management system, that the quality control measures are appropriate is quality assurance (see manual 8.2.3).

n.1: Project assurance is carried out on behalf of the project board; this auditor acts for the company's quality system instead (manual 8.2.3).
n.2: Quality control is the carrying out of the inspections and tests themselves, by the project, not an independent review of them (manual 8.2.2).
n.3: Quality planning is the project's own work of defining specifications, product descriptions and the quality management approach (manual 8.2.1).

9.q: Why does initiating a project agree the management approaches before preparing the project plan?
o: The plan must include the costs of the approaches, which the business layer sets in advance
The approaches set out how the project will be run, so the controls and plan can build on them
The board approves each approach separately before any planning is allowed to start
The approaches replace product descriptions, so the plan can be made without them
9.w: Once the management approaches are defined, project controls and the project plan can follow, because they need to reflect how risk, quality, issues, communication and the other areas will be managed (see manual 15.4.2, 15.4.4).

n.0: The business layer does not set the cost of the approaches in advance; the approaches are derived from business standards and the users' expectations (manual 15.4.2).
n.2: The board approves the approaches as part of the PID in authorize the project, at the end of initiation, not before planning (manual 14.4.2).
n.3: Product descriptions are still created as part of planning; the approaches describe how the project is managed, not what each product is (manual 15.4.4).

9.q: Which roles make up the project board in a PRINCE2 project?
o: Executive, project manager and senior supplier(s)
Executive, senior user(s) and senior supplier(s)
Senior user(s), senior supplier(s) and project assurance
Executive, senior user(s) and team manager(s)
9.w: The project board consists of the executive (one person), the senior user(s) and the senior supplier(s), so that the business, user and supplier interests are all represented (see manual 6.2.1, 6.2.4).

n.0: The project manager works at the managing level and is not a board member; the senior user role is missing (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: Project assurance is a board responsibility, not a board role, and the executive is missing (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Team managers work at the delivering level, not on the board (manual fig 6.2).

9.q: A hospital project must prepare nurses to move from paper notes to tablets on the wards. Separately, the board asks for a new report to be added to the approved specification. Which pairing reflects PRINCE2 7?
o: Both through the issues practice, as each is a change to the project
Both through the change management approach, as each affects users
Nurses' move through change management; new report through change control
Nurses' move through change control; new report through change management
9.w: Preparing nurses for a new way of working is organizational transition, planned through change management. Adding a report to an approved specification changes the baseline, so it goes through change control in the issues practice (see manual 3.2.1, 10.2.3).

n.0: Moving nurses to a new way of working is not a change to the baseline; it is planned in the change management approach (manual 3.2.1).
n.1: The new report changes an approved specification, so it must go through change control in the issues practice (manual 10.2.3).
n.3: This reverses the two: people's transition is change management and baseline changes are change control (manual 3.2.1, 10.2.3).

9.q: A stage has gone into exception. What is the effect of the project board approving the exception plan for that stage?
o: It extends the stage with no new boundary
It replaces the team plans for the stage
It marks a stage boundary for the revised stage
It resets the business layer's project tolerances
9.w: An exception plan is prepared in managing a stage boundary and, once the board approves it, its approval marks a stage boundary for the revised stage (see manual ch 18).

n.0: Approval of an exception plan creates a stage boundary; it does not just stretch the existing stage (manual ch 18).
n.1: An exception plan replaces a stage or project plan, not team plans (manual 7.2.2.4, ch 18).
n.3: A stage-level exception plan replaces the stage plan within existing project tolerances; the board does not reset them (manual 11.2.1, ch 18).

9.q: Which statement about the 'unique' characteristic of a project is correct?
o: A project that closely resembles an earlier one is treated as business as usual
Uniqueness means the project's outputs cannot be reused by the organization later
Uniqueness means the project should not draw on lessons from previous projects
Similar projects still differ in some way, such as team, customer or location
9.w: Every project is unique: an organization may run many similar projects with a familiar pattern of work, but each one differs in some way, such as its team, customer, supplier, location or timeframe (see manual 1.3).

n.0: A project that resembles an earlier one is still a project; it introduces change and differs in some way, so it is not business as usual.
n.1: Uniqueness is about each project differing from others; it says nothing to stop the organization reusing what a project delivers.
n.2: Similar projects create a familiar pattern of work, and PRINCE2's learn from experience principle expects lessons from previous projects to be used.

9.q: Why does PRINCE2 prefer a clear end to a project rather than letting it drift into operational use?
o: Costs stop, ownership passes to the business and the team disbands
The benefits can all be realized before the team is released
The board can carry out the post-project benefits reviews
The team can resolve every open issue before handover
9.w: A project is temporary. A clear end means project costs stop, ownership of the products passes to the business and the team can be disbanded, which is better than a slow drift into use (see manual 19.3).

n.1: Many benefits arise after closure and are checked in post-project benefits reviews (manual 19.2, 14.4.5).
n.2: Post-project benefits reviews are carried out by the business after closure, not by the board during the project (manual 19.2).
n.3: Open issues are passed on with follow-on action recommendations rather than all being resolved (manual 19.2).

9.q:
Which two statements about the work breakdown structure are correct?

1. It is a hierarchy of all the products of a plan.
2. It is used by the business layer to set the project-level tolerances.
3. It links the product breakdown structure to the work packages.
4. It helps the project manager decide how to structure teams and the boundaries between them.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
9.w: The WBS links the product breakdown structure to the work packages (statement 3) and supports the project manager in structuring teams and their boundaries (statement 4) (see manual 6.2.5).

n.0: Statement 1 describes the product breakdown structure, and statement 2 is false: project tolerances are not derived from the WBS (manual 7.3.1, fig 6.2).
n.1: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 1 describes the product breakdown structure, not the WBS (manual 7.3.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is correct, but statement 2 is false: the business layer sets project tolerances, and the WBS is a tool for structuring work and teams (manual fig 6.2, 6.2.5).

9.q: Why are most of a project's benefits realized after the project has closed?
o: Because benefits cannot be measured until the end project report has been approved
Because the business case is first prepared when the project is being closed
Because the senior supplier is responsible for realizing benefits after closure
Because projects deliver outputs, and benefits come from outcomes once outputs are in use
9.w: A project delivers outputs; outcomes (changes in behaviour) and the benefits they produce mostly follow once the outputs are used in operations, which is why benefits are largely confirmed after closure (see manual 5.1, 5.3.1).

n.0: The end project report reviews project performance; benefits are measured when outcomes occur, and some can be realized during the project (manual 5.3.1).
n.1: The business case is developed before and during initiation (outline then full), not at closure (manual 5.2.1).
n.2: The senior user, not the senior supplier, is responsible for the continued realization of benefits after closure (manual 6.2.4.2).

9.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
[?] is the procedure that ensures changes to the project baseline are identified and assessed, and then approved, rejected or deferred.
o: Quality control
Exception management
Change control
Change management
9.w: Change control is the procedure by which changes to the baseline are identified, assessed and then approved, rejected or deferred; in PRINCE2 7 it is part of the issues practice (see manual 10.2.3).

n.0: Quality control checks whether products meet their quality specifications; it does not decide on changes to the baseline (manual 8.2).
n.1: Exception management deals with forecast breaches of tolerance, escalated to the level above (manual 11.3).
n.3: In PRINCE2 7, change management means the organizational transition covered by the people element, not control of baselines (manual ch 3).

9.q: What is the difference between a threat and an opportunity?
o: A threat would have a negative effect on objectives if it occurred; an opportunity a positive one
A threat is likely to occur soon; an opportunity is likely to occur later in the project
A threat affects the project's objectives; an opportunity affects the business layer's objectives
A threat is recorded in the risk register; an opportunity is recorded in the issue register
9.w: PRINCE2 uses 'threat' for an uncertain event with a negative effect on objectives and 'opportunity' for one with a positive effect (see manual 9.1).

n.1: When a risk might occur is its proximity; it does not decide whether the risk is a threat or an opportunity (manual 9.1, 9.2).
n.2: Both threats and opportunities are defined by their effect on the project's objectives (manual 9.1).
n.3: Both threats and opportunities are recorded in the risk register (manual 9.5).

9.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
When a team is virtual or hybrid, building [?] needs more deliberate effort, for example by synchronizing co-location days for key people.
o: the project plan
risk tolerance
social cohesion
the product register
9.w: For virtual, remote or hybrid teams, social cohesion must be built more deliberately, for example through synchronized co-location days for key people focused on key relationships (see manual 3.3.3).

n.0: The project plan is built through the plans practice in initiating a project; co-location days are about relationships, not planning (manual ch 7).
n.1: Risk tolerance is set by the project board from the business's risk appetite; it is unrelated to bringing dispersed people together (manual 9.2.1).
n.3: The product register records products and their status; it is not built through co-location days (manual ch 7).

9.q: A housing association is starting its first ever project to fit heat pumps, a technology that its own staff have not worked with before. How does the 'learn from experience' principle apply?
o: Lessons cannot be sought, as there are no previous internal projects to review
Lessons should be gathered after the first stage, once the team has some experience
Seeking lessons is even more important, including from external organizations
Lessons should be left to the supplier, who has installed heat pumps before
9.w: When a project is a first for the business or includes novel content, learning from others is even more important, and that includes people and organizations outside the business (manual 2.2).

n.0: A lack of internal history does not stop learning: lessons can be sought from external people and organizations (manual 2.2).
n.1: Lessons should be sought when the project starts, not deferred until after a stage (manual 2.2, 13.4.2).
n.3: The project team as a whole seeks and applies lessons; it is not handed to one party (manual 2.2).

9.q: When the project board approves the project initiation documentation and authorizes the project, which objective of directing a project is it meeting?
o: There is authority to deliver the project product
There is authority to initiate the project
There is authority to close the project
Users have formally accepted the completed project product
9.w: Approving the PID in authorize the project gives the authority to deliver the project's product, one of the objectives of directing a project (see manual 14.2, 14.4.2).

n.1: Authority to initiate is given earlier, in authorize initiation, when the project brief and initiation stage plan are approved (manual 14.4.1).
n.2: Authority to close is given at the end of the project in authorize project closure (manual 14.4.5).
n.3: Confirming user acceptance of the project product is an objective of closing a project at the end of the final stage, not of approving the PID (manual 19.2).

9.q: Which role is accountable for specifying the benefits and for demonstrating to the business that the forecast benefits are on track to be realized?
o: Executive
Senior user
Project assurance
Project manager
9.w: The senior user specifies the benefits aligned to the business case, demonstrates that forecast benefits are on track and remains committed to realizing them after closure (see manual 6.2.4).

n.0: The executive owns the business case and secures funding; specifying benefits and showing they are on track is the senior user's role (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Project assurance monitors and advises on behalf of board members; it is not accountable for specifying benefits (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: The project manager runs the project day to day and maintains the business case, but the benefits are specified by the senior user (manual 6.2.4).

9.q: Why is culture considered in the change management approach?
o: Because culture determines the tolerances that the board sets for each stage
Because culture cannot change, so the products must be designed around it
Because culture is one of the things that changes between current and target states
Because culture problems are logged in the issue register as off-specifications
9.w: The change management approach describes the characteristics of each state, including culture, and the evolving culture is one of the factors in deciding how much detail it needs (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: Stage tolerances are set by the project board through the progress practice; culture is not what determines them (manual 11.2.1).
n.1: PRINCE2 refers to an evolving culture: culture shifts as the change takes place, which is why it is described for each state (manual 3.2.1).
n.3: Off-specifications concern products that will not meet their quality specifications; cultural matters are handled through the people element (manual 10.1, 3.2.3).

9.q: Which statement defines the project board in PRINCE2?
o: Accountable to the business for the project's success, with authority to direct it within the remit the business sets
Responsible for running the project day to day on behalf of the business, within the agreed project tolerances
The full set of roles, including assurance and support, that together hold the authority to direct the project
The commissioning party that provides the mandate and decides on any breach of the project-level tolerances
9.w: The project board is accountable to the business for the success of the project and has the authority to direct it within the remit set by the business (see manual 6.2.1).

n.1: Running the project day to day within tolerances is the project manager's role, on behalf of the board (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: This describes the project management team structure, which PRINCE2 says does not have authority to direct the project (manual 6.2.3).
n.3: Providing the mandate and deciding on breaches of project tolerance is the business layer, which sits above the board (manual fig 6.2).

9.q: Older PRINCE2 material lists six aspects of project performance. Which aspect did PRINCE2 7 add to make seven?
o: Sustainability
Benefits
Stakeholder engagement
Risk
9.w: PRINCE2 7 added sustainability as the seventh aspect of performance: projects affect their environment, so teams need sustainability performance targets for the project work and its products (see manual 1.4).

n.1: Benefits was already one of the six aspects in the 2017 edition.
n.2: Stakeholder engagement is covered by the people element, which is new in PRINCE2 7, but it is not an aspect of performance.
n.3: Risk was already one of the six aspects in the 2017 edition.

9.q: A director wants to run a very short internal project with as few stages as PRINCE2 allows. What is the minimum number of management stages?
o: One: a single stage covering initiation and delivery
Two: an initiation stage followed by one delivery stage
Three: initiation, delivery and a separate closing stage
Four: one stage for each level of the organization
9.w: A PRINCE2 project has at least two stages: the initiation stage, which is always first, and at least one delivery stage (see manual 2.4).

n.0: Initiation is a stage in its own right so that the project is properly set up before delivery work begins (manual 2.4).
n.2: Closing a project happens within the final delivery stage; it is not a separate stage (manual ch 19).
n.3: The four organizational levels describe who directs, manages and delivers; they do not set the number of stages (fig 6.2).

9.q: How does the business case practice support the 'manage by stages' principle?
o: The business case sets the tolerances the project manager uses for each work package
Decisions made at each stage boundary include checking that the project is still justified
The business case is prepared again from the project mandate at the start of each stage
The business case defines the products that each delivery stage must produce
9.w: Under 'manage by stages', the decisions taken at stage boundaries are checked for continued business justification, using the updated business case (see manual tab 5.2, 5.3.1).

n.0: Work package tolerances are set by the project manager in work package descriptions; this is not the business case link to manage by stages (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: The business case is developed once (outline then full) and then maintained; it is not recreated from the mandate each stage (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: Defining products and their delivery is the plans practice, through stage plans and product descriptions (manual 7.1).

9.q: Each PRINCE2 7 practice includes a table relating that practice to the principles. What does this table show?
o: That the practice can be used in place of a principle on small projects
That each principle belongs to a single practice and is applied there
How the principles are put into effect through that practice
Which principles may be set aside when that practice is tailored
9.w: Each practice chapter shows how the principles are applied through that aspect of project management, for example the business case practice supports ensure continued business justification and manage by stages (manual tab 5.2, 7.2, 8.3).

n.0: A practice never stands in for a principle; all seven principles apply on every project, whatever its size (manual ch 2).
n.1: Each practice relates to several principles, and each principle is applied through several practices, not through one (manual tab 5.2, 7.2).
n.3: Tailoring a practice does not set any principle aside; the principles are not tailored (manual 2.7).

9.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
A [?] is an issue whose timelines and impact still need to be assessed before the project manager can decide how serious it is.
o: problem
off-specification
concern
request for change
9.w: A concern is an issue whose timelines and impact need to be assessed; it is the issue type for matters whose seriousness is not yet clear (see manual 10.1).

n.0: A problem has an immediate and negative impact, so its effect is already evident rather than still to be assessed (manual 10.1).
n.1: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications (manual 10.2.3).
n.3: A request for change is a proposal for a change to a baseline (manual 10.2.3).

9.q: How does the planning horizon affect when each stage plan after initiation is prepared?
o: All of them are prepared in initiation so that the board can approve them together
Each is prepared by a team manager once the first work package in that stage has started
Each is prepared during closure to record what that stage actually delivered
Each is prepared near the end of the stage before it, when its work can be planned in detail
9.w: Because only the near future can be planned in detail, each later stage plan is prepared near the end of the current stage, close to when the work will be done (see manual 7.2.1, 7.2.2.2).

n.0: Initiation produces the project plan; later stage plans are prepared near the end of each preceding stage (manual 7.2.2.1, 7.2.2.2).
n.1: Stage plans are prepared by the project manager before the stage starts; team managers prepare team plans (manual 7.2.2.2, 7.2.2.3).
n.2: Stage plans are forward-looking plans for control; actual performance is reported in end stage and end project reports (manual 7.2.2.2, 11.5).

9.q: Which is an example of tailoring the PRINCE2 management products?
o: Setting no tolerances for the current stage to save the board's time
Leaving out the 'learn from experience' principle on a short project
Merging two management products into a single document
Letting the project manager take on the executive role
9.w: Management products can be merged, split, renamed or produced in different formats to suit the project (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Tolerances are how manage by exception delegates authority; removing them abandons a principle rather than tailoring a product (manual 2.5).
n.1: Principles cannot be tailored away; all seven must be applied (manual ch 2).
n.3: Combining the executive and project manager roles breaks a role rule that still applies after tailoring, and it concerns roles, not products (manual 6.2.4).

9.q: According to PRINCE2 7, what do pockets of resistance among stakeholders indicate?
o: Where communication efforts should be focused
That the project should be closed prematurely
That a request for change should be raised
That a stage tolerance has been exceeded
9.w: Pockets of resistance show where communication should be focused, so the project can understand and address the reasons behind them (see manual 3.4).

n.1: Premature closure is a project board decision, for example when the business justification is lost; resistance alone does not call for it (manual ch 19).
n.2: A request for change proposes a change to a baseline; resistance is a people matter addressed through engagement and communication (manual 10.1, 3.4).
n.3: Tolerance breaches are measured against plan targets; resistance does not itself mean a tolerance has been exceeded (manual 11.2.1).

9.q: What is meant by risk probability?
o: The estimated effect on the project's objectives if the risk were to occur
The degree to which a particular objective of the project is at risk overall
The measurable threshold for the tolerable range of outcomes of each objective at risk
The estimated chance that a risk will occur, judged from its likelihood or frequency
9.w: Risk probability is the estimated chance of a risk occurring, often estimated from its probability or frequency of occurrence (see manual 9.2).

n.0: This is risk impact, which is measured in the units of the objective affected (manual 9.2).
n.1: This is risk exposure, a neutral measure that can be positive or negative (manual 9.2).
n.2: This is risk tolerance, set by the project board (manual 9.2, 9.2.1).

9.q: Which feature of a PRINCE2 project makes the 'managing a stage boundary' process possible?
o: Each stage delivers benefits that can be measured at the end of the stage
The project has a fixed end date that is set by the business layer
Every team works to a team plan that is re-approved at each stage end
The project is divided into management stages, each ending in a decision point
9.w: Managing a stage boundary rests on the project being divided into management stages. Each stage end gives the board a point to review the stage and decide whether to continue (see manual 18.3).

n.0: Stages are management decision points; benefits may be realized after the project, so a stage need not deliver measurable benefits (manual 12, 19.2).
n.1: Stage boundaries depend on the project being divided into stages, not on a fixed end date (manual 18.3).
n.2: Team plans are optional and are not approved at stage boundaries; the board reviews stage and project plans (manual 17.4.1, 18.1).

9.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

A [?] sets out a product's purpose, composition, derivation, format, quality specifications and quality method.
o: work package description
project brief
product description
quality register
9.w: Under focus on products, product descriptions give clarity about each product: its purpose, composition, derivation, format, quality criteria or specifications and quality method (manual 2.6).

n.0: A work package description sets out work for a team manager; it refers to product descriptions rather than replacing them (manual ch 7).
n.1: The project brief describes the project as a whole for initiation, not each product's content (manual ch 13).
n.3: The quality register records planned and completed quality activities, not the product's definition (manual ch 8).

9.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

When a project manager forecasts that the current stage will exceed its agreed tolerances, the situation should be [?] to the project board using an exception report.
o: escalated
delegated
tailored
baselined
9.w: A forecast breach of stage tolerance takes the matter beyond the project manager's authority, so it is escalated to the project board in an exception report (see manual 11.2.6).

n.1: Delegation passes authority down a level, with tolerances; a forecast breach is passed up a level (manual 11.2.1, 11.2.6).
n.2: Tailoring adapts the method to the project; it is not how a forecast breach is handled (manual 2.7).
n.3: Baselining fixes an approved version of a product; it does not describe passing a forecast breach to the board (manual 4.3).

9.q: Why does PRINCE2 warn that generic, standard role descriptions are unlikely to be effective?
o: Because role descriptions are not one of the management products used in PRINCE2
Because role descriptions are agreed by the team managers rather than the project board
Because PRINCE2 requires each of its roles to be performed by a different person
Because people with the same skills perform a role differently and roles must fit them
9.w: Even people with the same capabilities perform the same role differently, so roles should reflect the individual's capability, authority, availability and key relationships rather than a standard template (see manual 3.3.2).

n.0: Role descriptions are a PRINCE2 management product of the organizing practice and form part of the PID (manual ch 6).
n.1: Role descriptions form part of the PID, which the project board approves when it authorizes the project (manual ch 6, 14.4.2).
n.2: One person may hold several roles and some roles can be shared, within the combination rules (manual 6.2.4).

9.q: Under which heading of a plan is the work in scope recorded as a work breakdown structure with its associated work package descriptions?
o: Planning assumptions
Monitoring and control
Work to be performed
External dependencies
9.w: A plan's 'work to be performed' heading shows the work in scope as a work breakdown structure together with the associated work package descriptions (see manual 7.5).

n.0: Planning assumptions record what the plan assumes to be true; they do not hold the work breakdown structure (manual 7.5).
n.1: Monitoring and control describes how the plan will be tracked, not the breakdown of the work itself (manual 7.5).
n.3: External dependencies record what the plan relies on from outside the project, not the work breakdown structure (manual 7.5).

9.q: Which tolerances are agreed with a team manager in a work package description?
o: Scope, cost, time and quality
Benefits, cost and time
Cost, time, risk and sustainability
Scope, cost and time
9.w: A work package description carries tolerances for scope, cost and time. Benefits, quality, risk and sustainability tolerances are not set at work package level (see manual 11.2.1).

n.0: Quality is controlled at work package level through the product descriptions, not through a quality tolerance in the work package description (manual 11.2.1).
n.1: Benefits are not managed at work package level; the tolerances are scope, cost and time (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Risk and sustainability tolerances are not set in a work package description, and this list leaves out scope (manual 11.2.1).

9.q: What does the project plan identify that typically forms the top level of the project's work breakdown structure?
o: The proposed work packages into which delivery activities will be organized
The team plans that each team manager will prepare for the project
The product descriptions for every product of every stage of the project
The stage tolerances that the executive will set for each delivery stage
9.w: The project plan identifies the proposed work packages into which product delivery activities will be organized; these typically form the top level of the work breakdown structure (see manual 7.2.2.1).

n.1: Team plans are optional plans prepared later by team managers; they are not the top level of the work breakdown structure (manual 7.2.2.3).
n.2: Product descriptions describe products; the work breakdown structure is organized around work packages (manual 7.3.1.1, 7.3.1.2).
n.3: Stage tolerances are set by the executive for each stage; they are not part of the work breakdown structure (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

9.q: According to PRINCE2 guidance on reviewing progress, what sets the limit on the level of detail at which progress can be controlled?
o: The frequency of highlight reports set by the board
The number of tolerance areas agreed for the stage
The level of detail held in the plans
The size of the change budget agreed for the stage
9.w: Progress can be controlled only at the level of detail contained in the plans, which is why detailed stage and team plans support the high-level project plan (see manual 11.2.3).

n.0: Reporting frequency affects how often progress is seen, but control is limited by the detail of the plans themselves (manual 11.2.3).
n.1: Tolerance areas set the limits of delegated authority, not the level of detail at which progress can be controlled (manual 11.2.1, 11.2.3).
n.3: The change budget funds approved changes; it does not limit the detail of progress control (manual 10.2, 11.2.3).

9.q: Which management product, held in the project log, lists all of the products required by a plan together with their status?
o: Product register
Quality register
Product breakdown structure
Project product description
9.w: The product register, one of the records in the project log, lists all the products required by a plan and their status (see manual 8.5).

n.1: The quality register records quality activities and their results, not the status of every product (manual 8.5).
n.2: A product breakdown structure is a planning diagram showing the hierarchy of products; it does not track their status (manual ch 7).
n.3: The project product description describes the project's major products, quality expectations and acceptance criteria; it is not a status list (manual 8.1.1).

9.q: Which list contains three of the PRINCE2 7 principles?
o: Manage by stages; focus on outcomes; learn from experience
Manage by exception; focus on products; tailor to suit the project
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships; manage risk; manage by stages
Ensure continued business justification; manage by tolerance; learn from experience
9.w: Manage by exception, focus on products and tailor to suit the project are all PRINCE2 7 principles. The other four are ensure continued business justification, learn from experience, define roles, responsibilities and relationships, and manage by stages (manual 2.1 to 2.7).

n.0: The principle is 'focus on products', not 'focus on outcomes': outcomes are a business case concept, not a principle (manual 2.6).
n.2: Risk is one of the seven practices, not a principle, so 'manage risk' is not a PRINCE2 principle (manual ch 4).
n.3: The principle is 'manage by exception'; tolerances are the means it uses, and 'manage by tolerance' is not a principle (manual 2.5).

9.q: In which management product is the project's benefits tolerance documented?
o: Sustainability management approach
Benefits management approach
Work package description
Risk management approach
9.w: Benefits tolerance, the permissible deviation in benefit targets before escalation, is documented in the benefits management approach (see manual 5.2.2).

n.0: The sustainability management approach documents sustainability performance targets and tolerances, not benefits tolerance (manual 5.2.2).
n.2: A work package description carries scope, cost and time tolerances; benefits tolerance is not agreed there (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: The risk management approach sets out how risks will be managed; benefits tolerance sits in the benefits management approach (manual ch 9, 5.2.2).

9.q: Where are the project's sustainability performance targets and tolerances documented?
o: Benefits management approach
Quality management approach
Communication management approach
Sustainability management approach
9.w: Sustainability performance targets and tolerances are documented in the sustainability management approach, which supports the business case and should reference the organization's ESG goals (see manual 5.2.2).

n.0: The benefits management approach documents benefits tolerance and benefits reviews, not sustainability targets (manual 5.2.2).
n.1: The quality management approach covers how quality will be achieved; sustainability targets are in the sustainability management approach (manual ch 8, 5.2.2).
n.2: The communication management approach covers the means and frequency of communication with stakeholders (manual ch 3).

9.q:
Which two statements about the authorize initiation activity are correct?
1. It must be carried out at a formal board meeting so that the business layer can attend.
2. It approves the full business case and the project plan for the delivery stages.
3. It can be done without a formal meeting if the board agrees and the executive gives a documented instruction.
4. It confirms that the investment in initiating the project is worthwhile.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
9.w: Statement 3 is correct: authorize initiation may be done with or without a formal meeting, but all board members must agree and the project manager must receive a documented instruction from the executive. Statement 4 is correct: the board confirms the investment in initiation is worthwhile (see manual 14.4.1).

n.0: Both are wrong: no formal meeting is required, and the full business case and project plan are approved later, in authorize the project (manual 14.4.1, 14.4.2).
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: authorize initiation can be done without a formal meeting when board members agree and the executive documents the instruction (manual 14.4.1).
n.2: Statement 2 is wrong: the full business case and project plan are prepared during initiation and approved in authorize the project (manual 15.4.4, 15.4.5, 14.4.2).

9.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
If the business case is no longer valid, the [?] may trigger a premature close, and the 'closing a project' process is still used, tailored to the situation.
o: project manager
team manager
change authority
project board
9.w: The project board can trigger a premature close, for example when the business case is no longer valid. Closing a project is still run, tailored to the circumstances (see manual 19.3).

n.0: The project manager prepares closure but does not decide to close the project early; that is the board's decision (manual 19.3).
n.1: The team manager delivers work packages in managing product delivery and has no authority to close the project (manual 17.3).
n.2: A change authority approves requests for change within delegated limits; it cannot close the project (manual 6.2.4).

9.q:
Which two statements about directing a project are correct?
1. The board takes part in managing product delivery so it can oversee team managers.
2. It gives the board a way to keep the project justified without hands-on management.
3. It ends when the project manager submits the end project report to the board.
4. Plans for realizing benefits after the project closes are managed and reviewed.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
9.w: Statement 2 is correct: directing a project lets the board ensure continued business justification without being overburdened by hands-on management. Statement 4 is correct: an objective is that plans for realizing post-project benefits are managed and reviewed (see manual 14.2, 14.3).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: the board is not involved in managing product delivery; team managers work under the project manager (manual 14.3).
n.1: Both are wrong: the board is not involved in managing product delivery, and directing a project continues until the board authorizes closure after closing a project (manual 14.3, 14.4.5).
n.3: Statement 3 is wrong: directing a project runs until after closing a project, when the board authorizes project closure (manual 12, 14.4.5).

9.q: In PRINCE2 7, for which aspects of performance can tolerances be set to manage a project's constraints?
o: Benefits, cost, time, quality, scope and risk
Cost, time, quality, scope, risk and stakeholder satisfaction
Benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, risk and resources
Benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk
9.w: PRINCE2 7 provides tolerances for seven aspects: benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk. Sustainability is new in PRINCE2 7 (see manual 7.2.4).

n.0: This is the older list of six; PRINCE2 7 adds sustainability as a seventh aspect (manual 7.2.4).
n.1: Stakeholder satisfaction is not a tolerance area, and the list misses benefits and sustainability (manual 7.2.4).
n.2: Resources are not a tolerance area; the seventh aspect is sustainability (manual 7.2.4).

9.q: Which statement best describes how the organizing practice differs from the plans practice?
o: Organizing defines the products to be delivered, while plans decides who is accountable for producing each one
Organizing sets out who is accountable and responsible, while plans defines the products and the means to deliver them
Organizing replaces the plans practice once the project management team has been appointed in starting up
Organizing records actual progress against each plan, while plans sets the baselines that progress is measured against
9.w: Organizing establishes the structure of accountability and responsibilities (the 'who'), whereas plans defines the products (the 'what') and the means of delivering them (see manual 6.1, 7.1).

n.0: This reverses the two practices: defining products is part of plans, and accountability is set by organizing (manual 6.1, 7.1).
n.2: All seven practices apply throughout the project; organizing does not replace plans after appointments are made (manual 4).
n.3: Comparing actual achievement with plans is the progress practice, not organizing (manual 11.1).

9.q: A project builds a new data centre using a fixed design, build and commission sequence, while the software that will run in it is developed in short cycles. Which delivery approach is the project using?
o: Linear-sequential
Hybrid
Iterative-incremental
Phased
9.w: A hybrid approach combines approaches within one project, for example linear-sequential for infrastructure and iterative-incremental for software (see manual 1.5.3).

n.0: The building work is linear-sequential, but the software is iterative, so the project as a whole is not linear-sequential.
n.2: The software work is iterative-incremental, but the building work follows a fixed sequence, so the project as a whole is not iterative-incremental.
n.3: Phased is not one of the three delivery approaches named in PRINCE2 7.

9.q: According to PRINCE2 guidance on the use of data and systems in progress management, which is a benefit of using data and technology?
o: Systems can set the tolerances for each management level from past data
Automated tracking removes the need for highlight reports to the board
Stored data on past performance can help to predict future performance
Dashboards can replace the board's decisions at the end of each stage
9.w: Guidance on data and systems notes that stored past performance helps predict future performance, automation saves manually consolidating data, and information can be presented in the format stakeholders prefer (see manual 11.2.7).

n.0: Tolerances are set by the management levels (business layer, board, project manager), not by data or systems (manual 11.2.1, 11.2.7).
n.1: Automation removes manual consolidation of data from different sources; the board still needs highlight reporting (manual 11.2.7).
n.3: Data supports decisions but does not replace the board's event-driven decisions at stage boundaries (manual 11.2.2, 11.2.7).

9.q: How does the communication management approach relate to the highlight reports produced during a stage?
o: It replaces highlight reports for the stakeholders outside the project board
It is updated by the team managers each time they send a highlight report
It sets the frequency at which the project manager produces highlight reports
It lists the stage tolerances that highlight reports must be measured against
9.w: In controlling a stage, the project manager produces highlight reports at the frequency set out in the communication management approach (see manual 16.4.8).
