n.0: Highlight reports are the project manager's regular status report to the project board; the communication approach does not replace them (manual 16.4.8).
n.1: Team managers send checkpoint reports to the project manager; highlight reports come from the project manager (manual 16.4.8).
n.3: Stage tolerances are set by the project board and recorded with the stage plan, not in the communication management approach (manual 11.2.1).

9.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

The change management approach describes the [?] before, during and after the transition, such as consultation, trials, training and a help line.
o: quality review steps
risk responses
enabling activities
tolerance levels
9.w: A typical content area of the change management approach is the enabling activities planned before, during and after the transition, such as consultation, trials, training and a help line (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: Quality review steps belong to the quality practice and its quality management approach (manual ch 8).
n.1: Risk responses are recorded against specific risks in the risk register under the risk practice (manual ch 9).
n.3: Tolerance levels are set through the progress practice and documented in the plans and approaches they apply to (manual 11.2.1).

9.q: Which outcome shows that the purpose of the issues practice is being achieved?
o: Issues are escalated to the project board so that the board makes each decision about them
Requests for change are refused once the project plan has been baselined and approved
Issues are recorded when the project closes so they can be included in the lessons report
Changes to approved products are made after their impact is assessed and they are authorized
9.w: The practice exists to assess issues and control changes to the baseline, so a sign of success is that approved products change only after their impact has been assessed and the change authorized (see manual 10.1, 10.2.3).

n.0: The board may delegate authority for changes and the project manager handles issues within tolerance, so escalating everything defeats manage by exception (manual 10.2.4, 2.5).
n.1: Change control does not forbid change; requests for change are assessed and then approved, rejected or deferred (manual 10.2.3).
n.2: Issues are captured and assessed as they arise, not stored up until closure; lessons are a separate record (manual 10.3.1, 11.5).

9.q:
Which two statements describe how the risk practice supports the PRINCE2 principles?
1. Setting risk tolerance supports manage by exception.
2. Recording risks in the daily log supports focus on products.
3. Weighing aggregated risk in the business case supports ensure continued business justification.
4. Letting the team manager set risk appetite supports define roles, responsibilities and relationships.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
9.w: Risk is one of the seven tolerance areas, so risk tolerance applies manage by exception (statement 1). The business case weighs benefits against costs and the associated risks, so aggregated risk informs continued business justification (statement 3) (see manual 2.1, 2.5, 9.7).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the daily log is not where identified risks are managed, and focus on products is about defining products and their quality (manual 2.6, 9.5).
n.2: Both are wrong: risks are recorded in the risk register, and risk appetite is set by the business, not by a team manager (manual 9.2, 9.5).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: risk appetite is determined by the business, and the project board sets tolerance from it (manual 9.2.1).

9.q: A project manager sets out how the risk practice will be applied on this project, with procedures and scales proportionate to its size and complexity. Which kind of tailoring is this?
o: Tailoring a principle through the risk register
Tailoring the terminology through the issue register
Tailoring the processes through the project mandate
Tailoring a practice through its management approach
9.w: The practices are tailored through the management approaches; the risk management approach sets out how the risk practice will be applied on this project (see manual 2.7 and 15.4.2).

n.0: Principles are not tailored, and the risk register holds specific risks rather than how the practice is applied (manual 2.7, ch 9).
n.1: Tailoring terminology means using the organization's own terms; the issue register records formal issues and does not set how risk is managed (manual 2.7, ch 10).
n.2: The mandate is the business layer's trigger for starting up a project; processes are tailored by combining or simplifying them, not through the mandate (manual 2.7, ch 13).

9.q: A project's environmental manager is to be held accountable for meeting the project's carbon-reduction target. In which management product should this accountability be recorded?
o: Project management team structure
Product description
Role descriptions
Benefits management approach
9.w: Role descriptions set out the roles in the project management team and their specific responsibilities, and should include accountability for sustainability targets (see manual 6.5).

n.0: The project management team structure shows who is involved, their relationships and how they will work together, not each role's specific accountabilities (manual 6.5).
n.1: A product description sets out a product's purpose, composition, derivation and quality specifications, not a person's accountabilities (manual 8.5).
n.3: The benefits management approach covers how benefits will be measured and reviewed; individual role accountabilities belong in role descriptions (manual 5.5, 6.5).

9.q: Which management product, agreed during initiating a project, describes how quality control will be organized, performed, monitored and reported?
o: Product description
Project product description
Quality register
Quality management approach
9.w: The quality management approach, part of the project initiation documentation, focuses on how quality control will be organized, performed, monitored and reported (see manual 8.3.1.1, 8.5).

n.0: A product description sets out one product's purpose, composition, derivation, format and quality specifications, not the project's quality control arrangements (manual 8.5).
n.1: The project product description holds the user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria for the project product, created in starting up a project (manual 8.1.1, ch 13).
n.2: The quality register records quality activities planned or performed and their results; it does not describe how quality control is organized (manual 8.5).

9.q: A project manager from a supplier organization is leading a team that includes several senior specialists from the customer. Which statement is consistent with PRINCE2's guidance on leading project teams?
o: The project manager should ask the executive to direct the specialists, as they outrank the project manager
The senior specialists should be moved out of the team, as their seniority weakens the project manager's authority
The project manager should use the formal role descriptions as the basis for instructing the specialists
It is not unusual for team members to outrank the project manager, so leading by influence is needed
9.w: PRINCE2 notes that it is not unusual for team members to be more senior than the project manager, so authority is harder to exercise and leadership through persuasion, influence and co-creation matters (see manual 3.3).

n.0: The project manager runs the project day to day on behalf of the board; asking the executive to direct team members bypasses that role and is unlikely to work for people who do not report to the executive (manual 3.3, 6.2.4).
n.1: Effective teams need a diverse mix of capabilities and perspectives; seniority is not a reason to remove people (manual 3.3.2).
n.2: Role descriptions do not give a temporary leader line authority over people from other organizations; leadership depends on influence and relationships (manual 3.3, 3.3.1).

9.q:
Which two statements about the characteristics of a project are true?
1. A project that closely repeats an earlier one is not unique.
2. Projects are the means by which an organization introduces change.
3. Uncertainty makes projects less risky than business as usual.
4. Every project differs from others in some way, even when it is similar.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
9.w: Statement 2 describes the 'change' characteristic and statement 4 the 'unique' characteristic (see manual 1.3).

n.0: Statement 2 is true, but statement 1 is false: even a project that repeats an earlier one differs in some way, such as team, location or timeframe, so it is still unique.
n.1: Both are false: similar projects are still unique, and uncertainty makes projects riskier than business as usual, not less risky.
n.3: Statement 4 is true, but statement 3 is false: the uncertainty projects carry makes them riskier than business as usual.

9.q: Which principle is being applied when a project team actively seeks, records and acts on lessons from earlier projects and from its own work as the project progresses?
o: Manage by exception
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Tailor to suit the project
Learn from experience
9.w: Learn from experience means the project team seeks, records and implements lessons from prior projects and throughout its own project, and shares them so others can apply them (manual 2.2).

n.0: Manage by exception is about tolerances and escalation between management levels, not lessons (manual 2.5).
n.1: This principle is about agreed roles and stakeholder relationships, not seeking and acting on lessons (manual 2.3).
n.2: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's context; gathering and applying lessons is learn from experience (manual 2.7).

9.q: Why does PRINCE2 keep the risk budget separate from the change budget?
o: The risk budget funds new user requirements, while the change budget funds contingent plans for threats
The risk budget is held by the business layer, while the change budget is held by the team manager
The risk budget funds responses to risks, while the change budget funds approved changes to the baseline
The risk budget is spent during initiation, while the change budget is spent in later delivery stages
9.w: The risk budget pays for specific risk responses, such as contingent plans. The change budget pays for authorized changes to the baseline. Keeping them apart stops one being used up by the other (see manual 7 (preparing the budget), 9.2).

n.0: This reverses the two: new requirements are changes funded by the change budget, and contingent plans are funded by the risk budget (manual 9.2).
n.1: Both budgets are part of the project's planned budget and are controlled within the project; team managers do not hold the change budget (manual 7, preparing the budget).
n.3: Both can be used in any stage; the difference is what they fund, not when they are spent (manual 7, 9.2).

10.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
Starting up a project is as much about preventing [?] projects from being initiated as it is about approving the initiation of viable ones.
o: high-risk
compulsory
poorly conceived
externally funded
10.w: A key part of the purpose of starting up a project is to stop poorly conceived ideas from going into initiation, as well as approving viable ones (see manual 13.1).

n.0: A project with significant risk can still be viable and worthwhile; risk is assessed rather than a reason in itself to stop initiation (manual 13.1, 9.1).
n.1: Compulsory projects still go through starting up and still need the chosen option justified; they are not what the process sets out to prevent (manual 13.1, 5.2.3).
n.3: The source of funding does not make an idea poorly conceived; the test is whether the project is viable and worthwhile (manual 13.1).

10.q: In PRINCE2 7, who does the 'people' element cover?
o: The members of the project management team and their reporting lines
Those working on the project, their relationships, and those it affects
The users who will operate the products once they have been handed over
The stakeholders listed in the communication management approach
10.w: PRINCE2 uses 'people' to mean those working on the project and the relationships between them, together with those impacted by the project (see manual ch 3 introduction, 3.1).

n.0: The project management team is part of the picture, but the people element also covers relationships and everyone affected by the project (manual ch 3).
n.2: Users are one affected group; the people element also covers everyone working on the project and their relationships (manual ch 3).
n.3: The communication management approach records stakeholders for communication purposes; the people element is defined by who works on or is affected by the project, not by a list (manual ch 3, 3.4).

10.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
Using a high-level project plan together with a detailed plan for each stage, with a decision at each stage boundary, applies the [?] principle.
o: manage by exception
focus on products
manage by stages
learn from experience
10.w: The project plan plus stage plans, with stage boundaries as decision points, is how the plans practice supports the manage by stages principle (see manual 7.7 tab 7.2).

n.0: Manage by exception is supported by setting tolerances at each plan level (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).
n.1: Focus on products is supported by product-based planning (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).
n.3: Learn from experience is supported by using lessons when estimating (manual 7.7 tab 7.2).

10.q: Which statement about the communicate step of the risk management technique is correct?
o: It runs in parallel with the other four steps throughout the project
It follows the implement step, once the planned responses have been actioned
It comes before the identify step, to agree the project's context with stakeholders
It takes place at each stage end, when the end stage report is being prepared
10.w: Identify, assess, plan and implement are carried out in sequence, while communicate runs alongside all of them, using the project's existing reports and channels (see manual 9.3.1, figure 9.2).

n.1: Communicate is not a final step: risk information is shared throughout, including while risks are still being identified and assessed (manual 9.3.1).
n.2: Defining context and objectives is part of identify; communicate runs alongside all the steps rather than preceding them (manual 9.3.1, 9.3.1.1).
n.3: The end stage report is one channel, but communication is continuous and uses checkpoint and highlight reports too (manual 9.3.1).

10.q:
Which two statements about ecosystems in PRINCE2 are correct?
1. The organizational ecosystem is created at initiation and dissolved when the project closes.
2. At closure, the project's products, people and learning move into the organizational ecosystem.
3. A project can affect people from across the organizational ecosystem, not just its own team.
4. The project ecosystem consists of the project board and the project manager.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 4
3 and 4
2 and 3
10.w: Statement 2 is correct: the final step of organizational design and development transitions the project's products, people and learning into the organizational ecosystem. Statement 3 is correct: projects impact people from across the organizational ecosystem (see manual 3.2.2, 6.3.1).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: the organizational ecosystem is the existing set of organizations; it is the project ecosystem that is temporary (manual 3.1).
n.1: Statements 1 and 4 are both wrong: the organizational ecosystem already exists, and the project ecosystem includes far more people and relationships than the board and project manager (manual 3.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: the project ecosystem covers the people, relationships, structures and ways of working across the business, user and supplier interests (manual 3.1, fig 3.2).

10.q: How does the quality practice support the principle of manage by stages?
o: Product descriptions for every product are written in full during initiation, before any stage plan
The quality register is checked at each stage end and feeds the end stage report for the next decision
Project acceptance of the project product takes place at the end of each delivery stage in turn
Quality assurance approves each stage plan before the project board authorizes the next stage
10.w: At each stage boundary the quality register is checked to confirm the stage's quality activities took place, and this feeds the end stage report the board uses at its stage decision point (see manual 2.4, tab 18.3).

n.0: Product descriptions are written for each stage as it is planned in managing a stage boundary, not all in full at initiation; this does not support stage-by-stage control (manual 2.4, ch 18).
n.2: Project acceptance concerns the project product as a whole and happens when the project closes, not at every stage end (manual 8.3.1.3, ch 19).
n.3: The project board approves stage plans in directing a project; quality assurance is independent and does not approve them (manual ch 14, 8.2.3).

10.q: Why does PRINCE2 regard communication as important to a project?
o: It removes the need for formal progress reports to the project board
It transfers responsibility for adoption from the senior user to the stakeholders
It helps avoid misconceptions and unnecessary barriers to implementing change
It allows the project manager to approve changes without the change authority
10.w: PRINCE2 explains that communication is important to avoid misconceptions and unnecessary barriers when implementing change (see manual 3.4).

n.0: Formal progress controls such as highlight and end stage reports still apply; communication does not replace them (manual ch 11).
n.1: The senior user remains responsible for handover, adoption and benefits realization; communication does not move this responsibility (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Approval of changes follows the issue management approach and delegated authority; communication does not change who approves (manual 10.2.4).

10.q: A stage is forecast to finish 2 weeks later than planned. The board set a time tolerance of plus 4 weeks for the stage. What should the project manager do?
o: Raise an exception report, as the stage plan's target date will be missed
Ask the business layer to widen the project's time tolerance
Ask the team manager to prepare an exception plan for the stage
Continue managing the stage, as it is forecast to stay within tolerance
10.w: Under manage by exception the project manager can take action within the delegated tolerance; escalation is needed when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, and a 2-week delay is within plus 4 weeks (manual 2.4, 2.5).

n.0: An exception report is needed when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, not when a target is missed within tolerance (manual ch 11).
n.1: Project tolerances are not affected, and the stage is still within its own tolerance, so nothing needs escalating (manual 2.5).
n.2: Exception plans are prepared by the project manager at the board's request after an exception report; none is needed within tolerance (manual ch 11, ch 18).

10.q: Which response to a threat makes the uncertain situation certain by removing the risk, for example by removing its cause?
o: Reduce
Transfer
Accept
Avoid
10.w: Avoid removes the threat, often by removing its cause, so the uncertain situation becomes certain (see manual 9.2.3.1, table 9.1).

n.0: Reduce takes definite action now to change the probability or impact, so some residual risk remains (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.1: Transfer passes part of the financial impact to a third party, such as an insurer; the threat itself remains (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.2: Accept takes the chance and monitors the risk, with no action now to remove it (manual 9.2.3.1).

10.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. In PRINCE2's description of the organizational context, the [?] specify the desired outputs, which PRINCE2 refers to as products.
o: suppliers
users
executives
sponsors
10.w: Users specify the desired outputs (products), suppliers provide the resources and expertise to deliver them, and business decision-makers keep the investment justified (see manual 1.5).

n.0: Suppliers provide the resources and expertise to deliver the products; users specify them.
n.2: The executive is a project board role representing the business interest; the organizational context description names users as the party that specifies outputs.
n.3: Sponsor is not a PRINCE2 role; the party that specifies desired outputs is the users.

10.q: What is the purpose of the risk management approach?
o: To keep a record of the identified risks related to the project, including their status and history
To describe how issues will be captured and how changes to the project baseline will be controlled
To describe how risk will be managed, including the procedures, techniques, standards and responsibilities
To describe how data and information will be created, used and managed across the project
10.w: The risk management approach describes how risk will be managed: the specific procedures, techniques, standards and responsibilities to be applied. It contains no specific risks (see manual 9.5).

n.0: This is the purpose of the risk register, which is part of the project log (manual 9.5).
n.1: This is the issue management approach (manual 10.5).
n.3: This is the digital and data management approach (manual 11.5).

10.q: Which principle does the people element apply when decisions are made at the most local level where the knowledge needed to make and own them resides?
o: Learn from experience
Manage by exception
Manage by stages
Focus on products
10.w: The people element applies manage by exception by keeping decisions at the most local level where the knowledge to make and own them resides, escalating when a decision could affect other areas (see manual 3.5.1).

n.0: Learn from experience is applied through knowledge sharing and social learning, not through where decisions are made (manual 3.5.1).
n.2: Manage by stages is applied by using stage boundaries to review changing influencers and relationships (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Focus on products is applied by co-creating products with the business, user and supplier communities (manual 3.5.1).

10.q: Which role works out, during initiation, how the business's standard project management method needs to be tailored for the project?
o: Project support
Project manager
Team manager
Senior supplier
10.w: In the 'agree the tailoring requirements' activity, the project manager may need to tailor PRINCE2 or the business's standard method to reflect internal and external factors; the result must be documented and agreed (see manual 15.4.1).

n.0: Project support provides administrative help, such as maintaining registers; it does not decide how the method is tailored (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Team managers deliver work packages in managing product delivery; they are not responsible for tailoring the project's method (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: The senior supplier represents supplier interests on the board and commits supplier resources; working out the tailoring falls to the project manager (manual 6.2.4, 15.4.1).

10.q:
Which two statements about progress reports are correct?

1. An end stage report is produced by the team manager.
2. A highlight report is sent by the team manager to the project board.
3. An exception report offers options and a recommendation to the project board.
4. An end stage report gives the project board the information it needs to decide what to do next.
o: 3 and 4
1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
10.w: An exception report sets out options and a recommendation for the board (3), and an end stage report summarizes progress so the board can decide what to do next (4) (see manual 11.5).

n.1: Both are wrong: the end stage report and the highlight report are both produced by the project manager for the board (manual 11.5).
n.2: Statement 3 is correct, but the end stage report is produced by the project manager, not the team manager (manual 11.5).
n.3: Statement 4 is correct, but highlight reports are produced by the project manager, not the team manager (manual 11.5).

10.q: In the 'prepare the full business case' activity of initiating a project, which role is responsible for preparing the full business case?
o: Project manager
Executive
Project assurance
Senior user
10.w: In 'prepare the full business case' the project manager is responsible, the executive is accountable, project assurance is consulted and the business layer is not involved (see manual 15.4.5 RACI).

n.1: The executive is accountable for the business case, but the project manager is responsible for preparing it (manual 15.4.5).
n.2: Project assurance is consulted on the full business case, not responsible for preparing it (manual 15.4.5).
n.3: The senior user specifies benefits but is not the role responsible for preparing the full business case (manual 15.4.5, 6.2.4).

10.q: When defining and analysing the products for the project plan, which step is carried out first?
o: Create the product breakdown structure
Write the project product description
Create the product flow diagram
Write the product descriptions
10.w: Defining and analysing the products has four steps in order: write the project product description (project plan only), create the product breakdown structure, write product descriptions, and create the product flow diagram (see manual 7.3.1.1).

n.0: The product breakdown structure is the second step, after the project product description (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.2: The product flow diagram is the last of the four steps, once the products are known (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.3: Product descriptions are written in the third step, after the products have been broken down (manual 7.3.1.1).

10.q: Which role is accountable for the business case throughout the project and for securing the funding for the project?
o: Senior user
Project manager
Senior supplier
Executive
10.w: The executive secures funding and owns the business case and continued business justification, as the single point of accountability for the project (see manual 6.2.4, tab 5.1).

n.0: The senior user specifies the benefits and is responsible for showing that forecast benefits are on track, but does not own the business case or secure funding (manual 6.2.4.2).
n.1: The project manager prepares and maintains the business case on the executive's behalf; accountability stays with the executive (manual 15.4.5).
n.2: The senior supplier represents the suppliers and is accountable for the quality of products they deliver, not for the business case (manual 6.2.4).

10.q: How does the business case practice support the 'ensure continued business justification' principle?
o: By setting benefits tolerances in each work package so that team managers can escalate
By defining quality specifications for each product so that the outcomes can be measured
By creating and maintaining a business case that shows the project is still worthwhile
By recording lessons from earlier projects in the lessons log for use in later stages
10.w: The business case practice puts this principle into effect by creating and maintaining a business case that assesses whether the project is (and remains) desirable, viable and achievable (see manual tab 5.2).

n.0: Work package descriptions carry scope, cost and time tolerances; benefits tolerance is in the benefits management approach (manual 11.2.1, 5.2.2).
n.1: Defining quality specifications in product descriptions belongs to the quality practice (manual ch 8).
n.3: Recording lessons supports the 'learn from experience' principle through the progress practice (manual 4.3.2).

10.q: A government agency in a heavily regulated environment has its own mandatory project standards. How does this affect tailoring?
o: The project replaces the PRINCE2 principles with the agency's standards
The project uses PRINCE2 unchanged so it can prove compliance to regulators
The method is tailored to align with the agency's standards and environment
The project leaves tailoring until the first delivery stage is authorized
10.w: The environment is a tailoring factor and organizational standards are an influence on tailoring: the method is aligned with the business processes and standards that govern the project (see manual 2.7).

n.0: Principles are not tailored or replaced; the method is aligned with the standards while all seven principles still apply (manual ch 2, 2.7).
n.1: PRINCE2 is meant to be tailored to its environment; using it unchanged ignores a named tailoring factor (manual 2.7).
n.3: Tailoring requirements are agreed in initiating a project, before delivery stages are authorized (manual 15.4.1).

10.q: In the plans practice, what is meant by the planning horizon?
o: The total duration of the project from its mandate to closure
The point at which the project board next reviews the business case
The period ahead for which it is possible to plan accurately
The latest date by which the project plan must be approved
10.w: The planning horizon is the period for which accurate planning is possible: only the near future can be planned in detail, so detail falls away further ahead (see manual 7.2.1).

n.0: The planning horizon is usually much shorter than the whole project; that is why the project plan is high level and detail is added stage by stage (manual 7.2.1).
n.1: That describes a decision point such as a stage end, not the planning horizon (manual 7.2.3).
n.3: This is not a PRINCE2 concept; the planning horizon concerns how far ahead detailed planning is possible (manual 7.2.1).

10.q:
Which two of the following actions apply the 'focus on products' principle?
1. Agreeing quality criteria for each product before work starts.
2. Setting a cost tolerance for each work package.
3. Reviewing at a stage boundary whether benefits still outweigh costs.
4. Identifying the products needed before planning the activities.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
10.w: Statement 1 applies focus on products: quality criteria are agreed in product descriptions before work starts. Statement 4 applies it too: product-based planning identifies products before activities (manual 2.6, ch 7).

n.0: Statement 2 applies manage by exception, as it sets a tolerance for delegated work (manual 2.5).
n.1: Statement 2 is manage by exception and statement 3 is ensure continued business justification, so neither applies focus on products (manual 2.1, 2.5).
n.2: Statement 3 applies ensure continued business justification, checking that benefits still justify costs (manual 2.1).

10.q: What should the project manager make sure of when organizing the work into work packages?
o: Each work package corresponds to one management stage of the project
Each work package has a team plan that is approved by the project board
There is no overlap in scope between any two work packages and no gaps
Each work package includes benefits and quality tolerances for its products
10.w: When organizing work packages, the project manager makes sure that no two work packages overlap in scope and that nothing is left out (see manual 7.3.1.2).

n.0: Work packages are grouped around products and delivery activities, not matched one to one with stages; a stage may contain several work packages (manual 7.3.1.2, 7.3.1.4).
n.1: Team plans are optional and are produced by team managers; the board does not approve them (manual 7.2.2.3).
n.3: Work package tolerances are for scope, cost and time; benefits and quality tolerances are not set at that level (manual 11.2.1).

10.q: Which principle does the quality practice most directly apply when each product's quality specifications are defined in a product description?
o: Manage by stages
Learn from experience
Ensure continued business justification
Focus on products
10.w: Focus on products centres the project on defining and delivering products, in particular their quality expectations and requirements; product descriptions with quality specifications are its main tool (see manual 2.6, tab 8.3).

n.0: Manage by stages is about planning, monitoring and controlling the project stage by stage with decision points, not defining product specifications (manual 2.4).
n.1: Learn from experience is about seeking, recording and applying lessons, not specifying products (manual 2.2).
n.2: Ensure continued business justification is about the project remaining justified, recorded in the business case, not specifying each product (manual 2.1).

10.q: Why is the benefits management approach updated during closing a project?
o: To plan the post-project benefits reviews that the business will carry out after closure
To record the results of the benefits reviews that the project team completed after closure
To transfer the benefits tolerance into the end project report for the board's approval
To replace the business case as the record of the project's business justification
10.w: In closing a project, benefits already realized are assessed and the benefits management approach is updated to include the post-project benefits reviews, which the business carries out after closure (see manual 5.5, ch 19).

n.1: The project team does not carry out post-project reviews; the business does, after the project team has disbanded (manual 5.5, ch 19).
n.2: The end project report reviews performance against the baselined PID; benefits tolerance is not transferred into it (manual ch 19).
n.3: The business case remains the record of justification and is updated with actual costs and benefits at closure (manual 5.5, ch 19).

10.q: In a project to merge two council call centres, a long-serving supervisor with no formal project role openly criticizes the new rota, and many colleagues follow her lead. What does PRINCE2 recommend?
o: Leave her out of project communications so her views do not spread further
Ask the executive to instruct her formally to support the new rota
Raise an exception report, because her resistance threatens the stage
Find out why she resists and involve her as a key influencer in the change
10.w: Resistance shows where engagement should be focused. PRINCE2 asks the project to understand why a stakeholder resists and to involve key influencers, who may have no formal role, in shaping the change (see manual 3.2.2, 3.4).

n.0: Sidelining a resisting stakeholder works against PRINCE2 guidance: pockets of resistance show where communication should be focused (manual 3.4).
n.1: PRINCE2 favours persuading, influencing and co-creating over formal instruction; the supervisor's influence comes from her relationships, not her role (manual 3.3, 3.2.2).
n.2: An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance; nothing here says a tolerance will be exceeded (manual 11.2.6).

10.q: What does PRINCE2 guidance on forecasting say that progress reviews should do?
o: Concentrate on work completed and leave prediction to the business case
Be replaced by forecasts produced by the project's data systems
Focus on recording lessons rather than predicting performance
Look forward to predict the likely outcome, as well as reviewing work done
10.w: Forecasting guidance says progress reviews should look forward as well as back, predicting likely future performance by extrapolation, data or judgement so that exceptions can be spotted early (see manual 11.2.5).

n.0: Progress reviews look forward as well as back; the forecasts they produce then feed the business case (manual 11.2.5).
n.1: Data and systems support forecasting, but they do not replace progress reviews or the judgement of the management levels (manual 11.2.7).
n.2: Lessons are reviewed too, but the forecasting guidance is that reviews predict future performance as well as reviewing the past (manual 11.2.3, 11.2.5).

10.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

Under the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, the justification for a project must remain [?] throughout its life, not only at the start.
o: unchanged
approved by the business layer
recorded in the project mandate
valid
10.w: The principle requires the justification to remain valid, and be revalidated, throughout the project (manual 2.1).

n.0: The justification can change during the project; the requirement is that it stays valid, not that it stays the same (manual 2.1).
n.1: The full business case is approved by the project board when it authorizes the project; the principle's test is continuing validity (manual 2.1, 5.3.1).
n.2: The project mandate triggers starting up a project; the justification is documented in the business case (manual 5.3.1).

10.q: Of which management product does the change management approach form part?
o: The project initiation documentation
The project brief
The daily log within the project log
The project product description
10.w: The change management approach is one of the nine management approaches, all of which form part of the project initiation documentation (PID) (see manual 3.2.1, 15.4.2).

n.1: The project brief is assembled in starting up a project; the management approaches are agreed later, in initiating a project, and form part of the PID (manual 15.4.2).
n.2: The daily log is part of the project log and records informal issues and actions; it does not hold the management approaches (manual ch 10, ch 11).
n.3: The project product description describes the project's main product, the user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria; it is not where the management approaches are kept (manual 8.5).

10.q: Which delivery approach evolves products through repeated cycles, refining quality and acceptance criteria alongside development by using a product backlog?
o: An iterative-incremental approach
A linear-sequential approach
A hybrid approach
A stage-gated waterfall approach
10.w: In an iterative-incremental approach, products evolve through repeated cycles, and quality and acceptance criteria are refined in parallel with development using a product backlog; there may be several delivery stages (see manual 1.5.3 and 7.2.3.1).

n.1: A linear-sequential approach defines products in detail up front and moves through stages in sequence.
n.2: A hybrid approach mixes linear and iterative work; the description is of the fully iterative approach.
n.3: A stage-gated waterfall is a linear-sequential way of working, with detail fixed up front rather than refined in repeated cycles.

10.q: Why does a plan include estimates of time and cost as well as describing the products to be delivered?
o: So that the plan can take the place of the business case once the project is authorized
So that benefits tolerances can be passed to team managers in work package descriptions
So that the project board can set the risk appetite of the business for the project
So the means of delivery can be checked against the business case that it must satisfy
10.w: A plan defines the products and the means of delivering them, including estimates of when and how much, so that the business case is satisfied. The estimates let the board check the plan against the business case (see manual 7.1, 7.7).

n.0: The business case remains the record of the why and is maintained throughout; a plan satisfies it but does not replace it (manual 5.1, 7.1).
n.1: Work package descriptions carry scope, cost and time tolerances; benefits tolerances are not set at work package level (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Risk appetite is set by the business, not derived from a plan's estimates (manual 9.2.1).

10.q: Why is leading a project team often harder than leading an established business team?
o: The team is temporary and crosses organizations, so authority is harder to exercise
The project manager is not permitted to give instructions to the team managers
Project teams have no governance arrangements until the project has been authorized
The project board leads the team directly, leaving the project manager to administer
10.w: Projects are delivered by temporary teams that typically work across organizational boundaries, so a temporary leader can find it harder to exercise authority and a different style of leadership is needed (see manual 3.3).

n.1: The project manager does instruct team managers, for example by authorizing work packages in controlling a stage (manual 16.4.1).
n.2: Governance applies before authorization: the business layer appoints the executive in starting up a project, and the project board directs initiation through 'directing a project' (manual ch 13, ch 14).
n.3: The project board directs; the project manager manages and leads the team day to day on the board's behalf (manual 6.2.4).

10.q: A team manager telephones the project manager about a fault found in a product. The project manager decides it is a problem, sets its priority and enters it in the issue register. Which step of the issues technique is this?
o: Assess
Recommend
Decide
Capture
10.w: Capture covers determining the issue type, determining its severity or priority and registering it; issues can be captured through formal or informal channels such as a phone call (see manual 10.3.1.1, fig 10.1).

n.0: Assess looks at whether and how the issue affects the project, such as its impact on the business case and risk profile; it follows registration (manual 10.3.1.2).
n.1: Recommend identifies and evaluates options and recommends one to the authority; no options have been considered yet (manual 10.3.1.3).
n.2: Decide is when the person or group with authority approves, rejects or otherwise responds to the recommendation (manual 10.3.1.4).

10.q: A project has an initiation stage and three delivery stages. Which process creates the stage plan for the second delivery stage?
o: Managing a stage boundary, near the end of the first delivery stage
Starting up a project, along with the initiation stage plan
Initiating a project, along with the project plan
Controlling a stage, at the start of the second delivery stage
10.w: Every stage plan after initiation is prepared in managing a stage boundary near the end of the previous stage, so the plan for the second delivery stage is made at the end of the first (see manual 18.1).

n.1: Starting up a project plans only the initiation stage; later stage plans are made at stage boundaries (manual 13.4.7, 18.1).
n.2: Initiating a project creates the project plan; each delivery stage plan is made near the end of the stage before it (manual 15.4.4, 18.1).
n.3: A stage cannot start until the board has approved its plan, which must already exist (manual 14.4.4).

10.q: An organization renames the 'highlight report' as its familiar 'fortnightly update' and agrees that its widely dispersed board will review reports online. Which principle is being applied?
o: Manage by exception
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Tailor to suit the project
Learn from experience
10.w: Using the organization's own terminology and adjusting the format of reporting and reviews to suit the project are examples of tailoring the method to suit the project (manual 2.7).

n.0: No tolerances or escalation limits are being set; terms and reporting formats are being adapted (manual 2.5).
n.1: Roles and relationships are not being defined; the method's terms and formats are being adapted (manual 2.3).
n.3: No lessons are being sought or applied; the action is adapting the method to the organization (manual 2.2).

10.q: The marketing manager on a website project asks for an extra page to be added to the site map that the project board has already approved. Which type of issue is this?
o: Off-specification
Concern
Business opportunity
Request for change
10.w: A request for change is a proposal for a change to a baseline. The approved site map is part of the baseline, so asking to add to it is a request for change (see manual 10.1, 10.2.3).

n.0: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications; nothing here says a product is failing its specification (manual 10.2.3).
n.1: A concern is an issue whose timing and impact still need to be assessed; this is a clear proposal to change an approved product (manual 10.1).
n.2: A business opportunity is an unanticipated positive consequence for the project or user organization, not a request to alter an approved product (manual 10.1).

10.q: Where should a project's agreed tailoring decisions be documented?
o: In the project brief from starting up
In the lessons log within the project log
In the project initiation documentation
In the project mandate from the business
10.w: How the method is applied and tailored is documented and agreed during initiation and recorded in the project initiation documentation (PID), which the board approves when it authorizes the project (see manual 2.7 and 15.4.1).

n.0: The project brief is prepared in starting up a project, before the tailoring requirements are agreed in initiation (manual ch 13, 15.4.1).
n.1: The lessons log records lessons that may inform tailoring, but the agreed tailoring is part of the PID (manual 2.2, 2.7).
n.3: The project mandate is the business layer's trigger for the project and exists before any tailoring is agreed (manual ch 13).

10.q: Which role usually maintains the quality register and the quality records on behalf of the project manager?
o: Project assurance
Quality assurance
Project support
Senior supplier
10.w: Project support, which is the project manager's responsibility, maintains registers such as the quality register and administers quality records (see manual ch 6, tab 8.2).

n.0: Project assurance works for the project board and must be kept separate from the administrative work of project support (manual ch 6).
n.1: Quality assurance is independent of the project management team, so it does not maintain the project's registers (manual 8.2.3).
n.3: The senior supplier is a board role providing supplier resources and accountable for supplier quality, not an administrator of registers (manual ch 6).

10.q: A stage plan allows some lower-priority products to be left out without the project manager needing to escalate. Which type of tolerance describes this permitted variation in the plan's products?
o: Quality tolerance
Scope tolerance
Benefits tolerance
Risk tolerance
10.w: Scope tolerance is the permissible variation of a plan's products, for example agreeing in advance which lower-priority products may be dropped without escalation (see manual 11.2.1).

n.0: Quality tolerance is the permitted variation from the agreed quality criteria of products, not variation in which products are delivered (manual 11.2.1).
n.2: Benefits tolerance is the permitted under- or over-delivery of benefits, not variation in the plan's products (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: Risk tolerance sets limits on the plan's aggregated risks, not on which products are delivered (manual 11.2.1).

10.q: A project manager is drafting the stage structure for a new project and proposes 'Closure' as the last stage. Which statement correctly describes where closing a project sits in the lifecycle?
o: It is planned and authorized as a separate stage after the final delivery stage
It runs at the end of each delivery stage before the next one is authorized
It is the last part of the final delivery stage, not a stage of its own
It is carried out by the project board as part of directing a project
10.w: Closing a project is not a stage. It takes place at the end of the final delivery stage, and the closure work is planned in that stage's plan (see manual chapter 12, fig 12.1, and 19.1).

n.0: Closure is not planned as a separate stage; its activities are part of the final delivery stage (manual 12, 19.1).
n.1: Work at the end of each non-final stage is done in managing a stage boundary, not closing a project (manual 12, 18.1).
n.3: The project manager carries out closing a project; the board then authorizes closure in directing a project (manual 12, 14.4.5, 19.1).

10.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The project board may delegate authority for approving requests for change and off-specifications to a [?], which acts within the limits the board sets.
o: change authority
project assurance role
quality assurance function
team manager
10.w: The board may delegate approval of requests for change and off-specifications to a change authority, a person or group acting within limits set by the board (see manual 10.2.4).

n.1: Project assurance advises the board and checks that the project is being run properly; it is not the body delegated to approve changes (manual 6.2, 10.2.4).
n.2: Quality assurance is a function independent of the project management team; it does not approve the project's changes (manual 8.2).
n.3: A team manager implements corrective actions in work packages; delegated approval goes to a change authority or the project manager (manual 10.2.4, 10.6).

10.q: In the 'receive completed work package' activity, what does the project manager make sure of for each product delivered?
o: The executive has approved it, as owner of the business case
Its benefits have been measured and recorded
It has the approval set out in its product description
The users have taken it into operational use
10.w: In receive completed work package the project manager checks that each product has its requisite approval, as defined by the quality and sustainability responsibilities in its product description, then updates the product register and stage plan (see manual 16.4.3).

n.0: Approval follows the quality responsibilities in each product description; the executive is not the approver of every product (manual 16.4.3).
n.1: Benefits are assessed through the benefits management approach, including reviews after closure, not when a work package is received (manual 19.2, 14.4.5).
n.3: Products are passed into the operational and maintenance environment in closing a project, in confirm project acceptance (manual 19.4.3).

10.q: Which management product describes the quality techniques and standards to be applied, and the roles and responsibilities for achieving the required quality?
o: Product description
Quality management approach
Quality register
Project product description
10.w: The quality management approach describes the quality techniques and standards to be applied and the roles and responsibilities for achieving the required quality specifications and acceptance criteria (see manual 8.5).

n.0: A product description defines one product, including its quality specifications, not the project's overall quality techniques and standards (manual 8.5).
n.2: The quality register records quality activities and results; it does not set the techniques and standards to be used (manual 8.5).
n.3: The project product description holds the user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria for the project product, not the techniques and responsibilities (manual 8.1.1).

10.q: Apart from the start of a new stage, what can trigger the 'authorize a work package' activity?
o: A team manager notifying that a work package is complete
The project board ordering a premature close
The business layer issuing a revised project mandate
A corrective action that needs new or amended work
10.w: Authorize a work package is triggered at the start of a stage and also by corrective action, which is put into effect through new or amended work packages (see manual 16.4.1, 16.4.6).

n.0: Notice of a completed work package triggers receive completed work package, not authorization of new work (manual 16.4.3).
n.1: A premature close notice from the board triggers closing a project, where work is made safe rather than newly authorized (manual 19.4.2).
n.2: The project mandate triggers starting up a project; it does not trigger work packages within a stage (manual 13.3).

10.q: Which three tests does the business case practice use to judge whether a project is, and remains, worth continuing?
o: Whether it is specific, measurable and achievable
Whether it is affordable, deliverable and sustainable
Whether it is desirable, feasible and compliant
Whether it is desirable, viable and achievable
10.w: The business case practice judges whether the project is (and remains) desirable, viable and achievable (see manual 5.1).

n.0: This resembles an objective-setting checklist, not the PRINCE2 business case tests of desirable, viable and achievable (manual 5.1).
n.1: Affordability and sustainability are aspects of performance; the business case tests are desirable, viable and achievable (manual 1.4, 5.1).
n.2: Two of these terms are not the PRINCE2 tests; the practice judges whether the project is desirable, viable and achievable (manual 5.1).

10.q: A team manager forecasts that a work package will exceed its cost tolerance, although the stage as a whole is still forecast to stay within tolerance. How does manage by exception apply?
o: The team manager raises an exception report directly to the project board
The team manager raises an issue to the project manager to resolve
The project manager asks the business layer for an exception plan
The team manager continues, as the stage tolerance will not be breached
10.w: The team manager escalates a forecast breach of work package tolerance to the project manager as an issue; work package exceptions are handled by the project manager in controlling a stage (manual 11.2.1, 11.2.6).

n.0: Team managers escalate to the project manager, not the board; only stage or project exceptions go to the board (manual 11.2.6).
n.2: No exception plan is needed while the stage is within tolerance, and the business layer handles project-level exceptions (manual 11.2.6).
n.3: The team manager's own tolerance is forecast to be breached, so it must be escalated to the project manager (manual 11.2.1).

10.q: Which of the following is an objective of the starting up a project process?
o: To ensure there is common understanding of how baselines will be established and controlled
To ensure alternative ways of doing the work are evaluated and a project approach is agreed
To ensure the business layer has an effective connection to the project throughout its life
To produce a project plan showing how and when products will be delivered and at what cost
10.w: One objective of starting up a project is that the various ways of approaching the project are evaluated and a project approach is agreed (see manual 13.2).

n.0: Understanding how baselines will be established and controlled is an objective of initiating a project (manual 15.2).
n.2: Keeping the business layer connected to the project is an objective of directing a project (manual 14.2).
n.3: Understanding how and when products will be delivered and at what cost comes from the project plan prepared in initiating a project (manual 15.2, 15.4.4).

10.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

The project board is accountable to the [?] for the success of the project and has authority to direct the project within the remit that has been set for it.
o: project manager
senior user
business
project assurance
10.w: The project board is accountable to the business for the success of the project, and directs it within the remit set by the business (see manual 6.2.1).

n.0: The project manager is accountable to the project board, not the other way round (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: The senior user is a member of the project board, not the party the board answers to (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Project assurance is carried out on behalf of the board members; the board is not accountable to it (manual 6.2.4).

10.q: A project manager is agreeing the management approaches in initiation. What does the digital and data management approach describe?
o: How the project's products will be quality checked and then accepted by the users
How issues will be captured and assessed and how changes to baselines will be controlled
How data and information will be created, used and managed during and after the project
How the project's stakeholders will be engaged and kept informed during the project
10.w: The digital and data management approach, part of the PID, sets out how data and information will be created, used and managed across the project ecosystem, through the lifecycle and afterwards, including security and privacy (see manual 11.5).

n.0: Quality checking and acceptance arrangements belong in the quality management approach (manual 8.5).
n.1: Handling issues and controlling changes to baselines is covered by the issue management approach (manual 10.5).
n.3: Engaging and informing stakeholders is planned in the communication management approach (manual 3.4).

10.q: In PRINCE2 7, what is the project baseline?
o: The current approved versions of the management and project products that are under change control
The original versions of the plans, kept unchanged so that later progress can be compared with them
The tolerances for the seven aspects of performance agreed for each stage of the project
The list of all the products required by a plan, together with the current status of each one
10.w: The project baseline is the current approved versions of the management products and project products that are subject to change control (see manual 10.1).

n.1: The baseline is the current approved version, not a frozen original: each approved change creates a new baselined version (manual 10.1, 10.2.1).
n.2: Tolerances are limits of delegated authority set under manage by exception; they are not the baseline itself (manual 2.5, 11.2.1).
n.3: A list of a plan's products and their status describes the product register in the project log, not the baseline (manual 4.3.2, 10.1).

10.q: Which statement about the supplier interest in a PRINCE2 project is correct?
o: Suppliers may be internal teams or external organizations, and the senior supplier represents them
Suppliers must be external organizations, because internal teams belong to the user interest
Suppliers are represented by the team managers, who sit on the project board for that purpose
Suppliers are accountable for specifying the benefits that the project's products will deliver
10.w: The supplier interest covers people with the skills and knowledge to deliver the products, whether from within the organization or external, and the senior supplier represents it (see manual 6.2.1, 6.2.4).

n.1: Suppliers may come from within the organization; the user interest is about using, operating or being affected by the products (manual 6.2.1).
n.2: Team managers work at the delivering level and are not board members; the senior supplier represents suppliers (manual fig 6.2, 6.2.4).
n.3: Specifying benefits is the accountability of the senior user, not the supplier interest (manual 6.2.4).

10.q: Which list gives the seven aspects of project performance that PRINCE2 7 manages?
o: Benefits, costs, time, quality, scope, risk and stakeholders
Benefits, costs, time, quality, scope, risk and resources
Benefits, costs, time, quality, scope, risk and governance
Benefits, costs, time, quality, scope, risk and sustainability
10.w: The seven aspects of project performance are benefits, costs, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk (see manual 1.4). Sustainability was added in PRINCE2 7.

n.0: Stakeholders matter to the people element, but they are not one of the seven aspects of performance; the seventh aspect is sustainability.
n.1: Resources are planned and managed through the plans, but resources are not one of the seven aspects; the seventh is sustainability.
n.2: Governance is provided by the project board and the method as a whole; it is not an aspect of performance. The seventh aspect is sustainability.

10.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
Risk [?] is determined by the business, and the project board applies it when setting measurable risk thresholds for the project.
o: tolerance
exposure
budget
appetite
10.w: Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk the business is willing to take; the board bases the project's risk tolerance on it (see manual 9.2, 9.2.1).

n.0: Risk tolerance is the measurable threshold itself, set by the project board, rather than the business's attitude it is based on (manual 9.2.1).
n.1: Risk exposure is the degree to which an objective is at risk; it is assessed, not determined by the business (manual 9.2).
n.2: The risk budget funds responses to risks; it is not the basis for setting tolerance (manual 9.2).

10.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.

The work breakdown structure is a hierarchy of all the work to be done during a project, and it forms a link between the product breakdown structure and the [?].
o: work packages
stage plans
team plans
product descriptions
10.w: The WBS links the product breakdown structure to the work packages (see manual 6.2.5).

n.1: Stage plans are one level of plan; the WBS links the product breakdown structure to the work packages rather than to a plan level (manual 6.2.5).
n.2: Team plans are optional plans produced by team managers; they are not what the WBS links to (manual 7.2.2.3).
n.3: Product descriptions describe each product in the product breakdown structure; the WBS goes further, to the work packages (manual 6.2.5, 7.3.1).

10.q: Which role is appointed as the single point of accountability for the project, is ultimately accountable for its success and secures its funding?
o: Senior user
Senior supplier
Executive
Project manager
10.w: The executive is appointed by the business as the single point of accountability, is ultimately accountable for the project's success and secures its funding (see manual 6.2.4.1).

n.0: The senior user represents the users and is accountable for requirements and benefits specification, not overall success and funding (manual 6.2.4).
n.1: The senior supplier commits supplier resources and is accountable for supplier product quality and technical integrity (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: The project manager runs the project day to day on the board's behalf; ultimate accountability stays with the executive (manual 6.2.4.5).

10.q:
Which two items would typically be included in the communication management approach?
1. An analysis of who is affected by the project and who can influence its success.
2. The purpose, frequency, channels and messages for each stakeholder group.
3. The scales used to estimate the probability and impact of each risk.
4. The prioritized acceptance criteria for the project product.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
10.w: Statement 1 is the stakeholder analysis and statement 2 is the communications schedule and procedures, both headings of the communication management approach (see manual 3.4).

n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: probability and impact scales belong in the risk management approach (manual ch 9).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: acceptance criteria are recorded in the project product description (manual ch 8).
n.3: Both statements are wrong: risk scales go in the risk management approach and acceptance criteria in the project product description (manual ch 8, ch 9).

10.q: Which 'closing a project' activity produces the end project report for the project board?
o: Evaluate the project
Confirm project acceptance
Request project closure
Prepare planned closure
10.w: In evaluate the project the project manager compares performance with the baselined PID, reviews lessons and prepares the end project report and lessons report (see manual 19.4.4).

n.1: This activity hands the products to the operational and maintenance environment and confirms acceptance (manual 19.4.3).
n.2: This activity briefs the board and asks it to authorize closure, using the end project report already prepared (manual 19.4.5).
n.3: This activity confirms the project can close, updates the project plan with actuals and closes the project log (manual 19.4.1).

10.q: How does PRINCE2 7 relate to the delivery approach a project uses?
o: It governs the project whichever delivery approach is used, without changing its principles
It replaces the delivery approach with its own processes for building specialist products
It requires a linear-sequential approach so that each stage can be approved in turn
It applies its principles to linear-sequential work and exempts iterative work from them
10.w: PRINCE2 7 is not specific to any delivery method: linear-sequential, iterative-incremental and hybrid delivery can all sit within its governance, and the principles always apply (see manual 1.1 and 1.5.3).

n.1: PRINCE2 works alongside specialist delivery methods; its processes direct and manage the project rather than replacing how products are built.
n.2: Stages are used with any delivery approach; PRINCE2 7 does not require linear-sequential delivery.
n.3: All seven principles must be applied for any PRINCE2 project, whatever the delivery approach.

10.q: What is the purpose of the directing a project process?
o: To ensure the prerequisites for initiating the project are in place and that the project is viable and worthwhile
To enable the project board to be accountable for success by making key decisions while delegating day-to-day management
To assign work, monitor it, deal with issues and report progress so that the stage stays within its tolerances
To control the link between the project manager and team managers by agreeing how work is accepted and delivered
10.w: Directing a project enables the project board to be accountable for the project's success by making key decisions and exercising overall control, while delegating day-to-day management to the project manager (see manual 14.1).

n.0: Ensuring the prerequisites for initiation are in place is the purpose of starting up a project (manual 13.1).
n.2: Assigning and monitoring work and reporting progress within stage tolerances is the purpose of controlling a stage, run by the project manager (manual 16.1).
n.3: Controlling the link between the project manager and team managers is the purpose of managing product delivery (manual 17.1).

10.q: The project manager forecasts that the whole project will exceed its project-level cost tolerance, and the project board agrees. Which organizational level should decide how to proceed?
o: Directing, because the project board is accountable for the success of the project
Business layer, because it defined the project-level tolerances in the first place
Managing, because the project manager runs the project on behalf of the project board
Delivering, because the team managers produce the products that incur the costs
10.w: The business layer defines project-level tolerances and decides on breaches of them; the board escalates a forecast breach of project tolerance to the business layer (see manual 6.2, fig 6.2, 11.2).

n.0: The board is accountable for success but can decide only within the project tolerances it was given; a forecast breach of them goes to the business layer (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: The project manager escalates forecast breaches of stage tolerance to the board; decisions on project tolerance are made above the board (manual 11.2).
n.3: Team managers work within work package tolerances and escalate to the project manager; they do not decide on project-level breaches (manual 6.2.4).

10.q: Which feature of PRINCE2 means the method can be tailored to meet the specific needs of the organizations involved?
o: Universal
Proven
Flexible
Outcome-focused
10.w: PRINCE2 is flexible: it can be tailored to meet the specific needs of the organizations involved (see manual 1.6 and the tailor to suit the project principle).

n.0: Universal is about applying to any project of any scale alongside specialist models; tailoring to the organizations involved is the flexible feature.
n.1: Proven means it is based on established and proven practice and governance.
n.3: Outcome-focused means keeping participants focused on the project's viability against its business case.

11.q: The project manager assesses a request for change and finds that it would cost more than the delegated authority allows. Who should make the decision on this request?
o: The team manager who would deliver the extra products in a work package
Project support, because it maintains the issue register for the project
The project board, or a change authority with enough authority
Project assurance, acting on behalf of the senior user and the executive
11.w: In the decide step, an issue beyond the decision-maker's delegated authority is escalated; decisions are made by the project board, a change authority or the project manager within the authority each holds (see manual 10.3.1.4, 10.2.4).

n.0: Team managers implement corrective actions in their work packages; they do not approve requests for change (manual 10.6).
n.1: Project support administers the procedures by maintaining the issue register; it has no decision authority over changes (manual 10.6).
n.3: Project assurance supports the board; it does not take decisions on requests for change on the board's behalf (manual 6.2, 10.2.4).

11.q: A team member assigned to write user training material is found to lack some of the skills needed for the task. Which action follows PRINCE2's guidance on building effective teams?
o: Record the skills gap as an off-specification and wait for the board's decision
Arrange upskilling or shift the training tasks to someone better suited
Ask the business layer to widen the project tolerances to allow for the delay
Leave the plan as it is, as building skills is the team member's responsibility
11.w: PRINCE2 says gaps in competency and capability should be identified and mitigated, for example by upskilling the person or shifting responsibility for certain tasks to more appropriate people (see manual 3.3.2).

n.0: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications; a gap in someone's skills is not one, and no product has been delivered yet (manual 10.1).
n.2: No breach of project tolerance is forecast; the response to a competency gap is mitigation such as upskilling, not changing tolerances (manual 3.3.2, 11.2.1).
n.3: Identifying gaps and putting mitigations in place is part of building an effective team, not something left to the individual (manual 3.3.2).

11.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
Issues that are being managed formally are recorded in the [?], which is one of the records held in the project log.
o: daily log
lessons log
risk register
issue register
11.w: The issue register, part of the project log, captures and maintains information on all issues that are being managed formally (see manual 10.5, 4.3.2).

n.0: The daily log is also in the project log, but it holds informal and sensitive issues rather than formal ones (manual 11.5).
n.1: The lessons log records lessons, not issues under formal management (manual 11.5).
n.2: The risk register records uncertain events, while formal issues have their own register (manual 9.5).

11.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the issues practice from the risk practice?
o: Issues are uncertain events that may happen later; risks are events that have already occurred
Issues need management consideration now; risks are uncertain events that may affect objectives
Issues are raised by team managers; risks are identified by the project board and the executive
Issues concern specialist products; risks concern management products such as plans and reports
11.w: An issue is a relevant event that requires project management consideration, whereas a risk is an uncertain event that, should it occur, would affect objectives (see manual 10.1, 9.1).

n.0: This reverses the two definitions: risks are the uncertain future events and issues are the events that need consideration now (manual 9.1, 10.1).
n.2: Issues can be raised by anyone at any time, and risks can be identified by anyone in the project too; the difference is certainty, not who raises them (manual 9.1, 10.1).
n.3: Both issues and risks can relate to any product, management or project; the distinction is between a present event and an uncertain one (manual 9.1, 10.1).

11.q: Which role uses the 'managing product delivery' process to carry out its work?
o: The project manager, who authorizes and receives work packages
The senior supplier, who directs supplier teams for the board
Project support, which keeps the registers for the team
The team manager, who agrees and delivers work packages
11.w: Managing product delivery is the delivering level of the process model: it is the team manager's view of the work, while controlling a stage is the project manager's view (see manual 12, 17.3).

n.0: Authorizing and receiving work packages are the project manager's activities in controlling a stage; managing product delivery is the team manager's view (manual 16.4.1, 17.3).
n.1: The senior supplier sits on the project board, and the board is not involved in managing product delivery (manual 17.3).
n.2: Project support helps the project manager with administration; it is informed of work package completion but does not run the process (manual 17.4.4).

11.q: Which aspect of project performance is concerned with when the project will start, when its key products will be delivered and when it will finish?
o: Scope
Costs
Time
Benefits
11.w: The time aspect covers when the project starts, when key products are delivered and when it finishes (see manual 1.4).

n.0: Scope covers what the project will deliver, not when.
n.1: Costs cover affordability and any overspend or underspend against the budget.
n.3: Benefits cover who the project is for and what must be achieved to justify the investment.

11.q: On a small project, the project manager plans fortnightly email updates to the board instead of formal weekly highlight reports. Which statement is correct?
o: It is acceptable tailoring of reporting frequency and formality
It is not allowed, as highlight reports follow a set weekly cycle
It departs from 'manage by exception', so needs an exception report
It is acceptable once the business layer has reissued the mandate
11.w: Making controls fit the project's scale includes adjusting the frequency and formality of reports and reviews; agreed lighter reporting is normal tailoring for a small project (see manual 2.7).

n.1: Highlight reports are time-driven at a frequency agreed for the project; there is no fixed weekly cycle (manual 2.7, ch 11).
n.2: Changing report frequency does not breach any tolerance, so no exception report is needed; exception reports are for forecast tolerance breaches (manual 2.5).
n.3: Reporting arrangements are agreed as project controls in initiation and recorded in the PID; the mandate does not need to be reissued (manual 15.4.3).

11.q: A project team is drawn from four departments. Nobody is sure who may approve changes to the design, and decisions keep stalling. Which challenge that PRINCE2 is designed to address does this BEST illustrate?
o: Uncertainty about which delivery approach the suppliers intend to use
Projects overrunning because tolerances have been set too widely
A lack of common vocabulary between organizations in different industries
Unclear roles, responsibilities and accountability in a temporary team
11.w: Temporary, cross-functional teams often suffer from confusion about who is responsible for what and who can decide. PRINCE2 addresses this with defined roles, responsibilities and relationships and a clear project management team structure (see manual 1.4 and 2.3).

n.0: The stem says nothing about how products will be delivered; the problem is that nobody knows who has authority to decide.
n.1: Tolerances are not mentioned and no overrun is described; decisions are stalling because authority is unclear.
n.2: The departments belong to one organization and the problem is who decides, not the meaning of project terms.

11.q:
Which two statements about risk owners and risk action owners are correct?
1. The risk owner is responsible for responding to the risk.
2. The risk action owner is responsible for managing the risk as a whole.
3. The risk action owner carries out agreed actions to respond to the risk.
4. Project support is the risk owner for each risk in the register.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
11.w: Statement 1 matches the definition of the risk owner, and statement 3 matches the risk action owner, who owns agreed actions for the risk owner (see manual 9.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: overall responsibility for responding to the risk sits with the risk owner, not the risk action owner (manual 9.2).
n.2: Both are wrong: the risk owner, not the action owner, responds to the risk, and project support administers the register rather than owning risks (manual 9.2, appendix B).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: project support provides risk administration but is not assigned as owner of every risk (manual 9.2, appendix B).

11.q: A customer and its main supplier each have their own quality management system. Why might the project tailor PRINCE2?
o: To align its processes and documents with both quality systems
To let the supplier's quality system replace the principles
To make the supplier's senior manager the executive
To remove the need for a quality management approach
11.w: A commercial customer-supplier relationship is an influence that gives cause to tailor: the project may need to align its management processes, practices and documentation with two or more quality systems (see manual 2.7).

n.1: Principles cannot be replaced or tailored; quality systems are aligned with, not substituted for, the principles (manual ch 2).
n.2: The executive represents the business interest and is accountable for the business case; the supplier is represented by the senior supplier (manual 6.2.1).
n.3: The quality management approach is still needed; tailoring adjusts it to align with both quality systems (manual 2.7, 15.4.2).

11.q: How does the organizing practice support the 'learn from experience' principle?
o: By adapting the role descriptions and the management approaches at each stage boundary
By creating a project management team suited to the capability of the people involved
By developing an explicit team structure so that everyone knows their responsibilities
By using lessons to inform the team structure, the WBS and a healthy project ecosystem
11.w: Organizing applies learn from experience by using lessons to shape the project management team structure, the work breakdown structure and a healthy project ecosystem, so the right people are in the right roles at the right time (see manual 6.7, tab 6.5).

n.0: Adapting role descriptions and approaches at stage boundaries is how organizing supports manage by stages (manual tab 6.5).
n.1: A team suited to the project's needs and people's capability is how organizing supports tailor to suit the project (manual tab 6.5).
n.2: An explicit team structure that makes responsibilities clear is how organizing supports define roles, responsibilities and relationships (manual tab 6.5).

11.q: A project will build a new visitor centre with several separate products. Where are the quality specifications for one of those individual products documented?
o: In that product's product description
In the project product description
In the quality register
In the quality management approach
11.w: Quality specifications, the measures and levels a specific product must meet, are documented in that product's product description (see manual 8.1.1, 8.5).

n.1: The project product description holds the user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria for the project product as a whole, not each product's specifications (manual 8.1.1).
n.2: The quality register records quality activities planned or performed and their results, not the specifications themselves (manual 8.5).
