n.3: The quality management approach sets out the quality techniques, standards and responsibilities for the project, not the specifications of individual products (manual 8.5).

11.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
People factors such as behaviours, culture and relationships are difficult to document and are best learned through [?] learning.
o: formal
individual
social
classroom
11.w: PRINCE2 explains that much valuable knowledge is hidden in the project ecosystem and that behaviours, culture and relationships are best learned through social learning, which is how the people element applies learn from experience (see manual 3.5.1).

n.0: Formal learning suits knowledge that can be written down; PRINCE2 says these people factors are hard to document and are learned socially (manual 3.5.1).
n.1: Individual learning keeps knowledge with one person; PRINCE2 calls for a collaborative environment that shares knowledge (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: Classroom learning is a form of formal teaching; people factors are best learned socially within the project ecosystem (manual 3.5.1).

11.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
The decision bias known as [?] makes people value cohesion within a group more than expressing a different view or reaching the right decision.
o: loss aversion
groupthink
optimism bias
proximity bias
11.w: Groupthink is the bias in which keeping the group together matters more than challenging a view or reaching the right decision (see manual 9.2.4).

n.0: Loss aversion values avoiding loss over making a gain (manual 9.2.4).
n.2: Optimism bias discounts disadvantageous risk on the assumption of success (manual 9.2.4).
n.3: Proximity bias treats nearer situations as riskier and more important (manual 9.2.4).

11.q: A housing association has completed ten kitchen refurbishment projects. Its next one will use a different contractor, at a new site, for a different group of tenants. Which characteristic of a project does this BEST illustrate?
o: Temporary
Change
Unique
Cross-functional
11.w: Every project is unique: even when an organization runs many similar projects, each one differs in some way, such as its team, customer, supplier, location or timeframe (see manual 1.3).

n.0: Temporary is about the project ending once its change is implemented; the stem is about how this project differs from earlier similar ones.
n.1: Change describes projects as the means of introducing change; the stem highlights the different contractor, site and tenants, which shows uniqueness.
n.3: Cross-functional is about people with different skills working together; the stem compares this project with previous ones rather than describing the team's skills.

11.q:
Which two statements about the project board and the project management team are correct?

1. The project board is made up of the executive, senior user(s) and senior supplier(s).
2. The project board is accountable to the project manager for directing each stage.
3. The project management team structure includes project assurance and project support roles.
4. The project board manages the work packages day to day on behalf of the team managers.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
11.w: The board comprises the executive, senior user(s) and senior supplier(s) (statement 1), and the project management team structure includes the assurance and support roles as well as the board, project manager and team managers (statement 3) (see manual 6.2.1, 6.2.3).

n.1: Statement 2 is false: the board is accountable to the business, and the project manager is accountable to the board (manual 6.2.1).
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both false: the board answers to the business, and day-to-day management is done by the project manager and team managers (manual fig 6.2).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is false: the board directs; it does not manage work packages day to day (manual fig 6.2).

11.q: In the plans practice, what is captured in a schedule?
o: The list of all the products of a plan together with the current status of each
The hierarchy of all the products to be produced during a plan
The timetable of reports and meetings agreed with the stakeholders
The sequencing, interrelationships and duration of work packages and their tasks
11.w: A schedule captures the sequencing, interrelationships and duration of work packages and their tasks; every work package for a stage must appear in that stage's schedule (see manual 7.3.1.4).

n.0: This describes the product register, which is held in the project log (manual 4.3.2).
n.1: This describes the product breakdown structure (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.2: Reporting and communication timings belong in the communication management approach and project controls, not the plan's schedule (manual 7.3.1.4).

11.q:
Which two statements about the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle are correct?
1. Stakeholders can be inside or outside the business.
2. The supplier interest is represented by the project manager.
3. Relationships matter within the project team and beyond it.
4. Roles are agreed once the first delivery stage has begun.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
11.w: Statement 1 is correct: stakeholders include internal groups and outside parties such as unions, customers, suppliers and communities. Statement 3 is correct: the team builds relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (manual 2.3).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the supplier interest is represented on the project board, not by the project manager (manual 2.3).
n.1: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: the supplier interest sits on the board, and roles are agreed before delivery begins (manual 2.3).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: roles and responsibilities are defined and agreed as the project is set up, not after delivery starts (manual 2.3, ch 13).

11.q: In a linear-sequential project, how detailed should product descriptions be when they are written?
o: Brief, because acceptance criteria will be refined during delivery through a product backlog
Limited to the project's major products, as recorded in the project product description
Written in full for the final stage's products, with earlier products left as titles
Detailed enough for cost and time to be estimated with an appropriate level of confidence
11.w: In a linear-sequential project, product descriptions should be detailed enough for cost and time to be estimated at an appropriate level of confidence. In iterative-incremental work, criteria are refined during delivery (see manual 7.3.1.1).

n.0: Refining criteria during delivery through a product backlog describes an iterative-incremental project (manual 7.2.3).
n.1: The project product description covers the major products; individual product descriptions go further, down to the products of each plan (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.2: Products are described as each plan is prepared, so earlier products need descriptions before their work starts (manual 7.3.1.1).

11.q:
Which two statements about people within and affected by a project are correct?
1. Members of the project board are people working within the project.
2. Someone who perceives that they will be affected by the project is a stakeholder.
3. People affected by a project fall outside the scope of the people element.
4. People with no formal role should be kept out of decisions about new ways of working.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
11.w: Statement 1 is correct: board members hold roles in the project management team, so they work within the project. Statement 2 is correct: a stakeholder includes anyone who perceives themselves to be affected by the project (see manual 3.1, 3.2.2).

n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: the people element explicitly covers those impacted by the project as well as those working on it (manual ch 3).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: PRINCE2 encourages co-creating products and ways of working with users and key influencers, many of whom hold no formal role (manual 3.3).
n.3: Statements 3 and 4 are both wrong: affected people are part of the people element and should be involved in shaping the change (manual ch 3, 3.3).

11.q: Which management products does quality planning produce, so that the project knows how its products will be checked?
o: The quality register entries and the results of each completed quality check
The outline business case and the project brief for the initiation stage
The product descriptions and the quality management approach for the project
The acceptance records and the end project report for the project board
11.w: Quality planning captures the quality specifications and produces the product descriptions and the quality management approach (see manual 8.2.1).

n.0: Recording quality checks and their results in the quality register is quality control, not quality planning (manual 8.2.2).
n.1: The outline business case and project brief are created in starting up a project under the business case practice (manual ch 5, ch 13).
n.3: Acceptance records and the end project report belong to project acceptance and closing a project, not quality planning (manual 8.3.1.3, ch 19).

11.q: How is the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle reflected in the make-up of the project board?
o: The board includes the project manager so that delivery is represented
The board has one member for each practice so that all practices are covered
The board brings together the business, user and supplier interests
The board is made up of line managers from each affected department
11.w: The principle requires the business, user and supplier interests to be represented, and this is reflected in the design of the project board (manual 2.3).

n.0: The project manager runs the project day to day for the board but is not a board member (manual ch 6).
n.1: Board membership follows the three stakeholder interests, not the seven practices (manual 2.3).
n.3: Membership is based on representing business, user and supplier interests, not on line positions (manual 2.3).

11.q:
Which two statements describe how the progress practice supports the PRINCE2 principles?

1. Setting tolerances and raising exception reports supports manage by exception.
2. Fixing the same reporting frequency for every project supports tailor to suit the project.
3. Recording lessons in the lessons log and passing them on supports learn from experience.
4. Producing highlight reports is how the focus on products principle is applied.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
11.w: Tolerances and exception reporting put manage by exception into practice (1), and the lessons log and lessons report support learn from experience (3) (see manual 2.2, 2.5, 11.7).

n.1: Statement 1 is correct, but tailoring means adjusting reporting frequency and formality to the project, not fixing one frequency for all (manual 2.7).
n.2: Both are wrong: tailoring adjusts reporting to suit each project, and focus on products concerns defining products, not highlight reporting (manual 2.6, 2.7).
n.3: Statement 3 is correct, but focus on products is applied by defining products and their quality requirements, not by highlight reports (manual 2.6).

11.q:
Which two statements about the business case technique are correct?
1. The 'do nothing differently' option is the baseline used to quantify the other options.
2. The project board checks the business case when assessing an exception plan.
3. The confirm step is completed before the project board authorizes the project.
4. The develop step begins with the end project report.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
11.w: Statement 1 is correct: 'do nothing differently' is the baseline against which the other options are measured. Statement 2 is correct: the board checks the business case at the end of starting up, the end of initiation, each stage end and when assessing an exception plan (see manual 5.3.1).

n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: confirming benefits happens mainly after closure, long after the project is authorized (manual 5.3.1).
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: the develop step starts from the project mandate, which triggers starting up a project (manual 5.3.1).
n.3: Statements 3 and 4 are both wrong: confirm is mainly post-project, and develop starts from the project mandate (manual 5.3.1).

11.q: A government agency is building an online licensing service. Members of the public will apply for licences through it, and agency staff will process the applications. How does PRINCE2 treat these two groups?
o: The public are external stakeholders rather than users, so the user interest is the agency staff
Both groups belong to the business interest, which the executive represents on the project board
Both groups are part of the user interest, which the senior user represents on the project board
The agency staff are part of the supplier interest, because they will operate the new service
11.w: Users can sit within the business (here, staff who will operate the service) or outside it as end users (here, the public), and the senior user represents the user interest (see manual 6.2.1).

n.0: PRINCE2 states that users can sit outside the business as end users, so the public are part of the user interest (manual 6.2.1).
n.1: The business interest concerns justification and value for money; people who use or are affected by the products form the user interest (manual 6.2.1).
n.3: Operating the products makes someone a user; suppliers are those with the skills to deliver the products (manual 6.2.1).

11.q: A project to merge two hospital pharmacies involves the hospital trust, the pharmacists who will use the new system and an external software supplier. Each has its own structures and culture. What does PRINCE2 call the temporary arrangement of people, relationships and ways of working created where these interests meet?
o: The organizational ecosystem
The business layer
The project ecosystem
The project management team structure
11.w: Where the business, user and supplier interests come together for the project, a temporary project ecosystem is created, made up of people, relationships, structures and ways of working (see manual 3.1, fig 3.2).

n.0: The organizational ecosystem is the existing trust, user and supplier organizations themselves, which continue after the project ends (manual 3.1).
n.1: The business layer is the commissioning level outside the project management team; here it would be part of the trust (manual 6.2).
n.3: The project management team structure is the set of roles in the project; the project ecosystem is wider, covering relationships and ways of working across the three interests (manual 3.1, 6.2.3).

11.q: Which is an objective of the 'managing product delivery' process?
o: To keep the business case under review during the stage
To give the board the information it needs to assess continuing viability
To make the team clear about the expected effort, cost and timescales
To ensure the business can support the products after closure
11.w: Managing product delivery aims to ensure that team managers and teams are clear about what is to be produced and the expected effort, cost and timescales (see manual 17.2).

n.0: Keeping the business case under review is an objective of controlling a stage (manual 16.2).
n.1: This is an objective of managing a stage boundary (manual 18.2).
n.3: This is an objective of closing a project (manual 19.2).

11.q: The project manager has completed the work of starting up a project. What triggers the directing a project process?
o: The project mandate from the business layer
The initiation notice from the board
The request to initiate a project
The first highlight report from the project manager
11.w: Directing a project starts when the board receives the request to initiate a project, the final output of starting up a project (see manual 14.3, 13.4.8).

n.0: The project mandate triggers starting up a project, which comes before directing a project (manual 13.3).
n.1: The initiation notice is an output of directing a project (authorize initiation) and triggers initiating a project (manual 14.4.1, 15.3).
n.3: Highlight reports are produced in controlling a stage, long after directing a project has begun (manual 16.1, 11.5).

11.q: PRINCE2 7 renamed the earlier 'defined roles and responsibilities' principle. What does the new wording add?
o: Tolerances agreed between each pair of management levels
A requirement for a full-time project manager
Building relationships with and between stakeholders
A separate role for each of the seven practices
11.w: PRINCE2 7 adds relationships: as well as defining roles and responsibilities, the project management team initiates and builds relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (manual 2.3).

n.0: Tolerances between management levels belong to manage by exception, not to the roles principle (manual 2.5).
n.1: The principle does not require a full-time project manager; it adds the building of relationships (manual 2.3).
n.3: Roles are not created per practice; the organizing practice defines the project management team roles (manual 2.3, ch 6).

11.q: A small, low-value internal project combines the project brief and the business case into a single short document. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Focus on products, as the merged document is a management product
Manage by stages, as the merged document is approved at a stage boundary
Tailor to suit the project, as the products are adapted to the project's scale
Learn from experience, as small projects reuse earlier business cases
11.w: Merging management products to fit a small project's scale is tailoring; the project still has a business justification, now held in a simpler document (see manual tab 5.2, 5.4.5, 2.7).

n.0: Focus on products concerns defining the products the project delivers; merging management documents for scale is tailoring (manual 2.6, 2.7).
n.1: The brief is approved when initiation is authorized; combining it with the business case is a tailoring choice, not a stage decision (manual 2.7, 14.4.1).
n.3: Nothing in the scenario involves reusing earlier lessons; adapting documents to the project's scale is tailoring (manual 2.2, 2.7).

11.q: Under which heading of the communication management approach should an analytics tool that tracks how many stakeholders read the project newsletter be recorded?
o: Stakeholder analysis
Communications schedule and procedures
Resources
Supporting tools and techniques
11.w: Supporting tools and techniques covers items such as communications platforms and tools for analytics or automation (see manual 3.4).

n.0: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is affected by the project or its delivery and who can influence its success; it does not record tools (manual 3.4).
n.1: The schedule and procedures set out purpose, frequency, channels and messages for each stakeholder group, not the tools used (manual 3.4).
n.2: Resources covers the resources for communication activities; an analytics tool belongs under supporting tools and techniques (manual 3.4).

11.q:
Which two statements about the activities of 'managing a stage boundary' are correct?
1. In 'request next stage', the project manager may highlight concessions granted for off-specifications during the stage.
2. In 'prepare next stage plan', the closure activities of the project are planned in the final stage's plan.
3. In 'evaluate the stage', the project board approves the end stage report and authorizes the next stage.
4. In 'update the business case', the post-project benefits reviews are carried out.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
11.w: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Request next stage briefs the board, including any concessions for off-specifications, and closure activities are part of the final stage plan (see manual ch 18).

n.1: Statement 3 is wrong: evaluate the stage is done by the project manager, and the board authorizes the next stage in directing a project (manual 14.4.4). Statement 1 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 2.
n.2: Statement 4 is wrong: post-project benefits reviews are planned during the project and carried out by the business after closure (manual 19.2, 14.4.5). Statement 2 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 1.
n.3: Statements 3 and 4 are both wrong. The board authorizes the next stage in directing a project (manual 14.4.4), and post-project benefits reviews happen after closure (manual 19.2).

11.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.

During quality planning, quality tolerances are set using the prioritized [?] and the quality specifications of the products.
o: acceptance criteria
benefits forecasts
risk responses
stage tolerances
11.w: Quality tolerance is set from the prioritized acceptance criteria and the quality specifications (see manual 8.2.1.2).

n.1: Benefits forecasts sit in the business case and drive benefits tolerance, not quality tolerance (manual ch 5).
n.2: Risk responses are planned under the risk practice and do not define how far a product's quality may vary (manual ch 9).
n.3: Stage tolerances are set by the project board for the stage plan; quality tolerance comes from acceptance criteria and quality specifications (manual 11.2, 8.2.1.2).

11.q: A construction firm is contracted to build a depot for a logistics company. Which statement about this commercial context is correct according to PRINCE2?
o: The supplier is covered by the customer's business case and needs no justification of its own
The contract between the parties replaces the need for a project board to direct the project
The project must use one management system, which the supplier chooses
The supplier will have its own business case for taking part in the project
11.w: In a commercial context each party has its own reasons for taking part: the supplier has its own business case, and the project may need to align with two or more management systems (see manual 1.5 and 2.1).

n.0: All parties, suppliers included, need a balance of benefits, costs and risks to justify their involvement, so the supplier has its own business case.
n.1: A contract governs the commercial relationship, but the project is still directed by a project board representing business, user and supplier interests.
n.2: A commercial project may need to align with two or more management systems, those of the customer and of the supplier.

11.q:
Which two statements about roles in the business case practice are correct?
1. The executive secures the funding for the project.
2. The senior supplier is responsible for realizing the benefits after closure.
3. The project manager owns the business case on behalf of the business layer.
4. The senior user's commitment to realizing benefits continues after the project closes.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
11.w: Statement 1 is correct: the executive secures funding and owns the business case. Statement 4 is correct: the senior user is responsible for the handover and adoption of products and for the continued realization of benefits after closure (see manual 6.2.4, tab 5.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: the senior user, not the senior supplier, is responsible for the continued realization of benefits after closure (manual 6.2.4.2).
n.1: Statements 2 and 3 are both wrong: the senior user is responsible for benefits realization, and the executive owns the business case (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: Statement 3 is wrong: the executive owns the business case; the project manager prepares and maintains it on the executive's behalf (manual 6.2.4, 15.4.5).

11.q: What is the minimum number of management stages in a PRINCE2 project, and what are they?
o: Two: an initiation stage and at least one delivery stage
One: a single delivery stage that includes initiation
Three: initiation, delivery and a closure stage
Two: a starting up stage and a delivery stage
11.w: A PRINCE2 project has at least two management stages: the initiation stage and one or more delivery stages. A simple project may need only initiation plus a single delivery stage (see manual 7.2.3).

n.1: Initiation is always a separate management stage, so a project cannot have fewer than two stages (manual 7.2.3).
n.2: Closing a project is not a stage; it takes place within the final delivery stage (manual 7.2.2.2).
n.3: Starting up a project happens before the project begins and is not a management stage; the first stage is initiation (manual 7.2.3).

11.q: Which integrated element recognizes that the needs, capabilities and motivations of those involved, and their relationships, are crucial to how a project is set up and managed?
o: People
Practices
Principles
Processes
11.w: People are at the centre of PRINCE2 7: understanding the needs, capabilities and motivations of those working on or affected by the project, and the relationships between them, is crucial (see manual 1.2 and chapter 3).

n.1: The practices describe aspects of project management such as plans and risk, not the needs and motivations of those involved.
n.2: The principles are the guiding obligations that make a project PRINCE2.
n.3: The processes set out the lifecycle activities; people apply them, but the element about needs and relationships is people.

11.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.
In the delivery stages, the business case is [?]: updated with progress data and the latest forecasts, and then checked at the end of each stage.
o: developed
outlined
maintained
superseded
11.w: Through the delivery stages the business case is maintained (updated with products delivered, costs, benefits realized and latest forecasts) and checked at each stage end before the next stage is authorized (see manual 5.2.1, fig 5.3, 5.3.1).

n.0: Developing the business case happens pre-project and in initiation, producing the outline and then the full version (manual 5.2.1).
n.1: The outline business case is produced in starting up a project, before the delivery stages (manual 13.4.3).
n.3: The business case is not superseded during delivery; it is the project brief that is superseded by the PID (manual 5.5).

11.q: During the initiation stage, which combination of processes is in use?
o: Directing a project, initiating a project and managing a stage boundary
Starting up a project, initiating a project and controlling a stage
Initiating a project, controlling a stage and managing product delivery
Directing a project, initiating a project and closing a project
11.w: In the initiation stage the board directs through directing a project, the project manager runs initiating a project, and managing a stage boundary is used near the end to plan the first delivery stage. Managing product delivery is not used in initiation (see manual chapter 12, fig 12.1).

n.1: Starting up a project is pre-project, before the initiation stage begins (manual 12, 13.3).
n.2: The process model shows no managing product delivery in the initiation stage; specialist delivery starts in later stages (manual 12).
n.3: Closing a project belongs to the final delivery stage, not to initiation (manual 12, 19.1).

11.q: Which term describes the completed set of project outputs that is required to deliver an outcome?
o: Capability
Benefit
Business objective
Outcome
11.w: A capability is the completed set of project outputs required to deliver an outcome. Outputs combine into capabilities, which lead to outcomes and then benefits (see manual 5.1, fig 5.1).

n.1: A benefit is the measurable improvement resulting from an outcome, not the set of outputs (manual 5.1).
n.2: A business objective is a measurable outcome that shows progress against the organization's strategy (manual 5.1).
n.3: An outcome is the result of change once the capability is used, not the set of outputs itself (manual 5.1).

11.q: A project board member asks what PRINCE2 means by a tolerance. Which definition is correct?
o: The total budget that the business layer has agreed to release for the whole project, including any contingency
The overall level of risk exposure that the business is willing to accept across all of its projects and operations
The permissible deviation above and below a plan's target before escalation to the next management level is needed
A situation in which a deviation beyond the levels agreed between two levels of management can be forecast
11.w: A tolerance is the permissible deviation above and below a plan's target for an aspect such as time or cost, beyond which the matter must be escalated to the next level of management (see manual 11.2.1).

n.0: A budget is a planned figure, not a permitted deviation; tolerance is the range above and below a target (manual 11.2.1).
n.1: This describes risk appetite, which the business determines; tolerance is a permitted deviation against a plan's target (manual 9.2.1, 11.2.1).
n.3: This is the definition of an exception, which is triggered when tolerance is forecast to be exceeded (manual 11.1).

11.q:
Which two statements about change management in PRINCE2 7 are correct?
1. It covers the move from the current state to the target state.
2. It is the procedure for approving requests for change to baselined products.
3. The organization may pass through interim states before reaching the target state.
4. It begins once the project has been closed and the products handed over.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
11.w: Statement 1 is correct: change management is how the organization transitions from the current state to the target state. Statement 3 is correct: the change management approach plans the move through any interim states (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: approving requests for change to baselined products is change control in the issues practice (manual 10.2.3).
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: approving requests for change is change control, and change management is planned in initiation as part of the PID (manual 10.2.3, 3.2.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the change management approach is agreed during initiating a project, long before closure (manual 15.4.2).

11.q:
Which two statements about the 'focus on products' principle are correct?
1. It helps to control scope creep.
2. Products are defined once the work to build them is complete.
3. Product descriptions include quality criteria or specifications.
4. It means each stage delivers exactly one product.
o: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
11.w: Statement 1 is correct: doing no more work than the agreed products need controls scope creep. Statement 3 is correct: product descriptions include quality criteria or specifications and the quality method (manual 2.6).

n.1: Statement 2 is wrong: products are defined and agreed before the work to deliver them (manual 2.6).
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: products are defined before the work, and a stage can deliver many products (manual 2.6).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: nothing in the principle limits a stage to one product (manual 2.6).

11.q: What does a sustainability tolerance set limits on in PRINCE2 7?
o: The plan's aggregated risks
The permissible variation of the plan's products
The agreed metrics for sustainability
The over- or under-delivery of benefits
11.w: A sustainability tolerance sets limits on the agreed sustainability metrics, alongside the other six tolerance areas (see manual 7.2.4, 11.2).

n.0: Limits on a plan's aggregated risks are risk tolerance (manual 7.2.4, 11.2).
n.1: Variation in the plan's products is scope tolerance (manual 7.2.4, 11.2).
n.3: Under- or over-delivery of benefits is benefits tolerance (manual 7.2.4, 11.2).

11.q:
Which two statements are correct for PRINCE2 7?
1. The 6th edition 'change' theme is now covered by the issues practice.
2. The change management approach describes how requests for change are approved.
3. Change management is part of the people element.
4. A change authority approves the organization's move from the current state to the target state.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
11.w: Statement 1 is correct: the old 'change' theme became the issues practice, which includes change control. Statement 3 is correct: change management is part of the people element (see manual 10.1, 3.2.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: how requests for change are assessed and controlled is set out in the issue management approach (manual 10.5).
n.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: requests for change are handled through the issue management approach, and a change authority approves requests for change and off-specifications (manual 10.5, 10.2.4).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: a change authority approves requests for change and off-specifications within delegated limits, not the organizational transition (manual 10.2.4).

11.q:
Which two statements about the organizational design and development technique are correct?

1. The design step is shaped by the work breakdown structure and the commercial management approach.
2. The transition step hands products, people and learning back to the business at closure.
3. The technique has four steps, ending with developing the project ecosystem.
4. The develop step is carried out once, in starting up a project, and is not repeated.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
11.w: The design step is shaped by the WBS and the commercial management approach (statement 1), and the final step transitions products, people and learning back into the organizational ecosystem (statement 2) (see manual 6.3.1, fig 6.5).

n.1: Statement 3 is false: the technique has five steps and ends with transitioning the project into the organizational ecosystem (manual fig 6.5).
n.2: Statement 4 is false: developing the project ecosystem is ongoing as needs, team members and relationships change (manual 6.3.1.3).
n.3: Both are false: there are five steps, and the develop step continues throughout the project (manual fig 6.5, 6.3.1.3).

11.q:
Which two statements about defining and analysing products are correct?
1. External products are left out of the product flow diagram because they are outside the project's control.
2. Product descriptions are written for products at all levels of plan.
3. A dependency means that one product depends on another, and dependencies can be internal or external.
4. The product flow diagram is drawn before the product breakdown structure is created.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 3
2 and 4
11.w: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Product descriptions are written for all levels of plan, and a dependency means one product depends on another, with at least internal and external types (see manual 7.3.1.1, 7.3.1.2).

n.0: Statement 1 is wrong: external products are included in the product flow diagram so that dependencies on others are visible (manual 7.3.1.1). Statement 2 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.
n.1: Statement 1 is wrong: external products are included in the product flow diagram so that dependencies on others are visible (manual 7.3.1.1). Statement 3 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 2.
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the product breakdown structure comes before product descriptions and the product flow diagram (manual 7.3.1.1). Statement 2 is correct, but it needs to be paired with statement 3.

11.q: Which statement describes the purpose of the 'closing a project' process?
o: To give the board enough information to review the stage and confirm continued justification
To ensure the prerequisites for initiating a project are in place
To provide a fixed point at which acceptance of the project product is confirmed
To let the board stay accountable while delegating day-to-day management
11.w: Closing a project provides a fixed point at which acceptance of the project product is confirmed and it is recognized that the objectives in the PID, or approved changes to them, have been achieved (see manual 19.1).

n.0: This is the purpose of managing a stage boundary, used at the end of every stage except the final one (manual 18.1).
n.1: This is the purpose of starting up a project, used before initiation (manual 13.1).
n.3: This is the purpose of directing a project, the board's process (manual 14.1).

11.q: A new team manager asks what a checkpoint report is for. Which statement describes the purpose of a checkpoint report?
o: To report a summary of stage status from the project manager to the project board
To tell the project board that stage tolerances are forecast to be exceeded
To summarize the stage at its end so the board can decide what to do next
To report the status of a work package from the team manager to the project manager
11.w: A checkpoint report is produced by the team manager for the project manager, reporting work package status at the frequency defined in the work package (see manual 11.5).

n.0: Summarizing stage status for the board is the purpose of the highlight report (manual 11.5).
n.1: Informing the board of a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance is the purpose of the exception report (manual 11.5).
n.2: A summary at the end of a stage to support the board's next decision is the end stage report (manual 11.5).

11.q: Which statement about the give ongoing direction activity is correct?
o: It takes place at each stage end so that the board can approve the next stage plan
It is the activity team managers use to obtain board decisions on their work packages
Board members can give guidance individually or collectively at any time during the project
It is the activity in which the board authorizes the project's first delivery stage
11.w: Give ongoing direction covers informal guidance and responses to requests for advice, given at any time by the board as a whole or by individual members, as well as responses to exception reports and to advice from the business layer (see manual 14.4.3).

n.0: Approving the next stage plan at a stage end is done in authorize a stage or exception plan (manual 14.4.4).
n.1: Team managers take direction from the project manager, not the board; the board is not involved in managing product delivery (manual 14.3, 17.1).
n.3: Authorizing a delivery stage, including the first, is done in authorize a stage or exception plan (manual 14.4.4).

11.q:
Which two statements about the purpose of the issues practice are correct?
1. It collects and assesses issues, which can be raised by anyone involved at any time.
2. It starts once the first delivery stage begins, after the project plan is approved.
3. It controls changes to the approved versions of management products and project products.
4. It sets how much risk the business is willing to take on the project.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
11.w: Statement 1 is correct: issues can be raised by anyone at any time and are collected and assessed by the practice. Statement 3 is correct: the practice controls changes to the project baseline, which is made of approved management and project products (see manual 10.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: issues are noted from starting up a project (in the daily log) and the issue register is set up in initiation, before any delivery stage (manual ch 13, ch 15).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: issues are handled from starting up a project, and risk appetite is set by the business, not by the issues practice (manual 9.2.1, ch 13).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: risk appetite is determined by the business and applied through the risk practice, not the issues practice (manual 9.2.1).

11.q: Who sets the risk tolerance for a project?
o: The business layer, as part of the project mandate it provides
The project manager, when writing the risk management approach
Project assurance, after it has reviewed the risk register
The project board, based on the business's overall risk appetite
11.w: Risk tolerance is set by the project board, based on the overall risk appetite determined by the business (see manual 9.2.1).

n.0: The business layer determines the risk appetite; the project board applies it by setting the project's risk tolerance (manual 9.2.1).
n.1: The project manager drafts the approach, which records the tolerance, but the tolerance itself is set by the project board (manual 9.2.1).
n.2: Project assurance reviews risk management on behalf of the board; it does not set the tolerance (manual 6.2.4.7, 9.2.1).

11.q: Which part of the quality management technique involves carrying out the quality methods and recording the results?
o: Quality planning
Project acceptance
Quality control
Quality assurance
11.w: In quality control the planned quality methods are carried out and the results are recorded in the quality register (see manual 8.3.1.2).

n.0: Quality planning defines the specifications, product descriptions and the quality management approach before any methods are carried out (manual 8.3.1.1).
n.1: Project acceptance follows the quality checks and transfers ownership of the project product (manual 8.3.1.3).
n.3: Quality assurance is an independent check that quality control measures are appropriate; it is not one of the three parts of the technique and does not carry out the methods (manual 8.2.3).

11.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
One objective of directing a project is to ensure that the [?] has an effective connection to the project.
o: project support function
business layer
team manager
quality assurance function
11.w: Directing a project aims to give the business layer an effective connection to the project, with the board communicating with it on the business's behalf (see manual 14.2, 14.3).

n.0: Project support works for the project manager inside the project; its connection is not an objective of directing a project (manual 14.2, 6.2).
n.2: Team managers take their direction from the project manager, not from the board, so linking them to the board is not a directing objective (manual 14.3, 17.1).
n.3: Quality assurance is an independent business function outside the project management team; the directing objective concerns the business layer as a whole (manual 14.2, 8.1).

11.q: Why is the delivery method one of the factors that influence how PRINCE2 is tailored?
o: Because quality activities need to suit how the products are delivered
Because PRINCE2 prescribes one delivery method for each type of project
Because the delivery method decides which principles the project applies
Because the delivery method replaces the need for a plan for each stage
11.w: How the products are delivered affects which controls and activities fit; for example, the quality practice tailors by requiring the quality activities that are appropriate to the delivery approach and product characteristics (see manual 2.7 and 8.7 tab 8.3).

n.1: PRINCE2 is not specific to any delivery method; it is tailored to whichever method the project uses (manual 1.1).
n.2: All seven principles apply whatever the delivery method; the delivery method affects how the method is tailored, not which principles apply (manual ch 2).
n.3: Manage by stages still applies whatever the delivery method, with a stage plan for each stage (manual 2.4).

11.q: In the risk practice, what is optimism bias?
o: A mindset that values avoiding a loss more highly than making an equivalent gain
A mindset that values the cohesion of a group more than voicing a different view
A mindset in which situations closer in time are seen as riskier and more important
A mindset that discounts disadvantageous risk, assuming that things are likely to succeed
11.w: Optimism bias leads people to discount risks that could harm them, on the assumption that things will be successful for them (see manual 9.2.4).

n.0: This describes loss aversion (manual 9.2.4).
n.1: This describes groupthink (manual 9.2.4).
n.2: This describes proximity bias, not optimism bias (manual 9.2.4).

11.q: PRINCE2 says projects should be output-oriented rather than work-oriented. What is the main advantage of this?
o: Team managers can start building before the products have been described
Activities can be planned without needing to involve the users
Waste is avoided, as no more work is done than the agreed products need
Progress can be measured by hours worked rather than by products delivered
11.w: A product focus makes projects more efficient and avoids waste: the project does no more work than needed to deliver its agreed products, which also helps control scope creep (manual 2.6).

n.0: Products are defined and agreed before the work is done, not after building has started (manual 2.6).
n.1: Products are defined around user quality expectations, so users are involved rather than left out (manual 2.6).
n.3: Measuring hours worked is a work-oriented view; PRINCE2 tracks the delivery of products (manual 2.6).

11.q: A project manager has a product breakdown structure for a new visitor centre and now needs to allocate responsibility for the work to teams. What should the work breakdown structure enable?
o: Approval of each product against its quality specifications before handover to the users
Measurement of the benefits once the visitor centre has opened to members of the public
Grouping of all the required work into work packages that can be allocated to teams
Selection of the executive and senior user who represent the interests on the board
11.w: The WBS sets out all the work needed to deliver the products and links it to work packages, so that responsibility can be allocated to teams with clear boundaries (see manual 6.2.5).

n.0: Checking products against quality specifications is quality control under the quality practice (manual 8.2).
n.1: Measuring benefits after the project is covered by the benefits management approach in the business case practice (manual 5.5).
n.3: The executive is appointed by the business layer and the rest of the board by the executive in starting up; the WBS is not used for this (manual 13.4.1, 13.4.4).

11.q: After reviewing an exception report, the project board asks for an exception plan. In which process does the project manager prepare the exception plan?
o: Managing a stage boundary
Controlling a stage
Directing a project
Managing product delivery
11.w: The project manager prepares the exception plan in managing a stage boundary ('prepare exception plan'), and the board then approves it in directing a project (see manual 11.3.1, 18).

n.1: Controlling a stage is where the exception report is raised, not where the exception plan is prepared (manual 11.3.1, 16.4.7).
n.2: Directing a project is where the board decides on the exception and later approves the exception plan (manual 11.3.1).
n.3: Managing product delivery is the team manager's process for executing work packages (manual 17).

11.q: Why does a project manager need to provide leadership as well as management?
o: Management directs tasks to agreed ways of working, but leading is needed to motivate and influence people
Leadership takes over from management once the team has agreed its ways of working
Management is used for people inside the project, while leadership is kept for stakeholders outside it
Combining the two allows the project manager to carry out project assurance for the board
11.w: Management instructs tasks within agreed ways of working, but on a temporary project the project manager often lacks formal authority, so leadership (motivating, persuading, influencing, co-creating) is also needed (see manual 3.3).

n.1: Leadership does not replace management at any point; both are needed throughout the project (manual 3.3).
n.2: Leadership applies to the team as well: it includes motivating team members and seeking their feedback to keep them aligned (manual 3.3).
n.3: The project manager can never carry out project assurance, which must be independent of the project manager (manual 6.2.4).

12.q:
Which two statements about the types of issue in PRINCE2 7 are correct?
1. A concern is an issue whose timing and impact still need to be assessed.
2. A request for change is a product that will not meet its quality specifications.
3. A business opportunity is an uncertain event that could have a positive effect on objectives.
4. An event external to the project that may affect it is one of the types of issue.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
12.w: Statement 1 correctly defines a concern. Statement 4 is correct: an event external to the project that may affect it is one of the types of issue the QRG lists, alongside problem, concern, business opportunity, request for change and off-specification (see manual 10.1).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: a product that will not meet its quality specifications is an off-specification; a request for change proposes a change to a baseline (manual 10.2.3).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: statement 2 describes an off-specification, and statement 3 describes a risk (an opportunity) because it is uncertain (manual 9.1, 10.2.3).
n.2: Statement 3 is wrong: an uncertain positive event is an opportunity in the risk practice; a business opportunity is an issue that has already arisen (manual 9.1, 10.1).

12.q: How is a programme BEST described in relation to the projects within it?
o: A temporary structure that leads several related projects and other work to achieve outcomes
A permanent function that runs all of an organization's routine operations and services
A single project large enough to need more than two management stages
The supplier's own management system for delivering contracted products
12.w: A programme is a temporary structure that leads multiple interrelated projects and other work to progressively achieve outcomes and benefits; a PRINCE2 project may sit within one (see manual 1.5, figure 1.2, and the glossary).

n.1: Running routine operations is business as usual, which is permanent; a programme is temporary and exists to achieve change.
n.2: A project with many stages is still one project; a programme coordinates several related projects.
n.3: A supplier's management system is part of a commercial context, not a programme.

12.q: Which statement about the exception management technique is correct?
o: Tolerances are delegated down through the levels, and forecast breaches go one level up
Each level sets its own tolerances, and forecast breaches go to the business layer
Tolerances are set by the team manager, and forecast breaches go to the project board
The board sets tolerances for every level, and forecast breaches go to project assurance
12.w: PRINCE2 delegates tolerances down through the four management levels (11.2.1); in the exception management technique, a level that forecasts a breach of its tolerances escalates to the level above, which set them (see manual 11.2.1, 11.3.1).

n.1: Tolerances are set by the level above, and a breach goes to the next level up, which may or may not be the business layer (manual 11.3.1).
n.2: Team managers work within tolerances set by the project manager and escalate to the project manager (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: The board sets stage tolerances only, and breaches go to the management level that set the tolerance, not to assurance (manual 11.2.1, 11.3.1).

12.q: Why does the business case practice judge whether a project 'remains' desirable, viable and achievable, rather than checking this once before the project starts?
o: Because the business case is replaced by the project plan once the project board authorizes the project
Because costs, risks, benefits and circumstances change, so a project that was justified may stop being so
Because the business layer must reissue the project mandate at the start of every delivery stage
Because the senior user must specify new benefits at the start of every work package
12.w: Justification established at the start can change as costs, timescales, risks and the business environment change, so it is kept under review and the project should be stopped if it is no longer justified (see manual 5.1, 2.1).

n.0: The business case is not replaced; it is maintained and checked at each stage boundary throughout the project (manual 5.3.1).
n.2: The mandate triggers starting up a project; it is not reissued at each stage. The board reviews justification at stage boundaries (manual 13.3, 5.3.1).
n.3: Benefits are specified for the project, not per work package; work package descriptions carry scope, cost and time tolerances (manual 11.2.1).

12.q: Which statement describes the project board's relationship with the business layer during directing a project?
o: The board passes accountability to the business layer once initiation is authorized
The board approves the project mandate on behalf of the business layer
The board stays accountable to the business layer and acts as its link to the project
The board receives checkpoint reports and forwards them to the business layer
12.w: The project board is accountable to the business for the project's success and, in directing a project, communicates with the business layer so that the business has an effective connection to the project (see manual 14.2, 14.3, 6.2.1).

n.0: The board remains accountable for the project's success throughout; accountability does not move back to the business layer after initiation (manual 14.1, 6.2.1).
n.1: The project mandate comes from the business layer itself and triggers starting up, before the board exists (manual 13.3).
n.3: Checkpoint reports go from team managers to the project manager; the board receives highlight reports (manual 17.1, 11.5).

12.q: In the risk practice, what is risk appetite?
o: A measurable threshold for the tolerable range of outcomes of each objective at risk
A sum of money set aside to fund specific responses to threats and opportunities
The amount and type of risk the business is willing to take in pursuit of its objectives
The degree to which a particular objective is at risk from the project's risks
12.w: Risk appetite is the business's attitude to risk taking: the amount and type of risk it will accept in pursuit of its objectives (see manual 9.2).

n.0: This is risk tolerance, which the project board sets based on the business's appetite (manual 9.2, 9.2.1).
n.1: This is the risk budget, which funds responses such as contingent plans (manual 9.2).
n.3: This is risk exposure, a neutral measure of how far an objective is at risk (manual 9.2).

12.q:
Which two statements about projects are true according to PRINCE2?
1. A project team is a permanent part of the organization's line structure.
2. A project continues after its change is implemented so that it can run the new service.
3. A project is created to deliver one or more business products.
4. A project is undertaken according to an agreed business case.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
12.w: Statements 3 and 4 restate the PRINCE2 definition: a temporary organization created to deliver one or more business products according to an agreed business case (see manual 1.3).

n.0: Statement 1 is false because the project organization is temporary, and statement 2 is false because the need for the project ends once its change is implemented.
n.1: Statement 3 is true, but statement 1 is false: the project team is temporary and is disbanded when the project closes.
n.2: Statement 4 is true, but statement 2 is false: running the new service is business as usual, which resumes once the change is in place.

12.q:
Identify the missing word(s) in the following sentence.
When the project board decides to address an exception, the [?] is prepared and, once approved, replaces the plan it covers from the current position to the end of that stage or project.
o: exception plan
next stage plan
team plan
project plan
12.w: An exception plan follows an exception report. If the board decides to address the exception, it is prepared and, once approved, replaces the stage or project plan from the current position (see manual 7.2.2.4).

n.1: A next stage plan is prepared near the end of the current stage for the following stage; it does not replace a plan after an exception (manual 7.2.2.2).
n.2: A team plan covers a team's work on work packages and is never used to replace a stage or project plan (manual 7.2.2.3).
n.3: The project plan is updated at stage boundaries; the plan prepared in response to an exception is the exception plan (manual 7.2.2.1, 7.2.2.4).

12.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.

Once the project manager has prepared an exception plan for a stage, the project board approves it in the [?] process.
o: managing a stage boundary
controlling a stage
directing a project
closing a project
12.w: The board approves exception plans in directing a project, through the 'authorize a stage or exception plan' activity (see manual 11.3.1, 14).

n.0: Managing a stage boundary is where the project manager prepares the exception plan, not where the board approves it (manual 11.3.1).
n.1: Controlling a stage is where the exception report is raised (manual 11.3.1).
n.3: Closing a project is for planned or premature closure, not for approving exception plans (manual 19).

12.q: How does PRINCE2 7 define culture?
o: The agreed procedures and standards set out in the management approaches
The set of shared attitudes, values, goals and practices of a group
The ability to relate to and work across different cultures in the ecosystem
Instructing the execution of tasks in line with agreed ways of working
12.w: PRINCE2 7 defines culture as the set of shared attitudes, values, goals and practices (see manual 3.2.3).

n.0: Procedures and standards in the management approaches are the project's defined ways of working; culture is how people actually think and behave (manual 3.2.3).
n.2: The ability to relate and work across cultures is cultural intelligence, a leadership capability, not culture itself (manual 3.3.1).
n.3: Instructing the execution of tasks in line with agreed ways of working is the PRINCE2 definition of management (manual 3.3).

12.q: While starting up a project, the project manager identifies several key risks. The risk register has not yet been created. Where should these risks be recorded?
o: In the daily log
In the lessons log
In the risk management approach
In the issue register
12.w: Starting up a project sets up the daily log, and the initial key risks are recorded there until the risk register is created during initiation (see manual 13, tab 13.3).

n.1: The lessons log holds lessons from previous and current projects, not the project's own risks (manual 13.4.2).
n.2: The risk management approach describes procedures, scales and responsibilities; it holds no specific risks and is not agreed until initiation (manual 15.4.2, 9.5).
n.3: The issue register is set up in initiating a project and records formal issues, not risks (manual 15, tab 15.3).

12.q: Which statement describes co-creation as PRINCE2 defines it?
o: A modification to any of the approved management products that make up the project baseline
Collaboration that involves users and key influencers in designing products and ways of working
The transfer of ownership of the completed products from the supplier to the user community
A quality review in which products are checked against their quality criteria before approval
12.w: Co-creation is a specific form of collaboration in which users and key influencers help design products and agreed ways of working, so that they are adopted (see manual 3.3).

n.0: A modification to an approved baselined management product is a change, handled through the issues practice (manual 10.1).
n.2: Transferring ownership of the project product to the users is project acceptance and handover, not co-creation (manual 8.3.1.3).
n.3: Checking products against quality criteria is quality control, for example a quality review (manual 8.2.2).

12.q: Which is NOT done by the project as part of managing benefits through the benefits management approach?
o: Planning when the post-project benefits reviews will happen
Carrying out the post-project benefits reviews
Defining how and when the benefits will be measured
Updating the approach with results of benefits actions at a stage end
12.w: The project plans post-project benefits reviews but does not carry them out: they take place after closure and are undertaken by the business (see manual 5.5, ch 19).

n.0: The project does this: the approach is updated in closing a project to include the post-project benefits reviews (manual ch 19).
n.2: The project does this: the benefits management approach sets out benefits measurement and timing (manual 5.5).
n.3: The project does this: in managing a stage boundary the approach is updated with the results of benefits actions (manual ch 18).

12.q: A government agency must update its licensing system to comply with new legislation by a fixed date. How does the 'ensure continued business justification' principle apply to this project?
o: It does not apply, because a compulsory project has no choice about proceeding
It applies at closure, when benefits are compared with costs to inform future work
It is replaced by the legal requirement recorded in the project mandate
It still applies, because the option chosen to meet the law must be justified
12.w: Even compulsory projects need business justification: the organization must still justify the option it chooses to meet the requirement, for example the one giving best value (manual 2.1, 5.2.3).

n.0: Compulsory projects are not exempt: the principle still requires justification of the chosen option (manual 2.1).
n.1: Justification must remain valid throughout the project, not just be considered at closure (manual 2.1).
n.2: A legal requirement explains why something must be done, but it does not replace the need to justify the option chosen (manual 2.1).

12.q: A project manager is designing the quality register. Which heading would you expect it to include?
o: Derivation, showing the source products from which an item is built
Result, showing whether the check passed or failed and any follow-up
Composition, listing the parts that together make up the product
References, naming the business's quality management system
12.w: The quality register records, for each quality activity, the quality method, planned and actual dates, who was responsible and the result, including the response to any failure (see manual 8.5).

n.0: Derivation is a heading of a product description, describing where the product comes from (manual 8.5).
n.2: Composition is a heading of a product description, describing what the product is made of (manual 8.5).
n.3: References, such as the business's quality management system, are a heading of the quality management approach (manual 8.5).

12.q: A project manager uses the work breakdown structure to agree which elements of the work an external supplier will deliver. In which management product should this delivery model be described?
o: Commercial management approach
Communication management approach
Quality management approach
Benefits management approach
12.w: The commercial management approach includes the delivery model, which identifies which elements of the WBS will be delivered by external suppliers (see manual 6.5, 6.3.2.1).

n.1: The communication management approach sets out how and when the project communicates with stakeholders, not which work suppliers deliver (manual 3.4).
n.2: The quality management approach describes how quality will be managed, not the commercial delivery model (manual 8.5).
n.3: The benefits management approach covers how benefits will be measured and reviewed, not which suppliers deliver the work (manual 5.5).

12.q: In which process is the activity 'assess previous lessons' carried out, so that the project applies learn from experience before it is initiated?
o: Initiating a project
Starting up a project
Directing a project
Managing a stage boundary
12.w: 'Assess previous lessons' is an activity in starting up a project: the lessons log is created and people with experience of similar projects are consulted (manual 13.4.2).

n.0: Initiating a project follows starting up; lessons are first assessed earlier, in starting up a project (manual 13.4.2).
n.2: Directing a project covers the board's decisions; the lessons activity named here belongs to starting up a project (manual ch 14, 13.4.2).
n.3: Lessons are recorded at stage boundaries, but 'assess previous lessons' is a starting up activity (manual 13.4.2, ch 18).

12.q: How does PRINCE2 7 link the 'focus on products' principle with the people element?
o: Co-creating products with users and suppliers improves their adoption
Products are designed by the supplier to keep ownership clear
User involvement ends once the project product description is agreed
Team members are assigned by product rather than by skills or capacity
12.w: Co-creating products, using agreed product descriptions, with the business, user and supplier communities unites perspectives, improves development and adoption and reduces handover risks (manual 3.5.1).

n.1: PRINCE2 7 encourages co-creation across business, user and supplier communities rather than leaving design to the supplier (manual 3.5.1).
n.2: Users stay involved, for example in co-creating and accepting products, not just in agreeing the project product description (manual 3.5.1).
n.3: The principle's people link is co-creation and adoption, not a way of assigning team members (manual 3.5.1).

12.q: A project manager reviews the lessons logs of similar past projects to find threats that affected them. Which principle does this apply to the risk practice?
o: Manage by stages
Ensure continued business justification
Focus on products
Learn from experience
12.w: Seeking lessons from previous projects, here about the threats they met, applies the learn from experience principle to identifying risks (see manual 2.2, 9.7).

n.0: Manage by stages concerns planning and authorizing the project a stage at a time, not drawing on past projects (manual 2.4).
n.1: This principle concerns keeping the project desirable, viable and achievable, not using lessons from earlier projects (manual 2.1).
n.2: Focus on products concerns defining and delivering products that meet quality requirements (manual 2.6).

12.q: In PRINCE2's description of the organizational context, which party ensures that the project investment can be justified and remains justified throughout the lifecycle?
o: Users
Suppliers
Business decision-makers
Specialist team members
12.w: PRINCE2 describes users who specify the desired outputs, suppliers who provide resources and expertise, and business decision-makers who ensure the investment is justified and stays justified (see manual 1.5).

n.0: Users specify the desired outputs (products) and will use them; they do not hold the responsibility for keeping the investment justified.
n.1: Suppliers provide the resources and expertise to deliver the products.
n.3: Specialist team members build the products within work packages; they do not decide whether the investment is justified.

12.q: Where does the 'closing a project' process sit in the project lifecycle?
o: As a closure stage after the final delivery stage
As the last part of the final stage
After the board has disbanded, run by the business
At each stage end, alongside managing a stage boundary
12.w: Closing a project is carried out within the final stage, as its last part. It is never planned as a separate management stage (see manual 12, 19.3).

n.0: Closure is not a stage of its own; planning it as a separate stage is a classic error (manual 12, 19.3).
n.2: The project manager prepares closure and the board authorizes it in directing a project, so the board is still in place (manual 19.3, 14.4.5).
n.3: Closing a project is used once, at the end of the project; stage ends use managing a stage boundary (manual 12).

12.q: What happens to the project initiation documentation in the 'managing a stage boundary' process?
o: It is replaced by the end stage report as the board's reference
It is created for the first time to support the next stage request
It is closed and archived together with the project log
It is reviewed and, where needed, updated for the next stage
12.w: One objective of managing a stage boundary is to review and, if necessary, update the PID, in particular the business case, project plan, management approaches, team structure and role descriptions (see manual 18.2).

n.0: The end stage report reviews the stage; the PID remains the reference and is updated where needed (manual 18.2).
n.1: The PID is assembled in initiating a project, before the first delivery stage (manual 15.4.6).
n.2: Project information is archived in closing a project, not at a stage boundary (manual 19.4.1).

12.q:
Which two statements about building effective teams are correct?
1. Some motivational factors, such as pay and career progression, may be outside the project manager's remit.
2. Roles are fixed at initiation and are not revisited during the project.
3. Structured team-building exercises can speed up the forming of a team.
4. Competency gaps are accepted as the team is temporary.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
12.w: Statement 1 is correct: pay and career progression are examples of motivators outside the project manager's remit (manual 3.3). Statement 3 is correct: structured exercises can accelerate team building (manual 3.3.2).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: roles should be reviewed and updated when key relationships shift (manual 3.3.2).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: roles are reviewed when relationships shift, and competency gaps should be identified and mitigated (manual 3.3.2).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: gaps should be identified and mitigated, for example by upskilling or shifting responsibilities (manual 3.3.2).

12.q: Which statement about tailoring and the PRINCE2 principles is correct?
o: It lets the project board select the principles that suit the project
It is a practice, applied through the management approaches
It applies to the principles but not to processes or practices
It adapts the method, while all seven principles still apply
12.w: Tailoring is itself one of the seven principles. It adapts the processes, practices, roles, management products and terminology, but the principles are not tailored: all seven must still be applied (see manual ch 2 and 2.7).

n.0: The board cannot select principles: if any principle is not applied, the project is not a PRINCE2 project (manual ch 2).
n.1: Tailoring is one of the seven principles, not a practice; it is the practices that are tailored through the management approaches (manual 2.7).
n.2: This is the reverse of the rule: processes and practices can be tailored, but the principles cannot (manual 2.7).

12.q: Which issues are typically managed formally, with an issue register entry and, where needed, an issue report?
o: Notes, actions and observations from the project manager's day-to-day work on the stage
Requests for change, off-specifications and problems or concerns needing formal review
Lessons the team wants recorded so that they can be passed on to future projects
Uncertain events that could affect the project's objectives later in the stage
12.w: Issue reports are used for requests for change, off-specifications, business opportunities and problems or concerns that need formal review; these issues are managed formally through the issue register (see manual 10.5).

n.0: Day-to-day notes, actions and observations belong in the daily log, the project manager's informal diary (manual 11.5).
n.2: Lessons are captured in the lessons log and reported in a lessons report, not managed as formal issues (manual 11.5).
n.3: Uncertain future events are risks, recorded in the risk register and managed through the risk practice (manual 9.1, 9.5).

12.q: Why is change management important to a PRINCE2 project?
o: Because it replaces the business case once the target state has been agreed
Because a project exists to deliver change that alters people's routines and responsibilities
Because it sets the tolerances that the project board delegates to the project manager
Because it controls which versions of products form the current project baseline
12.w: The purpose of a project is to deliver change, which affects people's business-as-usual activities, routines and responsibilities; how well that change lands drives how well the project performs (see manual ch 3 introduction, 3.2.1).

n.0: The business case remains in place throughout the project; the principle of continued business justification still applies (manual 2.1, ch 5).
n.2: Tolerances are set through the progress practice (manage by exception), not by change management (manual 11.2.1).
n.3: Controlling which product versions form the baseline is change control under the issues practice (manual 10.2.1).

12.q:
Which two statements are reasons why organizations use project management?
1. To keep a project team in place permanently after its change is implemented.
2. To remove the need for business as usual management.
3. To introduce change in a controlled way.
4. To check that an investment remains justified as the work progresses.
o: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
12.w: Project management lets an organization introduce change in a controlled way and keep checking that the investment is still worthwhile (see manual 1.3 and the ensure continued business justification principle, 2.1).

n.0: Both are false: a project team is temporary, and business as usual resumes in its new form once the change is in place.
n.1: Statement 3 is true, but statement 1 is false because the project organization is disbanded once the change is implemented.
n.2: Statement 4 is true, but statement 2 is false: projects change business as usual, which continues alongside and after them.

12.q: What does the 'prepare contingent plans' response involve?
o: Taking definite action now to change the probability or impact of the risk
Planning actions now that will be carried out if the risk occurs
Passing part of the financial impact of the risk to a third party
Taking the chance and monitoring the risk with no further plans made
12.w: Preparing contingent plans means deciding now what to do, and putting it in place to be used if the risk occurs; it is often funded from the risk budget (see manual 9.2, 9.2.3.1).

n.0: This describes reduce (for a threat) or enhance (for an opportunity) (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.2: This describes transfer, for example through insurance or a contract (manual 9.2.3.1).
n.3: This describes accept; a contingent plan is a prepared set of actions (manual 9.2.3.1).

12.q: How does PRINCE2 7 define change management?
o: The procedure for assessing and approving changes to the project baseline
The process of moving a project from one management stage to the next
The means by which an organization moves from its current state to its target state
The technique for capturing, assessing and deciding on issues raised in the project
12.w: In PRINCE2 7, change management is the means by which an organization transitions from the current state to the target state (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: Assessing and approving changes to the baseline is change control, which belongs to the issues practice (manual 10.1, 10.2.3).
n.1: Moving from one stage to the next is handled by managing a stage boundary and directing a project, not by change management (manual ch 14, ch 18).
n.3: Capturing, assessing and deciding on issues is the issue management technique of the issues practice (manual 10.3.1).

12.q: A team member mentions an informal concern to the project manager in conversation. Later the same day, a formal risk is identified that needs to be tracked. Where should each be recorded?
o: Both in the PID: the concern in the daily log and the risk in the risk management approach
Both in the project log: the concern in the issue register and the risk in the risk management approach
Both in the project log: the concern in the daily log and the risk in the risk register
Both in the business case: the concern in the lessons log and the risk under the major risks heading
12.w: Informal concerns can be noted in the daily log, while formal risks are recorded in the risk register. Both records sit in the project log (see manual 4.3.2; issues and risk practices).

n.0: The PID does not hold the daily log, and the risk management approach holds procedures and scales, not specific risks; both belong in the project log (manual 4.3.2, ch 9).
n.1: An informal concern can be handled in the daily log, and specific risks go in the risk register; the risk management approach is part of the PID (manual 4.3.2, ch 9).
n.3: The business case summarizes the major risks for justification; individual risks and concerns are recorded in the project log, and the lessons log is for lessons (manual 4.3.2, 5.5).

12.q:
Which two statements about the management products that support the issues practice are correct?
1. The issue register captures and maintains information on issues being managed formally.
2. An issue report is prepared for every entry that the project manager makes in the daily log.
3. The issue management approach lists the specific issues that have been raised so far.
4. The issue register records an issue owner for each issue it holds.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
3 and 4
1 and 4
12.w: Statement 1 is correct: the issue register captures and maintains formal issues. Statement 4 is correct: each issue on the register has an issue owner, who manages that issue while the project manager runs the procedure (see manual 10.5, 10.6).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: issue reports are for issues needing formal review, not for informal notes in the daily log (manual 10.5).
n.1: Both statements are wrong: daily log entries do not each need an issue report, and the approach describes procedures rather than listing specific issues (manual 10.5).
n.2: Statement 3 is wrong: the issue management approach describes how issues and changes are handled; specific issues go in the issue register (manual 10.5).

12.q: A team reports that a key supplier might go out of business before delivery, and also that a test server has failed. How should these be treated?
o: The possible supplier failure is a risk; the server failure, which has happened, is an issue
Both are risks, because each of them would affect the achievement of the project's objectives
Both are issues, because each of them is an event that needs project management consideration
The server failure is a risk, because its full effect on the stage is not yet known
12.w: A risk is an uncertain event that may occur; something that has already happened is an issue and is handled by the issues practice (see manual 9.1, 10.1).

n.1: The server failure has already happened, so it is not uncertain; it is an issue, even though it affects objectives (manual 10.1).
n.2: The supplier failure has not happened and may not happen, so it is an uncertain event: a risk (manual 9.1).
n.3: Uncertainty about the size of the effect does not make an event that has already occurred into a risk; it is an issue to be assessed (manual 10.1).

12.q: In the four-level structure, which level sets the tolerances for each stage, working within the project-level tolerances it has been given?
o: Directing (project board)
Business layer (commissioning)
Managing (project manager)
Delivering (team managers)
12.w: The project board, at the directing level, sets stage tolerances within the project tolerances defined by the business layer (see manual 6.2.4, 11.2).

n.1: The business layer defines project-level tolerances, not the tolerances for each stage (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: The project manager sets work package tolerances for team managers, not stage tolerances (manual 6.2.4).
n.3: Team managers set tolerances for their team members, not for stages (manual 6.2.4).

12.q: Why does PRINCE2 combine a high-level project plan with a detailed stage plan for the current stage?
