o: Because the project plan is fixed at initiation and cannot be updated during the project
Because the board approves stage plans while the business layer approves the project plan
Because team managers prepare the stage plans and the project manager prepares the project plan
Because only the near future can be planned in detail, so detail is added one stage at a time
12.w: The planning horizon limits how far ahead detailed planning is possible. PRINCE2 therefore uses a high-level project plan for the whole project and a detailed stage plan for the current stage (see manual 7.2.1, 7.2.2).

n.0: The project plan is updated at each stage boundary and at closure, so it is not fixed (manual 7.2.2.1).
n.1: The project board approves the project plan when it authorizes the project; the reason for two levels is the planning horizon (manual 7.2.2.1, 7.2.1).
n.2: The project manager prepares both the project plan and stage plans; team managers prepare team plans and work package schedules (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

12.q: Which statement describes a product breakdown structure?
o: A diagram of the order in which the products will be developed
A hierarchy of the activities and tasks needed to deliver a plan
A hierarchy of all the products to be produced during a plan
A list of all the products of a plan and their current status
12.w: A product breakdown structure is a hierarchy of all the products to be produced during a plan, breaking major products into their components (see manual 7.3.1.1).

n.0: The order of development and the dependencies are shown in the product flow diagram (manual 7.3.1.1).
n.1: A product breakdown structure lists products, not activities; activities are grouped into work packages later (manual 7.3.1.1, 7.3.1.2).
n.3: A list of products with their status is the product register in the project log (manual 4.3.2).

12.q: Which statement best explains why PRINCE2 places people at the centre of the method?
o: People can take the place of the practices on small and simple projects
The people element is applied once, in initiating a project, when the team is formed
The people element is the responsibility of the senior user, who represents the users
Performance depends on the team's capabilities, its relationships and the people affected
12.w: Projects deliver change that affects people, and how well a project performs depends on the capabilities of the team, the strength of their relationships and the people impacted by the change (see manual ch 3).

n.0: The people element integrates with the principles, practices and processes; it does not replace any of them (manual 3.5).
n.1: People factors are addressed continually throughout the project lifecycle, not just once (manual 3.5.1).
n.2: People duties are spread across roles: the board, project manager and team managers all have people responsibilities (manual 6.2.4).

12.q: In 'evaluate the project', what does the project manager compare the project's performance against?
o: The project mandate issued by the business layer
The outline business case approved at initiation
The most recent highlight report sent to the board
The baselined PID and its current approved version
12.w: Evaluate the project compares what was achieved with the original baselined PID and its current approved version, and analyses estimates against actuals to improve future estimating (see manual 19.4.4).

n.0: The mandate triggers starting up a project; performance is measured against the baselined PID (manual 19.4.4).
n.1: The outline business case was developed into the full business case in the PID, which is the baseline used (manual 15.4.5, 19.4.4).
n.2: A highlight report shows stage status at one point; it is not the baseline for evaluating the project (manual 16.4.8).

12.q: A charity's board asks what the quality practice will mainly be concerned with on its new fundraising database project. Which answer is correct?
o: Whether the project's activities are carried out in the sequence shown in the stage plan
Whether the project continues to be desirable, viable and achievable at each stage
Whether the project's products are fit for purpose and meet what the users require
Whether each management level in the project has clearly defined accountabilities
12.w: The quality practice is concerned with products being fit for purpose: it documents what users require of the products and how those requirements will be met (see manual 8.1).

n.0: The sequence of activities is a plans and progress concern, set out in the schedule and monitored against the stage plan (manual ch 7, ch 11).
n.1: Continuing desirability, viability and achievability is the concern of the business case practice (manual 5.1).
n.3: Defining accountabilities at each management level is the concern of the organizing practice (manual 6.1).

12.q: How does the 'manage by stages' principle support the 'manage by exception' principle?
o: Stage boundaries are when tolerances are first forecast to be exceeded
Each stage has its own exception report prepared by the team manager
The board sets project tolerances at the start of each delivery stage
The board delegates authority to the project manager one stage at a time
12.w: Manage by stages makes manage by exception workable: the board delegates authority one stage at a time, and while the stage is forecast to stay within tolerance the project manager can adjust as needed (manual 2.4).

n.0: A breach can be forecast at any time during a stage, not just at a boundary (manual 2.5, ch 11).
n.1: Exception reports are raised by the project manager when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, not by team managers each stage (manual ch 11).
n.2: Project tolerances are set by the business layer; the board sets stage tolerances (manual 11.2.1).

12.q: A project uses an external supplier whose teams follow their own delivery method. How does 'managing product delivery' still give the project manager control?
o: The supplier's teams adopt PRINCE2 before they accept any work package
The project board reads the supplier's reports and directs its team manager
Work is passed and returned through agreed work packages with checkpoint reporting
The senior supplier authorizes each work package instead of the project manager
12.w: Managing product delivery controls the link between project manager and team manager: work is agreed in work packages, progress comes back in checkpoint reports and completion is notified, so the supplier's own method does not matter (see manual 17.1, 17.3).

n.0: Suppliers do not need to use PRINCE2; the work package provides the interface (manual 17.3).
n.1: The board is not involved in managing product delivery; the team manager reports to the project manager (manual 17.3).
n.3: The project manager authorizes work packages in controlling a stage; the senior supplier does not take over that activity (manual 16.4.1).

12.q: What is the purpose of a product description?
o: To summarize all of the quality activities planned or carried out on the project
To list all of the products required by a plan, together with their current status
To describe a product's purpose, composition, derivation, format and quality specifications
To describe the quality techniques, standards and responsibilities for the whole project
12.w: A product description describes a product's purpose, composition, derivation and format, together with its quality specifications, quality method and quality responsibilities (see manual 8.5).

n.0: Summarizing all planned and completed quality activities is the purpose of the quality register (manual 8.5).
n.1: Listing all products of a plan and their status is the purpose of the product register (manual 8.5).
n.3: The quality techniques, standards and responsibilities for the project are described in the quality management approach (manual 8.5).

12.q:
Identify the missing words in the following sentence.
On a small, low-value project, the project brief and the [?] may be merged into one simple document.
o: project plan
lessons report
stage plan
business case
12.w: Small, low-value projects may merge the project brief and the business case into one simple business case document (see manual 5.4.5).

n.0: The project plan is created in initiating a project, after the project brief; the recognized small-project merger is brief and business case (manual 5.4.5, 15.4.4).
n.1: The lessons report passes on lessons at a stage or project end; it is not combined with the project brief (manual 19.4.4).
n.2: Stage plans are produced for each stage, the first in starting up and later ones in managing a stage boundary; they are not merged with the brief (manual 2.4, ch 18).

12.q:
Which two statements about the 'manage by exception' principle are correct?
1. An exception exists when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.
2. The project manager sets the tolerances for each stage.
3. It uses senior management time efficiently without removing their control.
4. Escalation waits until a tolerance has actually been exceeded.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
12.w: Statement 1 is correct: an exception is a forecast breach of tolerance. Statement 3 is correct: the principle reduces the burden on senior managers while keeping them in control (manual 2.5, ch 11).

n.0: Statement 2 is wrong: stage tolerances are set by the project board; the project manager sets work package tolerances (manual 11.2.1).
n.1: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: the board sets stage tolerances, and escalation happens on a forecast breach (manual 2.5, 11.2.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the next level should be alerted as early as possible, when a breach is forecast (manual 2.5).

12.q: Which statement about project assurance in a PRINCE2 project is correct?
o: It can be assigned to project support, because support already maintains the project's registers
It is the project manager's responsibility, and the project manager can delegate it to a project office
It can be carried out by board members, by people from the wider business or by an external party
It is another name for quality assurance, which the business manages from outside the project
12.w: Depending on who has the knowledge, skills and capacity, assurance tasks can be done by the board member themselves, by someone appointed from the wider business, or by an external party (see manual 6.2.4.7).

n.0: Project assurance cannot be assigned to project support; the two are kept separate to protect the independence of assurance (manual 6.2.4.7).
n.1: Project assurance is the board's responsibility and cannot be assigned to the project manager; it is project support that the project manager is responsible for (manual 6.2.4.7, 6.2.4.8).
n.3: Project assurance is a board responsibility within the project, whereas quality assurance is independent of the project management team; they are different (manual 8.2.3, 6.2.4.7).

12.q:
Identify the missing word in the following sentence.

Acceptance of the project product typically transfers [?] from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the user.
o: ownership
tolerance
funding
assurance
12.w: Project acceptance typically transfers ownership or responsibility for the project product from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the user (see manual 8.3.1.3).

n.1: Tolerance is delegated downwards from the board to the project manager and team managers; it is not what acceptance transfers (manual ch 11).
n.2: Funding is secured by the executive; acceptance concerns the product, not the money (manual ch 6).
n.3: Assurance is the board's responsibility throughout the project; acceptance does not transfer it (manual 8.2.3).

12.q: At the end of the authorize the project activity, what does the project board issue?
o: An initiation notice
A project authorization notice
A closure notification
A request for project authorization
12.w: Authorize the project ends with a project authorization notice, confirming that the project may proceed to its delivery stages (see manual 14.4.2).

n.0: The initiation notice is issued earlier, in authorize initiation, and triggers initiating a project (manual 14.4.1).
n.2: A closure notification is sent to the business layer in authorize project closure (manual 14.4.5).
n.3: The request for project authorization is sent by the project manager at the end of initiating a project; it is the input to authorize the project, not its output (manual 15.4.7).

12.q:
Which two statements about escalation in PRINCE2 are correct?

1. A forecast breach of work package tolerance is handled by the project manager.
2. An exception arises once a tolerance has actually been exceeded, and not before.
3. A team manager escalates a forecast work package breach directly to the project board.
4. A forecast breach of project tolerance is decided on by the business layer.
o: 1 and 2
2 and 3
1 and 4
3 and 4
12.w: Work package exceptions are handled by the project manager (1), and breaches of project tolerance are decided by the business layer, which sets project tolerances (4) (see manual 11.2.1, 11.2.6, 11.3.1).

n.0: Statement 1 is correct, but an exception is a forecast breach, so it arises before tolerance is actually exceeded (manual 11.1).
n.1: Both are wrong: an exception is based on a forecast, and a team manager escalates to the project manager, not the board (manual 11.1, 11.2.1).
n.3: Statement 4 is correct, but a team manager raises a forecast work package breach with the project manager as an issue (manual 11.2.1).

12.q: Before deciding on a request for change, the change authority compares the extra benefit the change would bring with its extra cost and the extra risk it adds. Which principle is being supported?
o: Manage by exception
Ensure continued business justification
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships
Manage by stages
12.w: Ensure continued business justification requires what the project delivers to stay consistent with its justification, so a request for change weighs the additional benefit against the additional cost and risk (see manual 2.1).

n.0: Manage by exception concerns delegated limits and escalation; the cost and benefit comparison is about justification (manual 2.5).
n.2: This principle concerns agreed roles and stakeholder relationships; it does not involve weighing a change's benefits against its cost and risk (manual 2.3).
n.3: Manage by stages provides decision points at stage ends; the comparison here is made for one change, on business grounds (manual 2.4).

12.q: Which is NOT one of the factors PRINCE2 suggests considering when deciding how much detail to include in the change management approach?
o: The skills and capabilities needed during and after the transition
The size of the change budget delegated to the change authority
The areas of the organizational ecosystem likely to be impacted
The key relationships and the evolving culture
12.w: The change budget belongs to the issues practice and funds approved requests for change. The factors PRINCE2 lists for the change management approach are skills and capabilities, impacted areas, key relationships, the evolving culture and how best to transition (see manual 3.2.1, 10.2.5).

n.0: Skills and capabilities needed during and after the transition are a listed factor for the level of detail (manual 3.2.1).
n.2: The areas of the organizational ecosystem likely to be impacted are a listed factor (manual 3.2.1).
n.3: Key relationships and the evolving culture are both listed factors (manual 3.2.1).

12.q: In a linear-sequential project, how detailed should product descriptions be when the work is planned?
o: Brief outlines, with detail added in each iteration from the product backlog
Limited to the project product description, with the rest written at closure
Detailed enough to show the delivery approach, but not to estimate cost or time
Detailed enough for cost and time to be estimated with appropriate confidence
12.w: In a linear-sequential project, product descriptions should be detailed enough for costs and time to be estimated at an appropriate level of confidence (see manual 7.3.1.1.3).

n.0: Adding detail iteration by iteration from a product backlog is how iterative-incremental projects work, not linear-sequential ones.
n.1: Product descriptions are needed to plan and build products; writing them at closure would be too late to guide the work.
n.2: The point of the detail in a linear-sequential project is to estimate cost and time with confidence.

12.q: Who sets the tolerances for the project as a whole, and where are they documented?
o: The executive, in each stage plan as it is approved by the project board
The business layer, in the project mandate or confirmed to the board for the project brief
The project manager, in the project plan that is prepared during initiating a project
Project assurance, in the quality management approach agreed during initiation
12.w: The business layer sets project tolerances and documents them in the project mandate, or confirms them to the project board for inclusion in the project brief (see manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

n.0: The executive defines tolerances for each stage; project-level tolerances come from the business layer (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).
n.2: The project manager sets work package tolerances, not project tolerances (manual 7.6 tab 7.1, 11.2).
n.3: Project assurance reviews progress against agreed tolerances; it does not set them (manual 7.6 tab 7.1).

12.q: A team manager says that, because she is a member of the project management team, she can approve a change to the current stage plan. Which statement is correct?
o: She is right, because every role in the project management team shares the board's authority
She is right, because team managers work at the directing level of the project's organization
She is wrong, because changes to a stage plan are approved by the business layer, not the board
She is wrong, because the authority to direct the project rests with the project board
12.w: The project management team structure is a set of roles and does not itself have authority to direct the project; that authority sits with the project board (see manual 6.2.3, 6.2.1).

n.0: Being in the project management team structure gives no authority to direct; PRINCE2 states the structure does not have that authority (manual 6.2.3).
n.1: Team managers work at the delivering level, within constraints set by the project manager (manual fig 6.2).
n.2: Stage plans are approved by the project board in directing a project; the business layer handles project-level matters (manual fig 6.2).

12.q: A project manager agrees with the board how much control it will exercise after initiation and how, and agrees how the project manager will control the work of team managers. Which activity is this?
o: Agree the tailoring requirements
Establish project controls
Prepare the project plan
Request project authorization
12.w: Establish project controls agrees the board's level of control after initiation and the mechanism for it, and the project manager's control over the work of team managers (see manual 15.4.3).

n.0: Agree the tailoring requirements decides how the method is adapted to the project, not the specific controls between levels (manual 15.4.1).
n.2: Prepare the project plan sets out the major products, timescales and costs; the control levels are agreed in establish project controls (manual 15.4.4).
n.3: Request project authorization asks the board for authority to deliver the project once the PID is ready (manual 15.4.7).

12.q: In product-based planning, what is the starting point for building a plan?
o: Defining and analysing the products that the plan must deliver
Listing the activities and tasks that the teams will carry out
Agreeing the budget and cost tolerances with the executive
Identifying the team managers who will accept the work packages
12.w: Product-based planning starts from defining and analysing the required products, and derives the rest of the plan, such as the work breakdown structure, estimates and schedule, from the product descriptions (see manual 7.2.5).

n.1: Activities are identified after the products are defined, when work packages are organized; they are not the starting point (manual 7.2.5, 7.3.1.2).
n.2: Preparing the budget comes late in the planning technique, after products, estimates and schedule (manual 7.3.1).
n.3: Work packages are organized and allocated after the products have been defined and analysed (manual 7.3.1.2).

12.q: During the 'controlling a stage' process, how should the project manager work with a team manager from a partner organization when defining a new work package?
o: Issue the work package description and ask the team manager to confirm receipt
Ask the executive to instruct the team manager to accept the work package
Build a working relationship and co-create the work package with the team manager
Let the team manager write the work package and approve it once work is under way
12.w: When authorizing a work package, the project manager builds a working relationship with the team manager, co-creates and reviews the work package with them, confirms acceptance and then authorizes the work (see manual 16.4.1, 3.3).

n.0: Issuing the work package one way misses the co-creation and confirmed acceptance that the activity expects (manual 16.4.1).
n.1: The project manager authorizes work packages; using the executive's authority over someone who does not report to them is unlikely to work (manual 16.4.1, 3.3.1).
n.3: The project manager defines and authorizes the work package before the team starts work; it is not approved after work is under way (manual 16.4.1).

12.q: A project board and project manager are agreeing how often progress should be reported during the next stage. What should mainly determine the reporting frequency?
o: The level of control required, reflecting factors such as team experience
A standard reporting frequency that PRINCE2 sets for every type of project
The preference of each team manager, agreed with the senior supplier
The number of products listed in the product register for the stage
12.w: The frequency of progress reporting should reflect the level of control required, for example more frequent reports for an inexperienced team or a high-risk stage (see manual 11.2.4).

n.1: PRINCE2 does not prescribe one frequency; it is tailored to the control needed (manual 11.2.4, 2.7).
n.2: Checkpoint frequency is set in the work package by the project manager, and highlight intervals by the board; it is not left to team managers (manual 11.5).
n.3: The number of products does not determine reporting frequency; the level of control required does (manual 11.2.4).

12.q: What is benefits tolerance?
o: The permissible variation of the plan's products allowed before escalation to the next management level
The measurable threshold for the tolerable range of outcomes for each identified risk to the project
The permissible deviation in benefit targets allowed before escalation to the next management level
The agreed limits on sustainability metrics allowed before escalation to the next management level
12.w: Benefits tolerance is the permissible deviation in the benefit performance targets that is allowed before the deviation needs to be escalated to the next level of management; it is documented in the benefits management approach (see manual 5.2.2).

n.0: This describes scope tolerance, the permissible variation of the plan's products (manual 11.2.1).
n.1: This describes risk tolerance, set by the project board based on the business's risk appetite (manual 9.2.1).
n.3: This describes sustainability tolerance, documented in the sustainability management approach (manual 5.2.2, 11.2.1).

12.q: Which role is accountable for the quality of the products delivered by the suppliers and for the technical integrity of the project?
o: Project executive
Senior user
Team manager
Senior supplier
12.w: The senior supplier represents the supplier community, commits supplier people and resources, and is accountable for the quality of supplier products and the project's technical integrity (see manual 6.2.4).

n.0: The executive is accountable for the project's overall success and business case, not specifically for supplier product quality (manual 6.2.4.1).
n.1: The senior user monitors products against the users' requirements, but supplier product quality and technical integrity sit with the senior supplier (manual 6.2.4).
n.2: A team manager delivers products to the agreed specifications but is not accountable for the project's technical integrity (manual 6.2.4).

12.q: Which statement BEST distinguishes the purpose of the business case practice from that of the plans practice?
o: Business case defines the products to be delivered; plans judges whether those products are still worth producing
Business case controls changes to the baselines; plans compares actual achievements with what was planned
Business case sets the tolerances for each stage; plans sets the tolerances for the whole project
Business case judges whether the project is worth doing; plans defines what will be delivered and how, when and at what cost
12.w: The business case practice establishes whether the project is (and remains) worthwhile, the 'why'. The plans practice defines the products and the means to deliver them (who, how, where, when, how much) to satisfy that business case (see manual 5.1, 7.1).

n.0: This reverses the two purposes: plans defines the products and the means to deliver them, and the business case judges worth (manual 5.1, 7.1).
n.1: Controlling changes to baselines is the issues practice and comparing actuals with plans is the progress practice (manual 10.1, 11.1).
n.2: Tolerances are set by management levels (business layer for the project, board for stages), not by these two practices (manual 11.2.1).

12.q: A team manager suggests tailoring away 'manage by stages' on a small project by skipping the initiation stage and going straight into delivery. Why is this unacceptable?
o: Because stage numbers are fixed by the business layer in the project mandate
Because principles are not tailored, and initiation precedes the delivery stages
Because tailoring proposals have to come from the executive, not a team manager
Because a project with one delivery stage would first need an exception plan
12.w: The principles cannot be tailored away, and manage by stages requires at least two stages: an initiation stage first, then one or more delivery stages, so the project is properly initiated before delivery work starts (see manual 2.4 and 2.7).

n.0: The business layer provides the mandate and project tolerances; the number and length of stages are planned for the project, not fixed in the mandate (manual 2.4, fig 6.2).
n.2: The problem is the proposal itself, not who made it: the principle cannot be tailored away whoever suggests it (manual 2.7).
n.3: A project with one delivery stage is valid if it also has an initiation stage; exception plans respond to forecast tolerance breaches (manual 2.4, ch 11).
